examples: Don't blame the intern for a policy she didn't write.
He blamed the missed deadline on the printer.
The report blames the outage on deferred maintenance.
She was blamed for everything that went wrong that summer.
Nobody is to blame for an honest mistake.
They blamed each other for the whole mess.
entries.русский: винить — blame smb for smth = blame smth on smb, аргументы меняются местами
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase or a gerund (blamed her for losing the file) — never a to-infinitive. on takes the person or thing held responsible. The two frames carry the same meaning with the arguments swapped, so each preposition goes with a fixed slot: ✗ blame the delay for the weather says the opposite of what you mean.
entries.pattern: blame [someone] for [something] · blame [something] on [someone] · [someone] be to blame for [something] · be blamed for [something]
entries.contrast: Same meaning, mirrored frames: They blamed the pilot for the crash = They blamed the crash on the pilot. Keep blame apart from accuse and charge: blame assigns fault and needs no wrongdoing at all (you can blame the rain), while accuse someone of alleges misconduct and charge someone with files it formally. The adjective frame keeps for: the contractor is to blame for the leak, never ✗ to blame of.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; assigning fault, with no wrongdoing implied (you can blame the rain).
entries.transitivity: transitive in both mirrored frames — blame the intern for the policy and blame the delay on the printer; the object is obligatory, and swapping the slots reverses the sentence: ✗ blame the delay for the weather.
entries.passive: yes in both — she was blamed for everything that went wrong that summer, the outage was blamed on deferred maintenance.
entries.see also: accuse of · charge with · punish for · forgive for · apologize for

entries.meaning: Talk with too much pride about something you have or have done.
examples: He boasts about his commute the way other people boast about their kids.
She never boasted about the award; we found out from the newsletter.
They boast of a hundred percent placement rate, which is technically true.
Boasting about how little you sleep is not the flex you think it is.
The company boasted about the acquisition for a year and then wrote it off.
The lodge boasts a wraparound porch and no cell service at all.
entries.русский: хвастаться чем-то — говорить о своём с излишней гордостью
entries.register: somewhat formal; brag about is the everyday word
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (boasted about winning) — never a to-infinitive (✗ boasted about to win). A clause takes no preposition: boasted that he had won.
entries.pattern: boast about / of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · boast that [clause] · [a place or thing] boast [a feature] — no preposition
entries.contrast: Two senses split on the preposition. With about or of, boast means brag, and it is unflattering. With a direct object and no preposition it means possess something worth showing off, and it is flattering — the hotel boasts three restaurants is advertising copy, not a criticism of the hotel. Boast of is a shade more formal than boast about; both are correct. In speech Americans overwhelmingly say brag about.
entries.verb type: both — action in the bragging sense (he boasts about his commute), stative in the possession sense, where a place or product is the subject: the lodge boasts a wraparound porch.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with about or of, and with a that-clause (boasted that he had won); transitive with no preposition in the possession sense.
entries.passive: no in either sense — the bragging frame is prepositional and awkward to promote (✗ the award was never boasted about by her), and the possession sense is stative, so it refuses outright: ✗ a wraparound porch is boasted by the lodge.
entries.see also: complain about · admit to · congratulate on · talk about

entries.meaning: Take something temporarily, intending to give it back.
examples: I borrowed a folding table from the church next door.
She borrowed the phrase from an essay she'd read in college.
Small businesses are borrowing from family instead of banks.
Can I borrow your charger?
The design borrows from Shaker furniture without copying it.
He borrowed against the equity in the house to cover tuition.
entries.русский: занимать, брать взаймы у — брать на время с возвратом
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause. The thing borrowed is a direct object and the source takes from: borrow a ladder from Ken. ✗ borrow of is archaic and ✗ borrow to someone reverses the direction entirely.
entries.pattern: borrow [something] · borrow [something] from [source] · borrow [an idea, a word, a style] from [a source] · borrow against [an asset]
entries.contrast: Borrow and lend point in opposite directions and are constantly swapped. You borrow from someone; they lend to you. ✗ Can you borrow me twenty dollars? is nonstandard in American English — the sentence you want is Can you lend me twenty dollars? or Can I borrow twenty dollars from you? Note that borrow from also covers influence (the score borrows heavily from Copland), and that borrow against a house or a policy means take a loan secured by it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a taking with a return understood, literal or figurative (the score borrows heavily from Copland).
entries.transitivity: transitive — the thing borrowed is the direct object and the source takes from: borrow a ladder from Ken. The object can be left implicit only where money is understood (borrowing from family instead of banks), and the direction is fixed: ✗ Can you borrow me twenty dollars? (say lend).
entries.passive: yes — the phrase was borrowed from an essay she'd read in college, the table was borrowed from the church next door.
entries.see also: provide with · escape from · learn from · from

entries.meaning: Think something matters, or look after someone — depending entirely on the preposition.
examples: Nobody on that committee cares about the deadline.
She cared for her father at home until the last month.
I don't care for his tone.
He cares about getting it right more than getting it done.
Would you care for another slice?
They care about what happens to the building after they sell it.
Take care of the paperwork and I'll handle the movers.
entries.русский: care about считать важным; care for ухаживать за; not care for не любить
entries.complement: about takes a noun phrase, a gerund (cares about winning), or a wh-clause (cares about what people think) — never a to-infinitive. for takes a noun phrase only. Care also takes a bare to-infinitive with no preposition (care to join us?), and a that-clause in the negative (I don't care that it's raining).
entries.pattern: care about [person / thing / issue] · care for [someone — tend] · care for [something — like, usually negative] · would you care for [a thing] · care to [verb] · take care of [someone / something] · not care (alone)
entries.contrast: Four patterns, four meanings, and they are not interchangeable. Care about = think it matters (she cares about the outcome). Care for = look after (he cared for his mother for six years) or, chiefly in the negative and in offers, like (I don't care for oysters; Would you care for coffee?). Care to do = be willing. Take care of = handle or look after, and is what Americans actually say for the tending sense. Note the idiom: I couldn't care less is the logical form, and the widespread American I could care less means exactly the same thing despite saying the opposite.
entries.verb type: both — stative in care about (✗ I am caring about the deadline) and in care for meaning like (I don't care for jazz); action in care for meaning tend: she is caring for her father at home.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object (✗ care the outcome); complements are prepositional, a to-infinitive (care to explain?), or a negative that-clause (I don't care that it's raining).
entries.passive: restricted — the tending sense passivizes well (patients cared for at home do better, she was cared for by her daughter); the two stative senses do not: ✗ the deadline is not cared about by anyone, ✗ jazz is not cared for by him.
entries.see also: take care of · look after · worry about · think about

entries.meaning: Have something as its main subject or its main point.
examples: The debate centered on whether the district could afford both schools.
Her research centers on migration between the wars.
The whole weekend centered around the wedding rehearsal.
The complaint centers on two paragraphs in the disclosure.
Most of the questions centered on the timing of the layoffs.
It is a quiet novel centered on one family and one street.
entries.русский: быть посвящённым чему-то, вращаться вокруг — иметь главной темой
entries.register: neutral; center on is the safe choice in edited prose, center around the one a copy editor may query
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (the argument centered on raising the cap) — never a to-infinitive (✗ centered on raise the cap) and never a that-clause (✗ centered on that costs were rising), though a wh-clause is fine: the hearing centered on what the city knew. The participial form is where most Americans meet it: a novel centered on one summer.
entries.pattern: [a discussion / a story] center on [a topic] · center around [a topic] · be centered on / centered around [something] · center [something] on [something] — transitive, position it
entries.contrast: Center around is the famous usage quarrel. The objection is geometric: a center is a point, and nothing can be around a point — so the purist demands center on or revolve around. The defense is that the phrase has been in respectable American prose since the 1860s and that center here means a cluster, not a dot. Practical advice: in a report, a brief, or a paper, write center on and lose nothing; in speech, center around passes unnoticed. Two neighbors do related work — focus on narrows to one thing, revolve around names what everything else moves in relation to.
entries.verb type: stative in the pattern that matters here — it reports what a thing is about, not something happening: her research centers on migration, and the progressive is rare. The positioning verb (center the title) is action.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with on or around in the subject-matter sense (✗ centered that costs were rising, though a wh-clause is fine); transitive in center the image on the page and center your efforts on one district.
entries.passive: yes, and the participle is the commonest form of all — a quiet novel centered on one family and one street, the questions were centered on the timing of the layoffs.
entries.see also: concentrate on · comment on · depend on · bear on · on

entries.meaning: Accuse formally, assign a duty, or bill money.
examples: He was charged with two counts of wire fraud.
The clinic charged us for a visit we never made.
The committee is charged with recommending a candidate by June.
How much do they charge for delivery?
She charged the whole dinner to the department.
Prosecutors declined to charge anyone with a felony.
entries.русский: обвинять в, поручать (with); брать плату за (for)
entries.register: charge with is legal or formal; charge for is everyday
entries.complement: with takes a noun phrase or a gerund (charged with defrauding investors) — never a to-infinitive. for takes a noun phrase or a gerund naming the service billed (charged us for parking). Neither takes a clause.
entries.pattern: charge [someone] with [an offense / verb-ing] · be charged with [a duty] · charge [someone] for [a service] · charge [an amount] for [a thing] · charge [something] to [an account] · charge at [someone]
entries.contrast: Three prepositions, three unrelated meanings. Charge with files an accusation (charged with arson) or assigns a responsibility (the panel is charged with reviewing appeals — note the -ing). Charge for bills money. Charge to puts it on an account. And charge at is a bull. Against its neighbors: accuse of is what a person does, charge with is what a prosecutor does, blame for assigns fault with no proceeding at all. In American criminal usage the person is charged with the crime, never ✗ charged of or ✗ charged for it — charged for would mean billed.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three prepositional senses: accusing, assigning a duty, and billing.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person is a direct object in charge her with arson and charge us for parking, and the amount can fill a second slot (they charge twelve dollars for delivery); how much do they charge for delivery? leaves the payer unstated.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the standard legal frame — he was charged with two counts of wire fraud, the committee is charged with recommending a candidate. Note ✗ charged of and ✗ charged for a crime (that would mean billed).
entries.see also: accuse of · blame for · pay for · suspect of · with

entries.meaning: Break the rules to gain an advantage — on a test, at a game, or on a partner.
examples: Two students were caught cheating on the midterm.
He cheats at cards and thinks nobody notices.
She found out he'd been cheating on her for a year.
Nearly a fifth of filers admit to cheating on their taxes.
The proctor rearranged the room so nobody could cheat on the final.
They cheated him out of six months' commission.
entries.русский: изменять (партнёру); списывать на (экзамене) — жульничать ради выгоды
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause. On takes either the test or the partner; at takes the game. Bare transitive cheat takes the victim (cheat a customer), and cheat someone out of something names what was taken.
entries.pattern: cheat on [a test, an exam, a tax return] · cheat on [a spouse or partner] · cheat at [a game] · cheat [someone] · cheat [someone] out of [something]
entries.contrast: American English says cheat on a test; British English says cheat in an exam. The preposition splits by the kind of activity: on for a test or a tax return, at for a game of cards or golf. With a person as object of on, the meaning is infidelity — he cheated on her — which is why cheat on the exam and cheat on his wife share a preposition and nothing else. Transitive cheat means defraud, and cheat someone out of names the loss (cheated out of a pension).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from a midterm to a tax return to a marriage.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with on (a test, a return, a partner) or at (a game); transitive when the victim is the object: cheat a customer, cheat him out of six months' commission.
entries.passive: yes — the transitive is straightforward (he was cheated out of a pension), and the infidelity sense has a fully idiomatic prepositional passive: she found out she'd been cheated on for a year. ✗ The midterm was cheated on is not idiomatic.
entries.see also: confess to · accuse of · punish for · suspect of

entries.meaning: Find out how someone or something is doing, often to make sure nothing is wrong.
examples: Would you check up on the dog while we're at the game?
Her manager keeps checking up on her, which is why she is job-hunting.
The state occasionally checks up on licensed facilities without warning.
I called the pharmacy to check up on the refill.
He drives past the rental every few weeks to check up on the place.
Nobody checked up on the numbers until the audit.
entries.русский: проверять, как дела у кого-то — наведываться, чтобы убедиться; разг.
entries.register: informal to neutral; everyday American speech
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun naming a person or a situation, or a wh-clause (check up on how she's settling in) — never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause. The three words are frozen in order and the object always follows all of them: check up on him, never ✗ check him up on.
entries.pattern: check up on [someone] · check up on [something] · check on [someone] — the two-word variant, slightly more neutral · have a checkup — the unrelated noun
entries.contrast: The object test separates the two constructions. In check out a book, out is a particle and the object can move — check the book out, check it out — but in check up on the tenant nothing can move: ✗ check the tenant up on, which is what marks on here as a fixed preposition. In meaning, check up on implies a little suspicion or supervision (he's checking up on me), while check on is neutral concern (check on the roast), and check in on is a friendly short visit (check in on your grandmother).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a visit or an inquiry, often repeated (her manager keeps checking up on her).
entries.transitivity: intransitive verb plus adverb plus preposition, frozen in that order — the object follows all three words and can never move: check up on him, ✗ check him up on.
entries.passive: yes, and the progressive passive is the everyday form — she could tell she was being checked up on. A full agentive passive (the numbers were never checked up on until the audit) is fine but less common.
entries.see also: look at, look for, look after, look into · cut down on · ask about · on

entries.meaning: Pick one of two or more options that are set against each other.
examples: She had to choose between the fellowship and the job offer.
Nobody should have to choose between rent and insulin.
Choose between the two color schemes and we'll order the paper.
Voters are choosing between two very different visions of the city.
You can choose from a dozen plans, which is exactly the problem.
He chose between staying in Tulsa and starting over in Austin.
entries.русский: выбирать между — брать одно из противопоставленных вариантов
entries.complement: between takes two items joined by and, or a plural noun phrase (choose between the two offers) — the joiner must be and, never or: ✗ choose between staying or going. It also takes a gerund pair (choose between staying and going). Choose itself takes a direct object or a to-infinitive with no preposition at all: choose a color, choose to stay.
entries.pattern: choose between [A] and [B] · choose between [plural noun phrase] · choose among / from [a set of three or more] · choose [something] · choose to [verb]
entries.contrast: Between is for options weighed one against another; among or from is for picking out of a pool. Choose between the two finalists against choose from a field of nine. The old rule that between is only for two is too strict — choose between the four candidates is fine when they are being weighed against one another — but choose among remains the safer formal choice with a large set. The fixed error is ✗ choose between X or Y; the coordinator inside between is always and.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a decision made at a point.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a bare object or a to-infinitive (choose a color, choose to stay); intransitive with between, among, or from, where the joiner inside between is always and: ✗ choose between staying or going.
entries.passive: yes for the transitive — a color was chosen that afternoon. The prepositional frame has no passive: ✗ the two offers were chosen between.
entries.see also: decide on · prefer to · compare to · vote for · between

entries.meaning: Point a reader to a source, especially to a particular page or authority.
examples: The brief cites to three Ninth Circuit cases and one treatise.
Please cite to the page in the transcript, not to the exhibit.
The opinion cites to a statute that had already been repealed.
Local rules require counsel to cite to the record for every factual claim.
She cited to the deposition twice and never quoted it.
In a seminar paper you simply cite the article — ✗ cite to it sounds like a filing.
entries.русский: ссылаться на конкретное место источника — юр.; вне права предлог to не ставят
entries.register: formal; legal writing almost exclusively — briefs, opinions, and law reviews (counsel cited to Brown, cite to the record). Outside law the to is not used, and an editor will strike it.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an authority, case, statute, page, or record — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, never a clause. The everyday construction is bare transitive: cite three sources, ✗ cite to three sources in ordinary prose.
entries.pattern: cite to [a case / a page / the record] · cite [a source] — standard, no preposition · cite [someone] for [an offense] — the ticket sense · cite [someone] as [an authority]
entries.contrast: Three constructions, three different jobs. Bare cite takes the source as a direct object and is what every writer outside a courtroom uses. Cite to is a term of art in American legal writing, where it points the reader to a specific place in an authority. Cite for is enforcement — cited for speeding, cited for a code violation — and has nothing to do with quotation. Spelling traps come free with this one: sight is vision and site is a place.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an act of pointing a reader somewhere, or, in cite for, of writing a ticket.
entries.transitivity: both — bare transitive everywhere outside a courtroom (cite three sources, and ✗ cite to three sources in ordinary prose); intransitive with to in American legal writing (cite to the record).
entries.passive: yes for the transitive frames — the article was cited eleven times, she was cited for speeding. The legal cite to passivizes poorly: ✗ the record was cited to by counsel.
entries.see also: refer to · allude to · attribute to · to

entries.meaning: Work jointly with someone to produce something.
examples: She collaborated with two other economists on the paper.
The studio wanted him to collaborate with a younger songwriter.
Our lab collaborates with a hospital group in Cleveland.
He refuses to collaborate with anyone he hasn't met in person.
The two agencies collaborated with each other for the first time in a decade.
Historians still argue about who collaborated with the occupiers and who had no choice.
entries.русский: сотрудничать с — работать вместе над чем-то
entries.register: neutral to formal; research, the arts, and business
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person or organization — never a gerund (✗ collaborated with writing the score; the work takes on: collaborated on the score). Never a to-infinitive and never a clause. There is no direct-object frame: ✗ collaborated the album.
entries.pattern: collaborate with [someone] · collaborate with [someone] on [a project] · collaborate in [an effort] — formal · a collaboration with [someone] — the noun keeps the preposition
entries.contrast: Collaborate with and cooperate with are not synonyms. Collaborating is making something together — a paper, a record, a design. Cooperating is not getting in the way: the company cooperated with investigators says it handed over documents, not that it helped write the report. And collaborate carries one sense cooperation does not: working with an occupying enemy, which is why he collaborated with the regime is an accusation. Note the two prepositions divide the roles — with a person, on a project — and cannot swap.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; joint work carried on over time, and the progressive is natural (our lab is collaborating with a hospital group).
entries.transitivity: intransitive always — no direct object (✗ collaborated the album); the person takes with, the project takes on, and the two prepositions cannot swap.
entries.passive: no — objectless, so nothing can be promoted: ✗ a younger songwriter was collaborated with, ✗ the paper was collaborated on by two economists. Recast with co-wrote or was written jointly.
entries.see also: cooperate with · work with · consult with · share with · with

entries.meaning: Say something in reaction to a subject.
examples: She declined to comment on the settlement.
Several reviewers commented on the length of the second act.
He commented on how little had changed in twenty years.
The mayor's office would not comment on the audit.
Feel free to comment on the draft in the margins.
Nobody commented on his new haircut, which disappointed him.
entries.русский: комментировать что-то — высказываться по поводу чего-то
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or wh-clause (commented on how quiet it was) — never a to-infinitive. Before a full clause the preposition drops: commented that the room was cold, never ✗ commented on that.
entries.pattern: comment on [noun phrase / verb-ing / wh-clause] · comment that [clause] · decline to comment on [something] · no comment on [something]
entries.contrast: Comment on is the standard American form; comment about is heard but is weaker in edited prose. The noun keeps on (a comment on the draft) and so does the fixed newsroom formula declined to comment on the report. Compare remark on (interchangeable, slightly more formal), note and observe (transitive, no preposition: he noted the discrepancy), and criticize (also transitive: criticize the plan, never ✗ criticize on the plan).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a speech act.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with on — no direct object (✗ comment the draft), and the preposition disappears before a full clause: commented that the room was cold, ✗ commented on that.
entries.passive: restricted — the length of the second act was widely commented on is acceptable in writing, and impersonal it was commented that… occurs, but the active is far commoner in American prose.
entries.see also: point to · complain about · talk about · refer to · on

entries.meaning: Bind yourself to a course of action.
examples: The board committed to replacing every lead service line by 2032.
She won't commit to a date until the permits clear.
Both candidates committed to three debates.
He's committed to getting the certification this year.
Don't commit to anything before you've read the fine print.
The district has committed to smaller classes without saying how it will pay for them.
entries.русский: обязываться, брать на себя обязательство — после to герундий
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (commit to hiring two more nurses) — to is a preposition here, not the infinitive marker, so ✗ commit to hire two more nurses is an error. Never a that-clause after the preposition. The reflexive frame follows the same rule: commit yourself to finishing it. A separate transitive commit takes a bare object and no preposition at all: commit a crime, commit funds, commit it to memory.
entries.pattern: commit to [noun phrase] · commit to [verb-ing] · commit [oneself] to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · be committed to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · commit [a crime, an error, resources] — no preposition
entries.contrast: Another member of the look forward to family, and the noun test settles it the same way: you can say commit to the plan, so to is a preposition, so it has to be commit to redrawing the plan. Notice how far the transitive senses sit from this one — commit a felony and commit a hundred thousand dollars take no preposition, and commit someone to an institution is a third thing again. The participle is the form you meet most often, and the -ing after it is not optional: a company committed to lowering emissions, ✗ committed to lower emissions. Against its neighbors, commit to is firmer than plan on and softer than promise to, which takes the infinitive because promise has no preposition at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; binding yourself at a moment. The participle committed to has drifted into an adjective: a company committed to lowering emissions.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with to (commit to a date), reflexive-transitive (commit yourself to finishing it), and plainly transitive in the unrelated senses: commit a crime, commit funds, commit it to memory.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — a felony was committed on the premises, a hundred thousand dollars has been committed to the project. The to frame passivizes only as the adjectival participle, not as an event.
entries.see also: look forward to · object to · dedicate to · plan on · agree to · to

entries.meaning: Exchange information with someone, or be connected to something.
examples: The hospital could not communicate with the family for two days.
Sales and engineering barely communicate with each other.
The buoy communicates with a satellite twice an hour.
He communicates with his students almost entirely by email.
Air traffic control communicated with the aircraft until 3:14 a.m.
Two of the rooms communicate with the courtyard through French doors.
entries.русский: общаться с; быть связанным с (о технике) — обмениваться информацией
entries.register: neutral to formal; management and HR writing, technical documentation (the sensor communicates with the hub), and clinical notes
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, group, or system — never a gerund (✗ communicate with telling them early), never a to-infinitive, never a clause. The message itself is never the object of with: it is a direct object, and the audience takes to: communicate the decision to staff.
entries.pattern: communicate with [someone] · communicate [something] to [someone] · [two systems] communicate with [each other] · communication with [someone] — the noun keeps the preposition
entries.contrast: With is two-way; to is one-way. She communicates with the field offices describes an exchange; she communicates the policy to the field offices describes a transmission — and mixing them (✗ communicate the policy with staff) is the usual error. There is no bare transitive frame for the person: ✗ communicate somebody. In speech Americans mostly say talk to or get in touch with and reserve communicate with for the formal register, which is why we are unable to communicate with the crew sounds like an official statement, because it is one.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an exchange, human or mechanical (the buoy communicates with a satellite twice an hour).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with with for the other party (✗ communicate somebody), transitive with the message as object and the audience in to: communicate the decision to staff, and never ✗ communicate the policy with staff.
entries.passive: yes for the message frame — the decision was communicated to staff on Friday. The with frame is restricted: the crew could not be communicated with for two days is official-register only.
entries.see also: talk to, talk with, talk about · consult with · cooperate with · share with · with

entries.meaning: Set two things side by side, or liken one to the other.
examples: He compared the reorganization to rearranging deck chairs.
Compare this year's numbers with the same quarter in 2022.
Revenue rose four percent compared with the prior year.
Critics compared her early work to Munro's, which she found irritating.
Nothing compares to the first cold morning in October.
It's hard to compare a rural district with an urban one on test scores alone.
entries.русский: сравнивать — with сопоставлять по признакам, to уподоблять одно другому
entries.register: neutral; the to / with distinction is formal-register only
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (compared moving to starting over) — no to-infinitive, no clause. Compare also takes two objects joined by and: compare the 2019 and 2024 figures. The passive participle compared to / compared with works as a preposition in its own right (compared with last year, sales are flat).
entries.pattern: compare [A] to [B] · compare [A] with [B] · compare [A] and [B] · [something] compare to / with [something — measure up] · compared to / with [noun phrase] (sentence adverbial)
entries.the textbook rule: compare to likens two unlike things to make a point (he compared the deficit to a leaky bucket), while compare with sets two like things side by side to weigh them (compare this quarter with last). In actual American usage the distinction is fading and compared to has taken over both jobs, especially in speech; compared with survives in statistical and scientific writing, where the side-by-side sense matters. What is not optional: in the intransitive sense, to is standard — nothing compares to a real vacation.
entries.verb type: both — action in the transitive sense, a mental operation performed on two things; stative in the intransitive measure-up sense: nothing compares to a real vacation, ✗ nothing is comparing to it.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with two slots (compare this year's numbers with the same quarter in 2022, or joined by and); intransitive in the measure-up sense, where to is standard.
entries.passive: yes for the transitive — her early work was compared to Munro's, which she found irritating. No for the measure-up sense: ✗ a real vacation is compared to by nothing.
entries.see also: resemble · differ from · prefer to · choose between · compared to · compared with

entries.meaning: Balance out a loss or a weakness, or pay someone for one.
examples: Extra rehearsal compensated for the missing week.
The airline compensated passengers for the canceled leg with vouchers.
She compensates for a weak serve with a very good net game.
Nothing compensates for losing that much institutional memory at once.
The system compensates for temperature drift automatically.
He tried to compensate for being new by staying late every night.
entries.русский: компенсировать, возмещать — восполнять потерю или слабое место
entries.register: neutral to formal; engineering, psychology, insurance, and payroll
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (compensate for arriving late) — never a to-infinitive (✗ compensate for arrive late) and never a that-clause. Two frames share the verb: compensate for [a loss] offsets it, and compensate [someone] for [something] pays them, with the person as a direct object.
entries.pattern: compensate for [a loss / a weakness] · compensate [someone] for [something] · compensate for [verb-ing] · overcompensate for [something]
entries.contrast: Two senses hang on the same preposition. The offsetting sense — thicker insulation compensates for the north exposure — has no money in it at all; the paying sense always has a person as direct object — compensate the homeowners for the damage. The everyday equivalent of the first is make up for; the technical neighbors are correct for and adjust for, which remove a distortion from a measurement rather than balancing a deficiency. And offset does the same work with no preposition: offset the loss, ✗ offset for the loss.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, offsetting a deficiency and paying for a loss.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with for when something offsets something else (extra rehearsal compensated for the missing week); transitive with the person paid as direct object (compensate the homeowners for the damage).
entries.passive: yes — the paying sense is idiomatic in the passive (passengers were compensated for the canceled leg), and technical writing passivizes the offsetting sense too: temperature drift is compensated for automatically.
entries.see also: pay for · correct for · substitute for · allow for · for

entries.term: compete with, compete against, compete for
entries.meaning: Try to win something that someone else also wants.
examples: Small presses can't compete with the big houses on advances.
She competed against her own sister in the semifinal.
Four firms are competing for the airport contract.
He competes in three or four triathlons a year.
Streaming services are competing for the same twelve hours of anyone's week.
Nothing in a jar competes with fresh basil.
entries.русский: соперничать — with/against с кем-то, for за что-то
entries.complement: with and against take a rival. for takes the prize. in takes the event (compete in the 400). No gerund and no clause follows any of them: ✗ compete for winning — say compete for the title. Compete is intransitive and never takes a bare object: ✗ compete the other firms.
entries.pattern: compete with / against [a rival] · compete for [a prize, a contract, attention] · compete in [an event, a market] · compete with [a rival] for [a prize]
entries.contrast: Compete with and compete against are genuinely interchangeable for the rival, with against a shade more adversarial and more common in sports. Keep the slots straight: the rival takes with or against, the prize takes for, the arena takes in — three firms competing with each other for one contract in a shrinking market. Note that compete with has a second, non-adversarial sense meaning match or rival in quality: no supermarket tomato competes with one out of the garden.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; also a quieter comparative sense meaning match in quality (nothing in a jar competes with fresh basil), which is closer to stative.
entries.transitivity: intransitive always — never a bare object: ✗ compete the other firms. The rival takes with or against, the prize takes for, the arena takes in.
entries.passive: no — there is no object to promote: ✗ the big houses can't be competed with on advances, ✗ the airport contract is being competed for. Recast in the active or use rival, which is transitive.
entries.see also: argue with · differ from · apply for · qualify for · against

entries.meaning: Say that something is wrong, unsatisfactory, or unfair.
examples: She complained to the building manager about the elevator.
Everyone complains about the parking and nobody goes to the meetings.
He complained of headaches for a week before anyone made him see a doctor.
Two neighbors complained to the city.
They complained about having to submit the same form twice.
You can't complain about a system you never voted in.
entries.русский: жаловаться — to кому-то, about на что-то
entries.complement: to takes the person or office hearing it. about takes a noun phrase, a gerund (complained about having to reapply), or a wh-clause. of takes a symptom, in medical and formal use (complained of dizziness). None takes a to-infinitive. A full clause drops the preposition: complained that the room was cold.
entries.pattern: complain to [person / office] · complain about [noun phrase / verb-ing] · complain to [person] about [thing] · complain of [a symptom] · complain that [clause]
entries.the person and the grievance take differ: ✗ complain to the noise, ✗ complain about the landlord when you mean you told the landlord. Complain of is the narrow medical and legal use — the patient complained of chest pain — and sounds odd elsewhere. Compare object to, which registers formal opposition, and criticize, which is transitive and takes no preposition at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a speech act, and habitually repeated in the commonest uses (everyone complains about the parking).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object (✗ complain the noise); the hearer takes to, the grievance about, a symptom of, and a full clause takes nothing: complained that the room was cold.
entries.passive: restricted — the elevator has been complained about for months passes in writing; the hearer cannot be promoted comfortably: ✗ the building manager was complained to.
entries.see also: object to · argue with · boast about · worry about · apologize to

entries.meaning: Do what a rule, an order, or a request requires.
examples: The lab failed to comply with federal handling standards.
All vendors must comply with the new security requirements by October.
The company complied with the subpoena within a week.
Buildings put up before 1978 don't comply with the current code.
He was fired for refusing to comply with a direct order.
The device complies with Part 15 of the FCC rules.
entries.русский: соблюдать, выполнять — делать то, чего требует правило или предписание; офиц.
entries.complement: noun phrase only, naming a rule, order, request, or standard. No gerund in normal use (✗ comply with reporting quarterly — write comply with the quarterly reporting requirement) and no clause. Comply is intransitive and never takes a bare object: ✗ comply the order.
entries.pattern: comply with [a rule, an order, a request, a standard] · fail to comply with [something] · in compliance with [something]
entries.contrast: Comply to and ✗ comply of are errors — the preposition is fixed at with. Its close neighbors each keep a different one: conform to a standard, adhere to a policy, abide by a rule, obey an order (transitive, no preposition), and follow instructions (also transitive). Comply with is heavier and more institutional than any of them; in ordinary speech an American says follow the rules.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; doing what a rule requires, often as a continuing state of affairs (the device complies with Part 15).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — never a bare object (✗ comply the order), and ✗ comply to, ✗ comply of are errors; the verb stands alone only elliptically: he refused to comply.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is standard in regulatory prose (the reporting requirement was complied with in full) but stiff anywhere else; ordinary speech says the rules were followed.
entries.see also: subscribe to · agree to · object to · in compliance with · in accordance with

entries.meaning: Give your full attention or effort to one thing.
examples: Concentrate on the first two chapters and leave the rest.
It's impossible to concentrate on anything with that leaf blower going.
The district is concentrating on third-grade reading scores.
She concentrated on getting the wiring right before touching the drywall.
Let's concentrate on what we can actually change this quarter.
Ninety percent of the growth is concentrated in the metro area.
entries.русский: сосредоточиваться на — отдавать всё внимание одному делу
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (concentrate on finishing the draft), or wh-clause — never a to-infinitive (✗ concentrate on finish the draft, ✗ concentrate on to finish it).
entries.pattern: concentrate on [noun phrase / verb-ing / wh-clause] · concentrate (alone) · be concentrated in [a place — distribution] · concentrate [efforts, resources] on [something]
entries.contrast: Concentrate in is a different verb. With on, it means direct your attention or effort — concentrate on the road. With in, and usually in the passive, it means be densely gathered somewhere: most of the state's jobs are concentrated in three counties. Focus on is exactly interchangeable with the on sense and is the more common word in American business speech; center on is the same again — and note that careful American usage prefers center on, since center around is widely criticized as illogical.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; directing attention or effort, and freely progressive (the district is concentrating on third-grade reading).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with on or alone (just concentrate); transitive when effort or resources are the object: concentrate its resources on two counties.
entries.passive: yes — chiefly in the in sense of distribution, which is normally passive: ninety percent of the growth is concentrated in the metro area. The attention sense passivizes only with a thing as object: the effort was concentrated on reading scores.
entries.see also: work on · insist on · think about · on

entries.meaning: Grant a right, a power, or an honor to someone.
examples: The charter confers broad zoning authority on the county board.
An honorary doctorate was conferred on her in 1998.
Nothing in the lease confers a right of first refusal on the tenant.
The medal is conferred upon fewer than a dozen people a year.
Membership confers borrowing privileges on the whole household.
The statute conferred jurisdiction on a court that did not yet exist.
entries.русский: присуждать, наделять кого-то (правом, званием, полномочием); юр./офиц.
entries.register: formal; statutes, charters, and ceremonies — the Act confers jurisdiction on the district courts, the university conferred an honorary degree on her
entries.complement: the thing granted is a direct object — a right, a power, an honor, a benefit — and on takes the recipient. Never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, never a clause. Both slots are required: ✗ conferred on the courts with nothing granted is incomplete.
entries.pattern: confer [a right / a power / a degree] on [someone] · be conferred on [someone] · confer with [someone] — a different verb, meaning consult · confer about [a matter]
entries.variants: confer upon — identical in meaning and the older form; standard in statutes, court opinions, and ceremonial citations, where upon still outnumbers on
entries.contrast: Confer on and confer with are two different verbs wearing one spelling. Confer on is transitive and means grant from a position of authority; confer with takes no direct object and means consult — may I confer with my client? You cannot mix them: ✗ conferred the degree with her, ✗ conferred on my client about the offer. Nearby, bestow on is the ceremonial synonym, grant to is the everyday one (granted the license to the applicant), and vest in is the drafting term for placing a power somewhere permanently.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a grant made from a position of authority, often ceremonial. The homonymous confer with (consult) is a different verb.
entries.transitivity: transitive in this pattern — the right, power, or honor is an obligatory direct object and the recipient takes on: ✗ conferred on the courts with nothing granted is incomplete. Confer with takes no object at all.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the ceremonial norm — an honorary doctorate was conferred on her in 1998, the medal is conferred upon fewer than a dozen people a year.
entries.see also: credit with · provide with, provide for · attribute to · consult with · on

entries.meaning: Say openly that you did something wrong.
examples: He confessed to the arson after nine hours of questioning.
She confessed to having read his email.
I'll confess to a certain fondness for the old logo.
Two of them confessed to the police and one never said a word.
He confessed that he had never actually read the report.
Nobody confessed to moving the thermostat.
entries.русский: признаваться в — открыто говорить о своей вине; после to герундий
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (confessed to taking the money) — never a to-infinitive (✗ confessed to take the money). The preposition is optional before a bare object: confess a crime, confess his sins. Before a clause it disappears: confessed that he had lied.
entries.pattern: confess to [a crime / verb-ing] · confess [a sin, a crime] · confess that [clause] · confess to [a priest, the police] · confess to [a small weakness]
entries.contrast: Confess to has two objects it can take and you must read which one is meant: confess to the police names the hearer, confess to the burglary names the deed. Against admit to, confess is heavier — it implies guilt and often a hearer — which is why I admit to liking bad television is light and I confess to liking bad television is arch. Own up to is the informal American equivalent, and it too takes a gerund: own up to breaking it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a speech act, heavier than admit and usually implying guilt.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with to, which can take either the hearer (confess to the police) or the deed (confess to the arson); transitive with the preposition dropped (confess a crime, confess his sins), and a that-clause takes none.
entries.passive: restricted — drop the preposition and the transitive passivizes (the crime was never confessed); the prepositional frame does not travel: ✗ the arson was confessed to after nine hours.
entries.see also: admit to · accuse of · look forward to · apologize for · boast about · suspect of

entries.meaning: Match a standard, a rule, or a type.
examples: None of the outlets in the basement conform to current code.
The proposal must conform to the format described in the RFP.
Her account conforms with what the two other witnesses said.
Products that fail to conform to the standard cannot carry the label.
He never much cared about conforming to what the neighbors expected.
The revised bylaws were conformed to the new state statute.
entries.русский: соответствовать чему-то — отвечать стандарту, норме или образцу
entries.register: formal and technical; building codes, specifications, standards, and social commentary
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a standard, code, specification, type, or expectation. A gerund is grammatical but rare (conform to using the approved fasteners); never a to-infinitive (✗ conform to use the approved fasteners) and never a that-clause. The verb also stands alone in the social sense, with no complement at all: the pressure to conform. There is no direct-object frame: ✗ conform the code (though conform something to something — bring it into line — exists in legal drafting).
entries.pattern: [a thing] conform to [a standard] · [a statement] conform with [another] · conform — no complement, social sense · conform [a document] to [a requirement] — formal transitive
entries.variants: conform with — interchangeable in most contexts and slightly more formal; American usage prefers to for matching a standard (conforms to code) and leaves with for two things that agree with each other (the summary conforms with the audited figures)
entries.contrast: Things conform; people comply. Comply with is what a person, a company, or an agency does about a requirement someone imposes — the plant complies with the permit — while conform to says a thing matches a specification: the wiring conforms to code. Beside them, adhere to is following a rule steadily over time and abide by is accepting a decision already made. Note the third life of the word, in social criticism, where conform needs no preposition and always sounds faintly like a criticism.
entries.verb type: both — stative where a thing matches a specification (the wiring conforms to code, ✗ is conforming to code); action in the social sense, where a person is the subject: he never much cared about conforming.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in normal use — no direct object (✗ conform the code) and the complement drops entirely in the social sense (the pressure to conform). Legal drafting keeps a transitive conform a document to a statute.
entries.passive: no for the stative matching sense — ✗ current code is not conformed to by the basement outlets. Restricted otherwise: the drafting transitive gives the revised bylaws were conformed to the new state statute.
entries.see also: comply with · adhere to · abide by · correspond to, correspond with · to

entries.meaning: Tell someone you are pleased about their good news or achievement.
examples: I want to congratulate you on the promotion.
She congratulated the team on a season nobody expected.
He congratulated himself on having avoided the whole argument.
Congratulations on passing the bar.
The dean congratulated every graduate on stage, one at a time.
They congratulated her on the book and then asked when the next one was due.
entries.русский: поздравлять с — выражать радость по поводу чужого успеха
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (congratulated her on winning) — never a to-infinitive (✗ congratulated her on to win) and never a clause. The person is a direct object and never takes a preposition: ✗ congratulate to her.
entries.pattern: congratulate [someone] on [noun phrase / verb-ing] · congratulate [someone] · congratulate [oneself] on [something] · Congratulations on [noun phrase / verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Congratulate for is nonstandard in careful American English, though it is common in speech; the fixed preposition is on, and the greeting keeps it too — Congratulations on the baby, ✗ Congratulations for the baby. British usage also allows congratulate upon, which sounds stiff in the U.S. Compare thank someone for something and praise someone for something, which take for and never on — three near-synonyms with three fixed and different prepositions.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a speech act performed in the saying; progressive is normal: they're congratulating themselves a little early.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person is a direct object and never takes a preposition (✗ congratulate to her); on adds the achievement. The object is obligatory: ✗ he congratulated on the promotion.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is very common: she was congratulated on the promotion by everyone in the office, he was congratulated on a season nobody expected.
entries.see also: thank for · apologize to · boast about

entries.meaning: Give permission for something.
examples: She would not consent to another round of tests.
The driver consented to a search of the trunk.
Both parties consented to the change of venue.
He consented to being photographed only from a distance.
Users must consent to the collection of location data.
Her father never consented to the marriage and never explained why.
entries.русский: давать согласие на — разрешать; мед. и юр. контексты
entries.register: neutral to formal; medicine, law, and privacy notices — consent to treatment, consent to the search, consent to the terms
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (consented to being recorded) — never a that-clause in modern American usage (✗ consented to that we record it). The one thing to keep straight: consent to be recorded, with a bare infinitive, is also correct — but there the to is the infinitive marker belonging to the verb consent, not this preposition, exactly as with agree. Both are good English and they mean the same thing; what is wrong is mixing them (✗ consented to be questioning).
entries.pattern: consent to [a procedure / a search / the terms] · consent to [verb-ing] · consent to [verb — infinitive, not preposition] · give consent to [something] · consent — no complement
entries.contrast: Consent to grants permission; the neighbors do other things. Agree to is the everyday word and carries no notion of authority; assent to formally approves; accede to gives in after resisting; acquiesce in merely fails to object. Legally the distinction matters: only the person with the right to permit can consent, which is why informed consent is a term of art and why ✗ consent with is not English. Note that object to, the opposite pattern, takes only the gerund — objected to being recorded, never ✗ objected to be recorded — so the two are not symmetrical.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a performative act of granting permission, not a state: she is consenting to the search on camera.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with a fixed preposition — no direct object (✗ consent the search), and the verb can stand alone: her father never consented.
entries.passive: restricted. Legal prose does passivize it — the search was consented to, a consented-to entry — but outside that register it sounds odd: ✗ another round of tests wouldn't be consented to.
entries.see also: agree to · assent to · accede to · object to · to

entries.meaning: Have as its essential nature — be constituted by.
examples: Her whole argument consists in one unproven assumption.
Real freedom, he wrote, consists in having nothing left to prove.
The difficulty consists in getting three agencies to sign the same document.
Virtue does not consist in never being tempted.
The novel's charm consists in how little it explains.
Most of the work consists in checking numbers somebody else typed.
entries.русский: заключаться в — составлять самую суть чего-то; книжн. (не путать с consist of)
entries.register: formal and philosophical; essays, theology, and academic prose — happiness consists in contentment — and rare enough in speech that many Americans know only consist of
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (consists in knowing when to stop) — never a to-infinitive (✗ consists in to know when to stop) and never a that-clause. The verb takes no direct object, has no passive (✗ is consisted in) and no progressive (✗ is consisting in).
entries.pattern: [an abstraction] consist in [its essence] · consist in [verb-ing] · the difficulty consists in [something]
entries.contrast: Consist in names the essence; consist of lists the parts. The committee consists of nine members is an inventory; good management consists in hiring well and then leaving people alone is a definition — swap them and you get nonsense: ✗ the committee consists in nine members. A useful test: consist of answers what is it made of, consist in answers what does it really amount to, and the second can almost always be replaced by lies in. Both refuse the passive and the progressive, which is the error learners make most often with either.
entries.verb type: stative — a relation of essence, never an activity; it rejects the progressive outright: ✗ the difficulty is consisting in the paperwork.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the verb takes no direct object at all; in plus its complement is obligatory: ✗ her whole argument consists.
entries.passive: no. The entry says so explicitly: ✗ is consisted in. Stative and objectless, there is nothing to promote — ✗ one unproven assumption is consisted in by her argument.
entries.see also: consist of · amount to · result in, result from · in

entries.meaning: Be made up of certain parts.
examples: The committee consists of five members and two alternates.
Breakfast consisted of cold toast and an apology.
The exam consists of forty questions and one essay.
Her job largely consists of answering email she didn't ask for.
The archive consists of letters, photographs, and one reel of film.
True courage, he said, consists in doing it anyway.
entries.русский: состоять из — быть составленным из частей
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (consists of filling out three forms) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause. Consist is intransitive: it has no passive (✗ is consisted of) and no progressive (✗ is consisting of).
entries.pattern: [a whole] consist of [its parts] · [something] consist in [its essence] — formal · be composed of / be made up of [parts]
entries.contrast: Is consisted of is an error — the verb is already active and cannot be passivized. Consist of lists the physical parts; the rarer consist in names where something's essence lies (freedom consists in the absence of coercion). The neighbors sort out like this: consist of and be made up of are the plain forms; be composed of is formal; and comprise means the same thing but takes a direct object and no preposition — the collection comprises 400 prints — so the very common is comprised of remains disputed in edited American prose. If you are unsure, consists of is always safe.
entries.verb type: stative — being made up of parts is a state, not an event, and the progressive is impossible: ✗ the committee is consisting of five members.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object; of plus the parts is required: ✗ the exam consists. Use comprise if you want a true direct object: the exam comprises forty questions.
entries.passive: no — the classic learner error. ✗ is consisted of does not exist; the verb is already active in meaning. Say be made up of or be composed of when you want that shape.
entries.see also: lack · belong to · contribute to · separate from · of

entries.meaning: Talk something over with someone, or look something up in a source.
examples: Let me consult with my partner before I commit to anything.
You should consult a tax attorney, not a message board.
The city consulted with residents about the bike lanes for eight months.
She consults for three startups and teaches one class.
Consult the appendix for the full list of exclusions.
The surgeon consulted with two colleagues before scheduling the operation.
entries.русский: советоваться с — обсуждать вопрос со специалистом
entries.register: consult with is neutral American; bare consult is more formal
entries.complement: noun phrase only, naming a person or body. No gerund, no clause. The bare transitive is a different pattern: consult a doctor, consult the manual — a reference source is a direct object and never takes with: ✗ consult with the dictionary.
entries.pattern: consult with [a person, a colleague, a firm] · consult [a doctor, a lawyer, a manual, a map] · consult [someone] about / on [a matter] · consult for [a client]
entries.contrast: Consult with someone is standard, everyday American English and is far more common in the U.S. than in Britain, where it can sound redundant next to plain consult. The useful distinction: you consult a source (it gives you information) and consult with a person (you talk it over together). A third pattern, consult for, means work as a paid consultant: she consults for two hospital systems. The matter under discussion takes about or on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both frames, talking something over (let me consult with my partner) and looking something up (consult the appendix); progressive fine: she's consulting with two colleagues.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with with before a person (consulted with residents), transitive before a source or a person consulted (consult a tax attorney, consult the manual), and consult for names a client.
entries.passive: restricted. The bare transitive passivizes cleanly — a tax attorney should be consulted, residents were consulted about the bike lanes — but the with frame is clumsy: ?my partner was consulted with first.
entries.see also: talk with · refer to · apply to · agree with · discuss

entries.meaning: Give something toward a total, or help bring something about.
examples: Everyone in the office contributed to the gift.
Deferred maintenance contributed to the failure of the pump.
She has contributed to the magazine for twenty years.
Three factors contributed to the drop in enrollment.
The tax credit contributed to lowering the uninsured rate.
He contributed a chapter to the anthology and never got paid.
entries.русский: вносить вклад в; способствовать чему-то — после to герундий
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (contributed to lowering the rate) — never a to-infinitive (✗ contributed to lower the rate, which changes the meaning to purpose). A wh-clause is possible after to whatever. Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: contribute to [a fund, a cause, a result] · contribute [something] to [something] · contribute to [verb-ing] · contribute [an article] to [a publication]
entries.contrast: Watch the to. In contributed to lowering the rate the to is the fixed preposition and the verb must be -ing; in contributed money to lower the rate the to is an infinitive of purpose and belongs to a different structure entirely. The two read almost alike and mean different things. Note also that contribute covers both giving and causing: contribute to a pension is generous, contribute to a collapse is not.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, giving (everyone contributed to the gift) and causing (deferred maintenance contributed to the failure); progressive normal: she's been contributing to that fund for years.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with to alone (three factors contributed to the drop), transitive when the thing given is named: he contributed a chapter to the anthology.
entries.passive: restricted. Passive only where there is a real direct object: a chapter was contributed to the anthology. The causal frame refuses it: ✗ the failure of the pump was contributed to by deferred maintenance.
entries.see also: add to · lead to · result in · participate in · invest in

entries.meaning: Come together from different directions toward one point.
examples: Reporters converged on the courthouse before the verdict was read.
Independent estimates have converged on about four percent.
Three storm systems converged on the valley in a single week.
The sequence converges to zero faster than the textbook example.
Both parties eventually converged on the same compromise figure.
The old logging road converges with the highway two miles north.
entries.русский: сходиться к одной точке — on съезжаться куда-то, to сходиться (мат.)
entries.register: neutral for converge on; converge to is technical, at home in mathematics and statistics
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a place, target, or value — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, never a clause. There is no direct-object frame: ✗ converged the plaza. The subject is plural or collective, because convergence takes at least two things: ✗ the reporter converged on city hall.
entries.pattern: [people / vehicles] converge on [a place] · [estimates / opinions] converge on [a figure] · [a sequence] converge to [a limit] · [two lines / two paths] converge with [each other]
entries.contrast: The preposition marks the field you are writing in. Converge on is the general word — crowds converge on a stadium, forecasters converge on a number. Converge to belongs to mathematics, where a series converges to a limit, and using it of a crowd sounds like a translation error. Converge with takes the other party rather than the destination (the trail converges with the highway). The opposite is diverge from, and note that converge has no passive: ✗ the plaza was converged on is at best jocular.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a process with duration; the progressive is normal: three storm systems are converging on the valley.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct-object frame at all (✗ converged the plaza), and the subject must be plural or collective: ✗ the reporter converged on city hall.
entries.passive: no, as the entry states: ✗ the plaza was converged on, ✗ four percent has been converged on by the estimates. Rewrite with surround or agree on.
entries.see also: agree on · arrive at, arrive in · amount to · on

entries.meaning: Find someone guilty of a crime in a court of law.
examples: He was convicted of wire fraud and sentenced in March.
The jury convicted her of the lesser charge only.
Anyone convicted of a felony loses the license automatically.
Two officers were convicted of falsifying the reports.
She was convicted on three counts and acquitted on the rest.
He was convicted of selling equipment that belonged to the county.
entries.русский: признавать виновным в — выносить обвинительный приговор; юр.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the crime, or a gerund naming it (convicted of lying to investigators) — never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause. The passive is the normal frame: was convicted of. Counts and charges take on instead: convicted on three counts, convicted on all charges; ✗ convicted for murder and ✗ convicted with murder are errors, though convicted for a crime he did not commit passes as causal for.
entries.pattern: [a jury / a court] convict [someone] of [a crime] · [someone] be convicted of [a crime] · be convicted on [counts] · a convicted felon · convict [someone] of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Convict of and acquit of are the two verdicts and share one preposition. Upstream of both, charge with is what the prosecutor files and indict for is what a grand jury returns, so the preposition changes at every stage: charged with fraud, indicted for fraud, convicted of fraud, sentenced to three years. Watch the stress: the verb is kun-VIKT, the noun KON-vikt. And convict never takes a that-clause — for that you need find: the jury found that he had lied.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a court's act at a point in time: the jury convicted her of the lesser charge.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person is the direct object and of names the crime; both slots are needed in the active: ✗ the jury convicted of wire fraud.
entries.passive: yes — and the passive is the normal frame in American reporting: he was convicted of wire fraud and sentenced in March, two officers were convicted of falsifying the reports.
entries.see also: acquit of · accuse of · charge with, charge for · absolve of · punish for · of

entries.meaning: Work together with someone, or help them rather than obstruct them.
examples: The airline cooperated with federal investigators from the first day.
Two states cooperated with each other on the watershed plan.
He declined to cooperate with the committee and was subpoenaed.
Local police cooperate with the sheriff's office on anything over the county line.
Tenants who cooperate with the inspection get the repairs done first.
If the weather cooperates with us, we'll be on the water by six.
entries.русский: сотрудничать с — содействовать, а не мешать (часто о следствии)
entries.register: neutral; extremely common in reporting on investigations
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, agency, or organization — never a gerund (✗ cooperated with handing over the files; the activity takes on or in: cooperated on the study, cooperated in the investigation). Never a to-infinitive, never a clause, and there is no direct object: ✗ cooperated the inquiry. The verb also stands alone: the witness cooperated.
entries.pattern: cooperate with [someone] · cooperate with [someone] on / in [something] · cooperate — no complement · cooperation with [someone] — the noun keeps the preposition
entries.contrast: Cooperating is not obstructing; collaborating is co-authoring. The company cooperated with regulators means it answered the questions and produced the documents; the company collaborated with regulators would oddly suggest they wrote the rules together. In criminal practice cooperate with has hardened into a term of art — a cooperating witness trades information for leniency — and refused to cooperate is nearly a formula. Note that ✗ cooperate to someone and ✗ cooperate someone are both impossible.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, something you do or refuse to do; progressive fine: the airline is cooperating with investigators.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object (✗ cooperated the inquiry), and the verb stands alone happily: the witness cooperated.
entries.passive: no. The prepositional passive is unusable here: ✗ federal investigators were cooperated with, ✗ the committee was refused to be cooperated with.
entries.see also: collaborate with · work with · comply with · consult with · with

entries.meaning: Deal successfully with something difficult.
examples: She's coping with a heavy caseload and a sick parent.
Small districts can't cope with an enrollment swing that size.
He coped with being passed over better than anyone expected.
The system wasn't built to cope with that kind of traffic.
How do you cope with the noise?
They're coping, but only just.
entries.русский: справляться с — успешно преодолевать трудность
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (cope with being alone) — never a to-infinitive (✗ cope with to be alone) and never a clause. Cope is intransitive and cannot take a bare object: ✗ cope the situation. It does stand alone: she's coping.
entries.pattern: cope with [a difficulty] · cope with [verb-ing] · cope (alone) · manage to [verb] — a different verb, different pattern
entries.contrast: Cope to and ✗ cope the problem are both errors. The preposition is fixed at with, and the verb never takes a direct object. Its neighbors split: deal with is the neutral everyday synonym, handle and manage are transitive with no preposition (handle the complaints, manage the fallout), and put up with means tolerate rather than manage. Bare cope, with nothing after it, has become the standard American shorthand for barely managing: I'm coping.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; managing is something you do over time, and the progressive is the commonest form: they're coping, but only just.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — cope never takes a bare object (✗ cope the situation) and with is fixed; the verb also stands alone: she's coping.
entries.passive: no in practice: ✗ a heavy caseload is being coped with, ✗ that kind of traffic couldn't be coped with. Switch to handle or manage, which are transitive: that traffic couldn't be handled.
entries.see also: take care of · object to · adapt to · suffer from

entries.meaning: Adjust a figure or a measurement to remove a known distortion.
examples: Wages have barely moved once you correct for inflation.
The model corrects for seasonal swings in construction hiring.
Their instruments correct for the curvature of the lens automatically.
The survey did not correct for the fact that only landlines were called.
Test scores corrected for school size tell a different story.
Blood values are corrected for altitude before they are compared.
entries.русский: вносить поправку на — устранять известное искажение; науч./техн.
entries.register: formal and technical; statistics, laboratory science, economics — corrected for inflation, corrected for altitude
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a distorting factor — inflation, seasonality, temperature, sample bias. A gerund is rare but possible (correcting for having oversampled retirees); never a to-infinitive and never a clause. Keep it apart from the plain transitive: correct the error takes no preposition, and correct someone on something is a third pattern.
entries.pattern: correct for [a distortion] · be corrected for [inflation / seasonality] · correct [an error] — no preposition · correct [someone] on [a point]
entries.contrast: Three technical near-neighbors, and the difference is real. Correct for and adjust for remove a known distortion from figures you already have — adjust for is the commoner word in finance. Control for is a design decision made in advance, holding a variable constant so it cannot vary; a study controls for age, and saying it corrected for age instead tells the reader the fix came afterward. And account for merely explains a number rather than changing it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an adjustment performed on figures: the model corrects for seasonal swings; progressive fine in describing a method.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with no preposition in correct the error, and intransitive with the fixed for when a distortion is removed: correct for inflation. Correct someone on something is a third frame.
entries.passive: yes, and the prepositional passive is standard technical English: blood values are corrected for altitude before they are compared, test scores corrected for school size tell a different story.
entries.see also: account for · allow for · compensate for · for

entries.meaning: Move together with something in a measurable way.
examples: Household income correlates with almost every health outcome in the study.
The two tests correlate with each other well enough to use either one.
Absenteeism correlates with the length of the commute.
Nothing in the data correlates with the change they expected to see.
The researchers correlated the sensor readings with hospital admissions.
Test scores correlate with having a parent who finished college.
entries.русский: коррелировать с — изменяться согласованно с чем-то; науч.
entries.register: formal and technical; statistics, medicine, and the social sciences, plus the business writing that borrows from them
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund naming the other variable (correlates with having gone to preschool) — never a to-infinitive (✗ correlates with to go to preschool) and never a clause. There is also a transitive frame in which the researcher is the subject: correlate the survey data with census figures. The verb can stand alone with a plural subject: the two measures correlate.
entries.pattern: [one variable] correlate with [another] · correlate [one set of data] with [another] · [two things] correlate · be strongly / weakly / negatively correlated with [something]
entries.variants: correlate to — heard in business and journalistic writing; with is the standard in scientific prose and the safer choice everywhere
entries.contrast: The whole point of the word is that it does not claim causation. Ice cream sales correlate with drownings asserts only that the two move together; cause, lead to, and result in assert direction, and swapping them in is the classic error. Two softer neighbors: relate to is vague about the relationship, and vary with describes co-movement without the statistical machinery (the fee varies with the size of the lot). Note the adjective frame is the commonest of all in papers: strongly correlated with income.
entries.verb type: stative in the relational sense — two variables simply move together, and the progressive is odd: ✗ income is correlating with health outcomes. Action (dynamic) in the researcher's frame: she was correlating the readings with admissions.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with with or with a plural subject alone (the two measures correlate), transitive when a researcher does the work: correlate the sensor readings with hospital admissions.
entries.passive: restricted. The researcher frame passivizes and the participle is everywhere in papers: the readings were correlated with admissions, strongly correlated with income. The relational sense does not: ✗ health outcomes are correlated with by income.
entries.see also: correspond to, correspond with · compare to, compare with · result in, result from · depend on · with

entries.meaning: Match something, or exchange letters with someone.
examples: Each color on the map corresponds to a census tract.
The two economists corresponded with each other for a decade before meeting.
The serial number does not correspond to anything in our records.
Roughly, a bachelor's degree there corresponds to an associate's here.
She corresponded with the family in Odessa until the mail stopped.
Revenue for the quarter fell short of the corresponding period last year.
entries.русский: соответствовать чему-то (to); переписываться с кем-то (with)
entries.register: neutral to formal; the letter-writing sense is formal and a little old-fashioned
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a gerund (✗ corresponds to being late; say corresponds to the delay), never a to-infinitive, never a clause. The verb has no passive (✗ is corresponded to) and no direct object.
entries.pattern: [one thing] correspond to [another] — match · [a person] correspond with [another] — exchange letters · [two things] correspond · the corresponding [figure / period] — the participle, very common in reports
entries.contrast: The two prepositions have drifted apart in American usage, and the split is worth keeping. Correspond to means match or be equivalent: the numbers on the invoice correspond to the packing list, the American term corresponds to the British one. Correspond with means write letters back and forth: they corresponded with each other for forty years. Older and British writing also uses with for matching, so the figures correspond with the audit is not wrong — but in a document where both senses could be read, to for matching keeps the sentence clear. Compare conform to, which measures a thing against a standard rather than pairing two things off.
entries.verb type: stative in the matching sense — a static equivalence, no progressive: ✗ each color is corresponding to a tract. Action (dynamic) in the letter-writing sense: they were corresponding with each other for forty years.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in both senses — no direct object at all (✗ correspond the invoice the packing list); the preposition is obligatory except with a plural subject: the two figures correspond.
entries.passive: no, as the entry states: ✗ is corresponded to, ✗ a census tract is corresponded to by each color. The participle the corresponding period is an adjective, not a passive.
