entries.see also: conform to, conform with · correlate with · compare to, compare with · communicate with · to

entries.meaning: Trust that someone or something will not let you down.
examples: You can count on her to have read every page.
Don't count on the mail getting there by Friday.
Half the neighborhood counts on that bus line.
I'm counting on you.
We were counting on a bigger turnout than forty people.
Count on it — he'll bring up the parking again.
entries.русский: рассчитывать на — быть уверенным, что не подведёт
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (counting on getting the grant) — never a to-infinitive after the preposition itself (✗ count on to get the grant). A to-infinitive is correct after a person: count on her to remember. A wh-clause is fine: don't count on what he tells you. Count on also takes a that-clause in speech (count on it that he'll be late), but the smoother form is count on his being late.
entries.pattern: count on [someone / something] · count on [someone] to [verb] · count on [verb-ing] · you can count on it
entries.contrast: Same family as depend on and rely on, with a difference of register: count on is the warm, spoken one, rely on the neutral one, depend on the one that also means be determined by. Count on almost never carries that second sense — That counts on the weather is not English; you want That depends on the weather. Note the unrelated phrasal verbs count in (count me in), count out (exclude), and count up (total), none of which are this pattern.
entries.verb type: stative in meaning — trust is a state, not an act — but unlike most statives it takes the progressive freely: I'm counting on you, we were counting on a bigger turnout.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with a fixed preposition — no bare object (✗ count her), though count on someone to do something adds an infinitive after the person. Bare count (total, matter) is a different verb.
entries.passive: yes — the prepositional passive is idiomatic: she can be counted on to have read every page, that bus line is counted on by half the neighborhood.
entries.see also: depend on · rely on · believe in · wait for

entries.meaning: Put a layer over something.
examples: Cover the dough with a damp towel and let it rest.
By morning the deck was covered with ice.
His desk is permanently covered in sticky notes.
She covered the stain with a rug and hoped nobody looked.
The whole field was covered with frost at sunrise.
The procedure isn't covered by our plan.
entries.русский: покрывать чем-то — накладывать слой поверх
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause. The passive takes either preposition: covered with snow and covered in snow are both standard, with in a shade more thorough. Cover itself is transitive: cover the pot, ✗ cover with the pot if the pot is the lid.
entries.pattern: cover [something] with [something] · be covered with / in [something] · cover [a topic, a distance, a shift] — no preposition · be covered by [insurance, a policy, a warranty]
entries.contrast: Covered with and covered in are genuinely interchangeable; in suggests more complete coverage (covered in mud beats covered with mud for effect). Covered by is a different thing entirely — it names an insurer, a policy, or a reporter: the surgery is covered by insurance, the trial was covered by three networks. And bare cover has a raft of transitive senses that take no preposition at all: cover the material, cover forty miles, cover for a colleague (that last one being cover for, meaning substitute or make excuses).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the resulting be covered with / in is a state rather than an event: his desk is permanently covered in sticky notes.
entries.transitivity: transitive — cover needs a direct object (✗ she covered with a rug), and with names the layer. Bare transitive cover the material / forty miles / a shift takes no preposition.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the commonest form: by morning the deck was covered with ice. Keep covered by apart — it names an insurer or a reporter: the procedure isn't covered by our plan.
entries.see also: consist of · provide with · dress in · protect from · with

entries.meaning: Say that someone deserves recognition for something.
examples: Reviewers credited the director with rescuing the second act.
She is credited with discovering two of the three isotopes.
Nobody credits the mayor with the drop in crime except the mayor.
He credits his sister with talking him out of dropping the case.
The bank credited the account with the disputed charge the next morning.
Historians now credit her with having written most of the report.
entries.русский: приписывать кому-то заслугу — признавать чей-то вклад
entries.register: neutral; standard in journalism, citations, and banking
entries.complement: the person or thing honored is a direct object, and with takes a noun phrase or a gerund (credited her with saving the account) — never a to-infinitive (✗ credited her with to save the account) and never a clause. Both slots are obligatory in the active: ✗ credited with the discovery alone needs a passive subject — she was credited with the discovery.
entries.pattern: credit [someone] with [an achievement] · credit [someone] with [verb-ing] · be credited with [something] · credit [an achievement] to [someone] · credit [an account] with [an amount]
entries.contrast: Credit with and blame for are mirror images, one for things that went right and one for things that went wrong, and they take different prepositions: credited her with the turnaround, blamed her for the collapse. Attribute to and ascribe to say the same thing with the arguments reversed — attributed the turnaround to her — so the achievement leads and the person follows. American speech also uses credit someone for something, which careful writers reserve for the effort or the reason (credit him for trying) while keeping with for the accomplishment itself. The banking sense runs both ways: credit the account with $50 or credit $50 to the account.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an act of ascribing recognition, performed by reviewers, historians, or a bank: historians now credit her with having written most of the report.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person honored is the direct object and with takes the achievement; both slots are obligatory in the active: ✗ reviewers credited with rescuing the second act.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the default frame: she is credited with discovering two of the three isotopes, the account was credited with the disputed charge.
entries.see also: attribute to · ascribe to · blame for, blame on · thank for · with

entries.meaning: Handle a problem or a person, be about a subject — or, with in, trade in a kind of goods.
examples: Somebody has to deal with the flooding in the basement before the drywall goes up.
I'll deal with him on Monday when everyone has cooled off.
The second chapter deals with the collapse of the savings-and-loans.
She dealt with being laid off better than anyone expected.
His uncle deals in rare coins out of a shop on Grand Avenue.
That firm deals in municipal bonds and nothing else.
entries.русский: иметь дело с, улаживать, быть о чём-то (with); торговать чем-то (in)
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (deal with getting the permits), or a wh-clause (deal with whatever the inspector finds) — never a to-infinitive (✗ deal with to get the permits) and never a that-clause (✗ deal with that he quit; use deal with the fact that he quit). Deal in takes a noun phrase naming goods or a kind of thing, and nothing else. The preposition is fixed in both: the object never moves, so ✗ deal it with is not English.
entries.pattern: deal with [a problem, a person, a subject] · deal with [verb-ing] · deal in [antiques, futures, rumor] · deal [someone] [cards, a hand] — no preposition · deal [a blow] to [someone]
entries.contrast: Deal with handles something; deal in trades in something. A manager deals with complaints; a gallery deals in prints. The two are never interchangeable: ✗ the gallery deals with prints says it is coping with them. Note also that deal with covers two jobs English usually splits — take action about a problem (deal with the leak) and be about a subject (the chapter deals with tariffs) — and that the transitive deal takes no preposition at all: deal the cards, deal a blow.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: handling a problem, trading in goods, or a chapter being about a subject (that last one shading stative: the second chapter deals with the savings-and-loans).
entries.transitivity: intransitive with both fixed prepositions — the object never moves (✗ deal it with) and there is no direct-object frame here. Bare transitive deal belongs to cards and blows: deal the cards, deal a blow to.
entries.passive: restricted. Deal with passivizes well: the flooding was dealt with before the drywall went up, he'll be dealt with on Monday. Deal in does not: ✗ rare coins are dealt in by his uncle.
entries.see also: cope with · put up with · take care of · dispose of · with

entries.meaning: Settle on one option after weighing them.
examples: They finally decided on the yellow one.
She decided against law school after two weeks of shadowing.
We haven't decided on where to hold it.
The board decided against raising dues this year.
He decided on the cheaper contractor and regretted it by March.
After all that, they decided to stay put.
entries.русский: останавливаться на чём-то (on); решать отказаться от чего-то (against)
entries.complement: on and against take a noun phrase, a gerund (decided against moving), or a wh-clause (decided on where to eat) — never a to-infinitive after the preposition (✗ decided on to move). Decide also takes a bare to-infinitive with no preposition (decided to move) and a that-clause (decided that it wasn't worth it).
entries.pattern: decide on [a choice] · decide against [a course / verb-ing] · decide to [verb] · decide not to [verb] · decide that [clause] · decide between [A] and [B] · decide [a case, a question]
entries.contrast: Decide to leave and decide on leaving are both correct and mean the same thing — the first is the infinitive frame, the second the prepositional one — but you cannot mix them: ✗ decide on to leave, ✗ decide leaving. Decide against is the negative of decide on, not of decide to: the negative of decided to sell is decided not to sell, and decided against selling is its prepositional twin. Note also transitive decide, which takes no preposition and belongs to courts and referees: the judge decided the case.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a punctual act of settling something: they finally decided on the yellow one; progressive fine while it is still open: we're still deciding on a date.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with on / against / between (decided against raising dues), transitive in the courtroom sense: the judge decided the case.
entries.passive: restricted. The transitive sense passivizes cleanly (the case was decided in March); the prepositional one is heavy but possible: ?the yellow one was finally decided on, ✗ raising dues was decided against by the board.
entries.see also: choose between · agree on · insist on · plan on · vote for

entries.meaning: Give something over entirely to a purpose or a person.
examples: The foundation is dedicated to restoring salmon habitat.
She devoted most of her thirties to getting the clinic open.
He dedicated the book to the teacher who failed him twice.
Two floors are devoted to storage that nobody has opened in years.
They devoted themselves to raising the money before the roof gave out.
The wing was dedicated to the founder's wife in 1961.
entries.русский: посвящать чему-то или кому-то — отдавать целиком; после to герундий
entries.register: neutral; dedicate is the more ceremonial of the two
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (devoted the summer to rebuilding the porch) — to is a preposition here, so a verb after it must be -ing: ✗ dedicated to preserve the wetland, ✗ devoted himself to restore it. Never a clause. In the active, both verbs need a direct object before the to — the thing given over, or a reflexive: dedicate the fund to scholarships, devote yourself to the work. In the participial forms that object drops away, but the to and its gerund do not: dedicated to ending hunger, devoted to running the shop.
entries.pattern: dedicate [something] to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · devote [time, money, oneself] to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · be dedicated to / be devoted to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · dedicate [a book, a building] to [a person]
entries.contrast: Dedicated to preserving and ✗ dedicated to preserve differ by a suffix and by a whole grammar. This is the look forward to trap wearing formal clothes, and it shows up constantly in mission statements, where an organization dedicated to ending hunger is right and ✗ dedicated to end hunger is not. The two verbs part company in one place: dedicate alone carries the ceremonial sense of naming something in someone's honor — dedicate the library to her memory, the album is dedicated to his father — which devote never does. In the other direction devote is the ordinary word for spending time (devoted three weeks to the appendix), where dedicate sounds grand. Note that the adjective devoted can stand alone meaning loyal (a devoted friend), and that ✗ dedicate on and ✗ devote for are errors.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of giving something over; the participial be dedicated to / be devoted to is a state: two floors are devoted to storage.
entries.transitivity: transitive — both verbs need a direct object before to in the active, often a reflexive: dedicate the fund to scholarships, they devoted themselves to raising the money. ✗ the foundation dedicates to restoring habitat.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is where these verbs live: the wing was dedicated to the founder's wife in 1961, the foundation is dedicated to restoring salmon habitat.
entries.see also: commit to · look forward to · object to · contribute to · specialize in · to

entries.meaning: Work something out by reasoning from what you already know.
examples: From the mud on the boots he deduced that she had come through the orchard.
You can deduce the missing figure from the two subtotals.
Nothing about his motive can be deduced from the emails alone.
She deduced from the silence on the call that the offer had already been made.
The students were asked to deduce the rule from eight sample sentences.
He deduced from watching two rehearsals that the show would run long.
entries.русский: выводить, заключать из — доходить рассуждением от известного
entries.register: neutral, leaning formal — logic, detective stories, and academic prose
entries.complement: from takes a noun phrase naming the evidence, or a gerund (deduced from watching the tape) — never a to-infinitive (✗ deduced from to watch the tape). What is deduced is the direct object, and it may be a noun phrase or a that-clause: deduced that the lock had been picked. The preposition disappears in front of that clause: ✗ deduced from that the lock had been picked.
entries.pattern: deduce [something] from [evidence] · deduce that [clause] from [evidence] · [something] can be deduced from [evidence] · deduce [something] — no preposition, when the evidence is understood
entries.contrast: Deduce from and infer from share a preposition and split the work. Deduce reasons down from a rule or a premise and claims certainty; infer reads a likely conclusion off the evidence and claims only probability. Derive from is about origin rather than reasoning (the word derives from Latin), and extrapolate from projects a known trend past the data you have. All four take from and none of them takes of: ✗ deduce of the evidence.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an act of reasoning carried out at a moment: from the mud on the boots he deduced that she had come through the orchard.
entries.transitivity: transitive — what is deduced is the direct object or a that-clause (deduced that the lock had been picked); from names the evidence and may be dropped when it is understood.
entries.passive: yes, and the modal passive is the natural frame: nothing about his motive can be deduced from the emails alone, the rule was deduced from eight sample sentences.
entries.see also: infer from · derive from · extrapolate from · follow from · from

entries.meaning: Fail to make a payment or meet an obligation you are bound to.
examples: Two homeowners on the block defaulted on their mortgages that spring.
If the company defaults on the note, the collateral goes to the bank.
He defaulted on a student loan in 2011 and spent a decade fixing his credit.
The country has defaulted on its external debt three times in forty years.
Tenants who default on rent get thirty days' notice under the ordinance.
Nobody expected a AAA borrower to default.
entries.русский: не платить по (кредиту), нарушать обязательство; фин./юр.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an obligation: a loan, a mortgage, a payment, a bond, a lease, an agreement. A gerund is unidiomatic (✗ defaulted on paying the rent — say defaulted on the rent), and no clause is possible (✗ defaulted on that he owed us). The verb is also fine with no object at all (the borrower defaulted in March), and there it is not a dependent preposition, just an intransitive verb.
entries.pattern: default on [a loan, a payment, an obligation] · default — intransitive · default to [a setting, a value] — a different verb · be in default on [a loan] · default judgment — the noun
entries.contrast: Default on is failing to pay; default to is falling back on a preset. The county defaulted on its bonds is a financial disaster; the form defaults to Eastern time is a software convenience, and the two never mix: ✗ defaulted to its bonds. The legal fixed phrase is in default of (in default of payment), which is a complex preposition rather than this verb. Compare renege on a promise, which is the same frame applied to a commitment nobody signed.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an event with a date: he defaulted on a student loan in 2011.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object (✗ defaulted the loan), and the verb is fine with nothing after it: nobody expected a AAA borrower to default.
entries.passive: restricted. Financial writing allows the prepositional passive — loans defaulted on during the crisis, the note was defaulted on in March — but the ordinary phrasing is be in default on: ✗ their mortgages were defaulted on by two homeowners.
entries.see also: foreclose on · dispose of · pay for · in default of · on

entries.meaning: Yield to somebody else's judgment or authority instead of your own.
examples: On anything involving the tax code I defer to her.
The panel deferred to the trial judge's findings of fact.
Younger associates learn quickly which partners expect to be deferred to.
He deferred to his brother's wishes about the funeral arrangements.
Reviewing courts defer to the agency where the statute is genuinely ambiguous.
She rarely defers to anyone on questions of structural engineering.
entries.русский: уступать чьему-то мнению или власти — полагаться на чужое суждение
entries.register: neutral to formal — courts, committees, and polite disagreement
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, a body, or somebody's judgment or expertise. A gerund is grammatical but rare (deferred to having the committee decide), and a to-infinitive is impossible (✗ defer to decide — that is the infinitive of a different verb, meaning postpone). No clause: ✗ defer to that she knows more.
entries.pattern: defer to [a person, a court, an authority] · defer to [someone's judgment, expertise, wishes] · defer [a decision, payment, maintenance] — postpone, no preposition · defer [something] to [a later date, the next meeting]
entries.contrast: One spelling, two verbs. Defer to the board is yielding to somebody else's authority; defer the vote is putting it off, and that second verb takes a direct object, not to. Both can appear with to and mean different things: we deferred to the chair (yielded) versus we deferred the item to June (postponed). In appellate writing defer to is a term of art — the court defers to the agency's reading — and deference to is its noun. Do not confuse it with differ from.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the sense of yielding on a given occasion (the panel deferred to the trial judge), and habitual-stative in she rarely defers to anyone on structural engineering.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with a fixed to — no direct object here (✗ defer her judgment in this sense). The homonym meaning postpone is transitive: defer the vote, defer maintenance.
entries.passive: yes — the prepositional passive is idiomatic and the entry uses it: younger associates learn which partners expect to be deferred to, the agency's reading was deferred to.
entries.see also: refer to · comply with · go along with · rely on · to

entries.meaning: Leave a place, or break with an established practice or text.
examples: The 6:12 to Chicago departs from Track 9.
The opinion departs from thirty years of settled precedent in two paragraphs.
He never departs from the recipe, which is why the bread is always the same.
The translation departs from the original in ways the preface never admits.
Delegates departed from the capital before the vote was certified.
Any departure from the protocol has to be logged.
entries.русский: отправляться из; отступать от (правила, традиции, текста)
entries.register: formal — travel announcements for the literal sense, policy and legal prose for the figurative one
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a place, or a practice, text, precedent, or norm. A gerund is possible but stiff (departed from following the script); no to-infinitive (✗ depart from to follow the script) and no clause. Depart is also intransitive with no object at all (the train departs at six), and there nothing is a dependent preposition.
entries.pattern: depart from [a city, a gate, a station] · depart from [precedent, the text, standard practice] · depart for [a destination] · depart — intransitive · a departure from [the norm] — the noun keeps from
entries.contrast: From is where you leave; for is where you are headed. Departed from Denver and departed for Denver are opposite trips. In the figurative sense the neighbors divide finely: depart from a practice is a deliberate break, deviate from a plan is a step off a required path, diverge from a route is a gradual separation, and differ from is not motion at all but a static comparison. Note that in ordinary American speech nobody departs from a house — that is leave — and the verb belongs to airports, timetables, and briefs.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both the travel sense (the 6:12 departs from Track 9) and the figurative one (the opinion departs from settled precedent).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no object at all (✗ depart the practice in this sense), and depart stands alone with a time: the train departs at six. Note depart for is the opposite trip.
entries.passive: restricted. Legal and technical prose allows it — thirty years of precedent were departed from in two paragraphs — but the travel sense refuses: ✗ Track 9 was departed from.
entries.see also: deviate from · diverge from · differ from · derogate from · from

entries.meaning: Rely on, or be determined by.
examples: The whole schedule depends on whether the permit clears.
She has three kids depending on her.
You can depend on him to be five minutes late.
How long it takes depends on traffic.
Funding for next year depends upon the audit.
Everything depends on getting the roof done before November.
entries.русский: зависеть от; полагаться на — определяться чем-то или доверять кому-то
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (depend on winning) · also a wh-clause (it depends on what she says) — never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause. A to-infinitive is correct only after a person: depend on him to be late.
entries.pattern: [subject] depend on [noun phrase] · depend on [someone] to [verb] · depend on [verb-ing] · it depends on [wh-clause]
entries.variants: depend upon — identical in meaning, more formal and more common in writing
entries.contrast: Depend of and depend from are errors — the preposition is fixed. Bare depend with no preposition works only in the elliptical It depends. Note the two senses: depend on someone (rely on) versus depend on something (be determined by), which is why That depends on the weather is not about trust. Against its neighbors, rely on is the neutral synonym of the first sense only, and count on the warm spoken one; neither carries the be-determined-by sense.
entries.verb type: stative in both senses — trusting and being determined by. The rely sense takes the progressive (she has three kids depending on her); the be-determined-by sense does not: ✗ how long it takes is depending on traffic.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with a fixed preposition — no bare object (✗ depend him), though depend on someone to do something adds an infinitive after the person. Bare depend survives only in It depends.
entries.passive: restricted by sense. The rely sense passivizes: he can be depended on to be five minutes late. The be-determined-by sense cannot: ✗ traffic is depended on by how long it takes.
entries.see also: rely on · count on · believe in · on · depending on

entries.meaning: Take something away from someone, or keep them from having it.
examples: The blackout deprived half the county of power for three days.
He was deprived of counsel for the first thirty-six hours.
A newborn deprives both parents of sleep for about a year.
The redistricting deprived the neighborhood of a representative it had had since 1974.
Deprived of sunlight, the seedlings went pale and leggy.
She refused to deprive herself of one small pleasure a day.
entries.русский: лишать чего-то — отнимать или не давать иметь
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (deprived of seeing his kids) — never a to-infinitive (✗ deprived of to see them) and never a clause. The person deprived is a direct object: deprive someone of something, never ✗ deprive of someone something.
entries.pattern: deprive [someone] of [something] · be deprived of [something] · sleep-deprived, oxygen-deprived (compounds)
entries.contrast: Deprive from is an error. Compare the family: deprive someone of takes something away that they had or needed; rob someone of does the same thing with more violence or unfairness; strip someone of a title or a rank is formal and public. All three keep of. Contrast prevent someone from doing, which blocks an action rather than removing a thing — a different preposition because a different structure. The past participle has become a productive compound: sleep-deprived, deprived neighborhoods.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an act or event of taking something away: the blackout deprived half the county of power.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person deprived is the direct object and of names what is taken; the order is fixed: ✗ deprive of someone something.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the commonest form: he was deprived of counsel for the first thirty-six hours, deprived of sunlight, the seedlings went pale.
entries.see also: rob of · prevent from · protect from · save from · of

entries.meaning: Come from a source, or take something from a source.
examples: Most of the county's revenue derives from a single property tax.
The word derives from an Old French verb meaning to trap.
She derives an unusual amount of satisfaction from labeling things.
The board's authority derives from a 1974 ordinance nobody has read since.
Their advantage derives from being the only supplier within four hundred miles.
The drug is derived from a fungus that grows on rye.
entries.русский: происходить от; извлекать из — брать начало в источнике
entries.register: neutral, leaning formal — etymology, finance, and academic prose
entries.complement: from takes a noun phrase naming a source, or a gerund (derives from being the only supplier in the county) — never a to-infinitive (✗ derives from to be the only supplier) and never a clause. Two frames share the verb: transitive derive [pleasure, income, authority] from [a source], and intransitive derive from, where the subject is the thing that came out of the source.
entries.pattern: derive [something] from [a source] · [something] derive from [an origin] · be derived from [a source] · a derivative of [something] — the noun takes of
entries.contrast: Derive from is about where something came from; deduce from is about how you reasoned. A word derives from Latin, but a conclusion is deduced from the evidence, and swapping them is a real error in student writing. Against the neighbors: stem from points at a cause (the delay stems from a supply problem), result from names the outcome of an event, and follow from is strictly logical. Note the noun switches prepositions — a derivative of morphine, never ✗ a derivative from morphine.
entries.verb type: stative in the origin sense — no progressive: ✗ the word is deriving from Old French. Action (dynamic) in the transitive sense of extracting: she derives satisfaction from labeling things.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when the subject is the thing that came out of the source (most of the revenue derives from one tax), transitive when someone takes something from a source: derive income from a trust.
entries.passive: restricted. Only the transitive frame passivizes, and it does so constantly: the drug is derived from a fungus. The intransitive origin sense has no passive: ✗ Old French is derived from by the word.
entries.see also: stem from · result in, result from · deduce from · follow from · from

entries.meaning: Take away from a right, a rule, or a standard — chiefly in legal drafting.
examples: Nothing in this section shall derogate from the tenant's statutory remedies.
The amendment does not derogate from the treaty's core protections.
Counsel argued that the waiver derogated from rights the legislature made non-waivable.
No local ordinance may derogate from the state minimum.
None of this derogates from the achievement of the people who built it.
The court refused to read the clause as derogating from the warranty.
entries.русский: умалять, ущемлять (право, норму) — юр., оговорка в договорах
entries.register: formal and legal — contract boilerplate, treaties, and judicial opinions. An American meets it in one place above all: the clause reading nothing in this Agreement shall derogate from the rights of either party. It is not a word anyone says out loud.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a right, an authority, a standard, or a reputation. No gerund, no infinitive, no clause in real use: ✗ derogate from being paid. The verb has no everyday intransitive life; the fixed legal phrase in derogation of covers the same ground as a complex preposition.
entries.pattern: derogate from [a right, an obligation, an authority] · nothing herein shall derogate from [something] · derogate from [someone's reputation, achievement] — literary · in derogation of [a right] — the fixed phrase
entries.contrast: Do not reach for it when you mean denigrate. Derogate from takes something away from a right or a standard; denigrate attacks a person's character, and it is transitive: denigrated his work, never ✗ denigrated from his work. The plain-English equivalents are detract from and take away from, and either is better anywhere outside a contract. The adjective derogatory belongs to the denigrate side of the family, which is exactly why the verb gets misused.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in form but abstract in effect, a drafting term for cutting into a right; the progressive is rare outside participles: a clause derogating from the warranty.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with a fixed from — no direct object (✗ derogate the tenant's remedies), and no everyday objectless use; the noun phrase in derogation of covers the same ground.
entries.passive: no in real use: ✗ the tenant's statutory remedies shall not be derogated from is not how drafters write it — they keep the active nothing shall derogate from. For a passive, switch to be diminished or be waived.
entries.see also: depart from · desist from · divest of · in derogation of · from

entries.meaning: Stop doing something, usually because you have been told to.
examples: The letter demanded that he desist from using the company's logo.
The court ordered the contractor to cease and desist from further excavation.
She was told to desist from contacting the witnesses directly.
The agency asked two clinics to desist from advertising the treatment as a cure.
Neither side would desist from the filings long enough to talk.
They desisted from the practice only after the fine doubled.
entries.русский: прекращать что-то делать — обычно по требованию; юр. (cease and desist)
entries.register: formal and legal. In American life it is nearly a one-phrase word: the cease and desist letter, and the injunction ordering a party to cease and desist from something. Using it conversationally sounds like a joke about lawyers.
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (desist from contacting her) — never a to-infinitive (✗ desist from to contact her) and never a clause. The verb also stands alone with no object (the picketing did not desist), where nothing follows it at all.
entries.pattern: desist from [conduct] · desist from [verb-ing] · cease and desist from [verb-ing] · desist — intransitive
entries.contrast: Refrain from is the neutral version and stop is what people actually say. All three take the same complement — refrain from smoking, desist from smoking — but desist implies an order already given, usually in writing, while refrain is a request or a personal choice. Its formal cousin abstain from is about deliberately going without something (food, alcohol, a vote). None of them takes an infinitive.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the ceasing of an activity, usually after an order: the letter demanded that he desist from using the logo.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object (✗ desist the excavation), and the verb stands alone: the picketing did not desist.
entries.passive: no. The prepositional passive does not occur: ✗ the practice was desisted from, ✗ the witnesses were desisted from contacting. The order itself goes passive instead: he was ordered to cease and desist.
entries.see also: refrain from · prevent from · discourage from · derogate from · from

entries.meaning: Leave a course, a rule, or a standard you were expected to follow.
examples: Do not deviate from the checklist, even when you are sure of the next step.
The pilot deviated from the filed route to get around the weather.
This year's numbers deviate from the ten-year average by about four percent.
He gave the same talk for a decade and never once deviated from it.
Any lab that deviates from the published method has to say so in the writeup.
The remodel deviated from the approved drawings in three places.
entries.русский: отклоняться от — отступать от курса, правила или стандарта
entries.register: neutral to formal — protocols, procedures, statistics
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a plan, a script, a protocol, a norm, or a value. A gerund is possible but uncommon (deviated from following the checklist); no to-infinitive (✗ deviate from to follow the checklist) and no clause. The verb is otherwise intransitive: the readings deviated sharply takes no object at all.
entries.pattern: deviate from [a plan, the script, the mean] · deviate — intransitive · a deviation from [the norm] — the noun keeps from · standard deviation — the fixed statistical term
entries.contrast: Deviate from implies there was a rule to leave. You deviate from a protocol, a flight path, or an agreed script — something prescribed. Depart from is the same move made deliberately and often defensibly (depart from precedent); diverge from is a gradual parting of two things that started together; differ from is not movement at all, just unlikeness. And the noun of deviate is deviation: a deviation from the norm, never ✗ a deviation of the norm.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a step off a required path; progressive fine: the readings are deviating from the mean again.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object (✗ deviate the checklist), and the verb works alone with an adverb: the readings deviated sharply.
entries.passive: restricted. Clinical and technical writing allows it (the protocol was deviated from in two cases), but ordinary prose does not: ✗ the checklist must not be deviated from, ✗ the filed route was deviated from by the pilot.
entries.see also: depart from · diverge from · differ from · derogate from · from

entries.meaning: Pass down to somebody by default, succession, or operation of law.
examples: On his death the estate devolved on his sister.
If the chair resigns, the duties devolve upon the ranking member.
Responsibility for the audit devolved on the one accountant who had not quit.
Under the 1998 act, substantial powers were devolved to the regional assemblies.
The title devolves upon the eldest surviving child, whatever the will says.
Everything the founder used to handle personally has devolved on a committee.
entries.русский: переходить к кому-то по наследству или по закону; юр./книжн.
entries.register: formal and legal — wills, constitutions, and successions; an American meets it in an estate document or a line about who takes over when an office falls vacant
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the person or body that receives the duty, estate, or power. No gerund, no infinitive, no clause: ✗ the duty devolved on running the office. The subject is the thing handed down — a duty, a title, an estate, an authority — not the person taking it.
entries.variants: Devolve upon is the same pattern in a more formal key, and older drafting prefers it. Devolve to appears where the point is transfer downward to a smaller unit — powers devolved to the states, devolved government. Keep all three apart from devolve into, which is the everyday word meaning degenerate.
entries.pattern: [a duty, an estate, a title] devolve on / upon [someone] · [powers] be devolved to [a body] · devolve into [chaos, a shouting match] — a different sense · devolution of [power] — the noun
entries.contrast: Devolve on is passive inheritance; delegate to is a deliberate handoff. A responsibility devolves on whoever is left standing; a manager delegates it to somebody chosen. And devolve into is not this word at all — the meeting devolved into a shouting match means it deteriorated, and swapping the prepositions produces nonsense: ✗ the chairmanship devolved into the vice chair. In plain American English the whole first sense is usually fall to: the job fell to me.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an event of passing down by succession or default: on his death the estate devolved on his sister. Keep it apart from devolve into, meaning degenerate.
entries.transitivity: both by frame — intransitive with on / upon, where the duty or estate is the subject (✗ his sister devolved on the estate); transitive in devolve powers to a body, where the power is an object.
entries.passive: restricted. Only the devolve X to Y frame passivizes, and there it is standard: substantial powers were devolved to the regional assemblies. The on frame refuses: ✗ his sister was devolved on, ✗ the ranking member was devolved upon.
entries.see also: impose on, impose upon · preside over · inhere in · belong to · upon

entries.meaning: Stop living — and the preposition names the cause.
examples: Her grandfather died of emphysema at eighty-one.
Two firefighters died from smoke inhalation.
He nearly died of embarrassment when the microphone stayed on.
Thousands died from the complications rather than the infection itself.
She died in a crash on the interstate.
I'm dying of thirst — is there anything cold in there?
entries.русский: умирать от — предлог называет причину смерти
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (died from falling) — never a to-infinitive, never a clause. Die also takes for (a cause), in (an event or place), and by in a small set of fixed phrases (die by suicide, die by the sword).
entries.pattern: die of [a disease, a condition] · die from [an injury, a cause, complications] · die for [a cause] · die in [a crash, a fire, a war] · be dying to [verb] — idiom, infinitive
entries.contrast: Die of and die from overlap heavily in American English and reversing them will not confuse anyone. The tendency, not a rule: of goes with diseases and internal conditions (died of pancreatic cancer, died of a heart attack), from with external causes, injuries, and chains of consequence (died from his injuries, died from complications of surgery). Die by is restricted — by suicide, by fire, by his own hand — and died by suicide is now the preferred American phrasing over the older committed suicide. Note the hyperboles, which take of: dying of thirst, died of embarrassment.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an event, not a state, and the progressive is normal both literally (he was dying from the injuries) and in hyperbole: I'm dying of thirst.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no object of any kind; the cause is always in a prepositional phrase (of, from, in, by, for). ✗ he died emphysema.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is no passive at all: ✗ emphysema was died of, ✗ smoke inhalation was died from by two firefighters. For an agent, switch verbs: two firefighters were killed by smoke inhalation.
entries.see also: suffer from · recover from · result from · save from

entries.meaning: Be unlike something else — or, with with, disagree.
examples: This year's model differs from last year's in almost every respect.
American practice differs from the European standard here.
The two accounts differ from each other on every material point.
Her reading of the statute differs from mine in one important way.
I differ with him about how much of this the public needs to see.
On the question of timing, reasonable people differ.
entries.русский: отличаться от — быть непохожим; differ with расходиться во мнениях
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause. Differ is intransitive and never takes an object: ✗ differ the other model. In the disagree sense it takes with: I differ with her on that. The related adjective takes its own preposition — see the contrast.
entries.pattern: [A] differ from [B] · [A] differ from [B] in [respect] · differ with [someone] on / about [something] · differ (plural subject, alone): opinions differ
entries.variants: different from — the safe standard everywhere · different than — established American, and the natural form before a clause · different to — British; avoid in American writing
entries.contrast: The adjective is where the trouble is. Different from is standard everywhere and always safe. Different than is fully established in American English, and is the natural choice before a clause (a different city than I remembered), where from forces an awkward rewrite. Different to is British and sounds wrong to American ears. The verb itself allows only from for unlikeness — ✗ differs than, ✗ differs to — and with only when people disagree: the two economists differ with each other about the cause.
entries.verb type: stative — unlikeness is a static fact, not an event, and the progressive is out: ✗ this year's model is differing from last year's.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — never takes an object (✗ differ the other model); with a plural subject the preposition can drop: opinions differ. Disagreement takes with: I differ with him about the timing.
entries.passive: no. Stative and objectless, it has no passive: ✗ last year's model is differed from, ✗ mine is differed from by her reading of the statute.
entries.see also: compare with · separate from · compete with · different from · from

entries.meaning: Think that something is wrong or unacceptable.
examples: My mother disapproved of the whole arrangement and said so once, at length.
He disapproves of eating at your desk.
The faculty disapproved of the change but voted for it anyway.
She disapproved of his taking the money.
Nobody actually disapproves of a shorter meeting.
They disapprove of almost everything the new coach does.
entries.русский: не одобрять — считать неправильным или неприемлемым
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or possessive plus gerund (disapproved of her going) — never a to-infinitive (✗ disapprove of to go) and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: disapprove of [noun phrase] · disapprove of [verb-ing] · disapprove of [someone] -ing · disapprove (alone) · a disapproving look
entries.contrast: Unlike approve, disapprove has no ordinary transitive use. The board approved the budget is authorization; ✗ The board disapproved the budget is not the mirror image American editors want — write rejected or voted down. So disapprove survives almost entirely in the of frame, where it means think badly of. Note the register: it is a mild, slightly prim word, which is why she disapproves of him is funnier than she dislikes him.
entries.verb type: stative — a settled attitude rather than an act; the progressive is marginal (?she is disapproving of the arrangement), though the participle is common as an adjective: a disapproving look.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with a fixed of — and, unlike approve, it has no ordinary transitive use: ✗ the board disapproved the budget (write rejected). The verb can stand alone: she disapproves, loudly.
entries.passive: restricted. The prepositional passive is grammatical but stiff — ?his taking the money was disapproved of — and the participle survives mainly as a modifier: a disapproved-of arrangement. ✗ he is disapproved of by my mother is best rewritten.
entries.see also: approve of · object to · complain about · comment on

entries.meaning: Try to persuade someone not to do something.
examples: The counselor discouraged him from taking five APs at once.
Steep fees discourage small filers from appealing at all.
She was discouraged from applying by an advisor who barely knew her.
Nothing discourages a reader from finishing a book like a bad first paragraph.
The policy is designed to discourage people from driving downtown.
Don't let one rejection discourage you from sending it out again.
entries.русский: отговаривать от — убеждать не делать чего-то; после from герундий
entries.complement: gerund or noun phrase (discouraged him from applying) — never a to-infinitive (✗ discouraged him to apply). This is the classic asymmetry: encourage takes an infinitive and discourage takes from plus -ing.
entries.pattern: discourage [someone] from [verb-ing] · discourage [an activity] · be discouraged from [verb-ing] · encourage [someone] to [verb] — the mirror pattern
entries.contrast: The pair does not mirror. Encourage her to apply / discourage her from applying — same idea, opposite structures, and ✗ discourage her to apply is one of the most persistent advanced errors in English. The same shape governs prevent from, stop from, keep from, ban from, prohibit from, and bar from: all of them take from plus -ing while their positive counterparts take an infinitive. Note also that discourage has a plain transitive use meaning dishearten (the results discouraged her), which takes no preposition.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an act of persuading someone away from something: steep fees discourage small filers from appealing. The plain transitive sense (dishearten) is dynamic too: the results discouraged her.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person is the direct object and from plus -ing follows; the object is obligatory: ✗ the policy discourages from driving downtown.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is very common: she was discouraged from applying by an advisor who barely knew her, filers are discouraged from appealing at all.
entries.see also: prevent from · punish for · allow for · protect from

entries.meaning: Get rid of something, sell it off, or settle a matter finally.
examples: There is a fee for disposing of paint and motor oil.
The estate had to dispose of the house before the taxes came due.
The panel disposed of the objection in two sentences.
Nobody could say how the company disposed of the old servers.
She disposed of her shares the week before the merger closed.
He disposed of the last three questions without looking at his notes.
entries.русский: избавляться от; распродавать; окончательно решать (дело); книжн. к get rid of
entries.register: neutral to formal — waste rules, estate documents, and court dockets
entries.complement: noun phrase naming what is being got rid of, sold, or settled: dispose of the packaging, dispose of the assets, dispose of the motion. A gerund is rare and stiff (dispose of having to store it), and there is no infinitive and no clause: ✗ dispose of to sell the house. The preposition is fixed and the object never moves: ✗ dispose the trash of.
entries.pattern: dispose of [waste, property, a body, an argument, a case] · be disposed of [properly, at auction] · dispose [someone] to [something] — a different verb · be disposed to [verb] — an adjective with an infinitive · at [someone's] disposal — the noun
entries.contrast: Dispose of is the formal twin of get rid of, and it does three jobs: throw away (dispose of the solvent), sell off (dispose of the property), and settle for good (the court disposed of the appeal in a footnote). Keep it clear of be disposed to, which is an adjective meaning inclined and takes an infinitive: disposed to agree, never ✗ disposed to agreeing. And the noun is disposal — the disposal of hazardous waste, the money at your disposal.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: throwing away, selling off, and settling a matter for good (the panel disposed of the objection in two sentences).
entries.transitivity: intransitive with a fixed of — nothing may come between verb and preposition (✗ dispose the trash of), and the of is not optional: ✗ dispose the old servers. Keep it clear of the adjective be disposed to + infinitive.
entries.passive: yes — the prepositional passive is standard: paint and motor oil must be disposed of at the transfer station, the appeal was disposed of in a footnote.
entries.see also: get rid of · divest of · deprive of · take care of · of

entries.meaning: Move apart, or come to differ, from something you started out matching.
examples: The bike path diverges from the highway just past the reservoir.
Her account diverges from his in every detail that matters.
After 1994 the two economies diverged from one another for good.
This year's figures diverge from the model's forecast by a wide margin.
The screenplay diverges from the novel about halfway through.
Where the sources diverge, the footnote says so.
entries.русский: расходиться с — начать отличаться от того, чему прежде соответствовал
entries.register: neutral to formal — mathematics, data, narrative, and commentary
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a path, a text, a norm, or another account. A gerund is unidiomatic (✗ diverged from following the trail), and there is no infinitive and no clause. The verb is very often intransitive with a plural subject and no preposition at all: the two roads diverge, their estimates diverge sharply.
entries.pattern: diverge from [a route, an account, the consensus] · [two things] diverge — intransitive · diverge on / over [a question] — disagree about · a divergence from [the mean] · divergent [views]
entries.contrast: Four verbs, one preposition, four pictures. Diverge from is a gradual parting of two things that started together; deviate from is a step off a path you were required to keep to; depart from is a deliberate break with a practice or a text; differ from is not motion at all, only unlikeness. So the trail diverges from the creek (they separate), the driver deviated from the route (he broke a rule), the opinion departs from precedent (a considered break), my copy differs from yours (a static fact). Its opposite is converge, which takes on or toward rather than from.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic where two things gradually part (the bike path diverges from the highway), stative where it reports a fixed unlikeness: her account diverges from his in every detail.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no object (✗ diverge the route), and with a plural subject the preposition drops entirely: where the sources diverge, the footnote says so.
entries.passive: no. There is nothing to promote: ✗ the highway is diverged from by the bike path, ✗ the model's forecast was diverged from.
entries.see also: deviate from · depart from · differ from · derive from · from

entries.meaning: Give up a holding, a power, or an illusion — usually deliberately and formally.
examples: The company divested itself of three regional papers in a single quarter.
Cabinet nominees are expected to divest themselves of conflicting holdings.
The statute divested the board of any say in the appointment.
Two decades on the road had divested him of every romantic idea about touring.
The endowment finally voted to divest from coal and tar sands.
Once divested of its patents, the firm was worth very little.
entries.русский: лишать(ся) чего-то, продавать (активы, доли); фин./юр.
entries.register: formal — securities filings, trust documents, and university endowment fights; the literary sense (divested of illusions) belongs to essays rather than speech
entries.complement: a person, company, or fund is the object, and of takes a noun phrase naming what is given up: holdings, powers, a title, illusions. A gerund is rare (divested itself of having to run the plant), and there is no infinitive and no clause. The reflexive frame is extremely common: divest itself of the subsidiary.
entries.variants: Divest from — the trustees voted to divest from fossil fuels — has become standard American usage in the divestment-campaign sense, where the object of the verb disappears and from names the sector being exited. Older editors still prefer divest itself of, but divest from is now the ordinary way the argument is phrased.
entries.pattern: divest [someone / a fund] of [holdings, power, a title] · divest oneself of [something] · be divested of [something] · divest from [a sector] · divestiture / divestment of [assets] — the nouns keep of
entries.contrast: Divest of removes something formally; deprive of takes it away against your interest. A board divests itself of a money-losing division on purpose; a storm deprives a town of power. Rob of and strip of are the hostile members of the same family, and get rid of is the plain-English one. Note that the of is not optional in the transitive frame: ✗ divested the subsidiary means something quite different — that you sold the subsidiary itself.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a deliberate and usually formal act: the company divested itself of three regional papers in a single quarter.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person, fund, or company is the direct object (very often a reflexive) and of names what is given up; the of phrase is not optional: ✗ divested the subsidiary means something else. Divest from a sector drops the object.
entries.passive: yes: the board was divested of any say in the appointment, once divested of its patents, the firm was worth very little.
entries.see also: deprive of · rob of · dispose of · get rid of · of

entries.meaning: Use a store of money, experience, or material as a source.
examples: The essay draws on three unpublished diaries.
They had to draw on savings for the second year of treatment.
She draws on twenty years in emergency medicine every time she teaches.
The company drew on its credit line to make payroll in February.
His novels draw upon a childhood he describes only obliquely.
The report draws on interviews with forty-one former employees.
entries.русский: черпать из — использовать запас денег, опыта или материала как источник
entries.register: neutral to formal — scholarship, journalism, and banking (draw on a line of credit)
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a resource — savings, experience, sources, a reserve — or a gerund (drew on having run a kitchen for ten years). No to-infinitive (✗ draw on to have run a kitchen) and no clause. The preposition is fixed, not a movable particle: ✗ draw my savings on, ✗ draw it on.
entries.variants: Draw upon is the same pattern one register higher, common in academic prose and prefaces; the meaning is identical.
entries.pattern: draw on / upon [a resource, an account, experience] · draw [something] from [a source] · draw down [a balance] · draw on — intransitive, of time (as evening drew on)
entries.contrast: Do not confuse the fixed draw on with the separable phrasal verbs. Draw up a contract, draw out a meeting, and draw in a crowd all allow the object to move — draw the contract up — which is what makes their second words particles rather than prepositions; those belong with the phrasal verbs, not here. This draw on never separates. Note the sister frame draw [something] from [a source] — drew her material from letters — where the resource follows from and what you took becomes the object. And as evening drew on is a third, intransitive verb meaning approach.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; using up a store of money, material, or experience: they had to draw on savings for the second year of treatment. The unrelated intransitive as evening drew on means approach.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with a fixed preposition — the object never moves (✗ draw my savings on, ✗ draw it on), which is what separates it from the separable draw up / draw out. The sister frame draw something from a source is transitive.
entries.passive: yes — the prepositional passive is natural in reports: the credit line had already been drawn on twice, three unpublished diaries are drawn on throughout.
entries.see also: rely on · depend on · count on · derive from · on

entries.meaning: See something while asleep, or long for something while awake.
examples: I dreamed about that house for years after we sold it.
She dreams of opening a bakery somewhere with a real winter.
He dreamed that every tooth in his head fell out at once.
They dreamed of going back and never did.
I wouldn't dream of charging you for that.
Half the class dreams about the exam the night before it.
entries.русский: видеть во сне (about); мечтать о (of)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (dreamed of playing at Carnegie Hall) — never a to-infinitive (✗ dream of to play there). A clause takes no preposition: dreamed that the house was on fire. American English prefers dreamed; dreamt is chiefly British.
entries.pattern: dream about [what happened in a dream] · dream of [an ambition] · dream of / about [verb-ing] · dream that [clause] · wouldn't dream of [verb-ing] · dream up [an idea]
entries.contrast: Dream about reports what your sleeping brain did; dream of names what your waking self wants. I dreamed about my old apartment is a night's event; I dream of a corner office is an ambition. The two overlap freely for daydreaming (dreaming about / of retirement), but the fixed idiom takes only of: I wouldn't dream of asking means I would never — note the gerund, since ✗ wouldn't dream of to ask is impossible.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; the progressive is normal for sleeping (half the class is dreaming about the exam) and for wishing: she's been dreaming of opening a bakery for years.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with the fixed prepositions — no bare object here (✗ dream the old apartment); a clause takes no preposition (dreamed that every tooth fell out), and dream up an idea is a separate transitive phrasal verb.
entries.passive: no. Neither frame passivizes: ✗ that house was dreamed about for years, ✗ a bakery is dreamed of by her. Only the attributive participle survives: the long dreamed-of bakery.
entries.see also: hope for · long for · wish for · think about · plan on

entries.meaning: Wear, or put on, a particular kind of clothing.
examples: She came to the reading dressed in head-to-toe corduroy.
Everyone at the funeral was dressed in black except the deceased's brother.
He dresses in the same three shirts on rotation.
The kids came dressed as characters from books nobody had read.
Dress for the weather; it's supposed to drop twenty degrees by four.
The waiters were dressed in white jackets that had clearly seen better decades.
entries.русский: одеваться во что-то — носить одежду определённого вида
entries.complement: noun phrase naming clothing or a color — no gerund, no clause. As takes a character or role (dressed as a pirate), and up as is the costume version. Dress on its own is intransitive (dress warmly) or transitive with a person (dress the baby), and takes no preposition either way.
entries.pattern: be dressed in [clothing / a color] · dress in [a style] · dress as / up as [a character] · dress [someone] · dress for [an occasion, the weather] · dress up / down
entries.contrast: Dressed in is about the clothes; dressed as is about who you are pretending to be. Dressed in black describes fabric; dressed as a nun describes a costume. Dress for names the occasion or condition you are dressing to suit (dress for the weather, dress for the job you want). Note that dressed with is wrong for clothing but right for salad — dressed with a little vinaigrette — and that dress down means both wear casual clothes and reprimand someone.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic when someone does the dressing (he dresses in the same three shirts, dress the baby); the far commoner be dressed in is a resultant state, close to an adjective: everyone was dressed in black.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with a manner or a for phrase (dress warmly, dress for the weather), transitive with a person or a reflexive (dress the baby, she dressed herself). In takes the clothing, never a bare object: ✗ dress black.
entries.passive: yes, though most examples are stative rather than eventive: she came to the reading dressed in head-to-toe corduroy describes a state, while the child was dressed by her father is a true action passive.
entries.see also: cover with · provide with · in · as

entries.meaning: Say more about something you have already mentioned.
examples: Would you elaborate on the second recommendation?
She declined to elaborate on the reasons for her resignation.
The memo elaborates on a policy that had been one sentence long.
He elaborated on being the only engineer in a building full of salespeople.
The witness was asked to elaborate on what he had seen from the porch.
I'd rather not elaborate in front of the whole committee.
entries.русский: развивать мысль о — рассказывать подробнее о уже сказанном
entries.register: neutral, common in interviews, seminars, and reporting
entries.complement: noun phrase (elaborate on the second point), gerund (elaborate on being passed over), or a wh-clause (elaborate on what went wrong) — never a to-infinitive (✗ elaborate on to explain the delay) and never a that-clause: ✗ elaborate on that the delay was ours. The verb also stands alone with no object (Could you elaborate?), and there it takes no preposition at all.
entries.variants: Elaborate upon is the formal-register twin, at home in an academic paper or a brief; the meaning is identical, and on is what an American says.
entries.pattern: elaborate on / upon [a point, a claim, a topic] · elaborate on [verb-ing] · elaborate — intransitive · elaborate [a theory, a design] — transitive, meaning develop in detail
entries.contrast: Elaborate on and expand on are interchangeable; comment on is a step lighter, meaning simply to say something about a subject rather than to say more about it. Watch two things. First, transitive elaborate exists and means something else — elaborate a theory is to work it out in detail, not to say more about it. Second, explain takes no preposition before the thing explained (explain the rule, ✗ explain on the rule); the to in explain to me points at the listener, not the topic. And the adjective elaborate is stressed differently: /ɪˈlæbərət/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of saying more; progressive fine: he's elaborating on a point nobody questioned. The transitive homonym (elaborate a theory, work it out in detail) is dynamic too.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with on / upon and also with nothing at all (Could you elaborate?); transitive in the develop-in-detail sense: elaborate a design.
entries.passive: restricted. The prepositional passive is acceptable in formal prose — the second recommendation was elaborated on at length — and the transitive sense passivizes freely: a theory elaborated over three decades.
entries.see also: comment on · explain to · concentrate on · refer to · on

entries.meaning: Advance gradually onto somebody else's land, rights, or time.
examples: The new deck encroaches on the setback by almost two feet.
He argued that the ordinance encroaches on rights the state constitution protects.
Work has begun to encroach on the one evening a week she keeps for herself.
Sagebrush is encroaching upon what used to be grassland.
The agency's new rule encroaches on territory Congress reserved to the states.
Each department resented any attempt to encroach on its budget.
entries.русский: посягать на, вторгаться в — понемногу захватывать чужое
entries.register: formal-leaning — property law, zoning disputes, and civil-liberties commentary. An American most often meets it in a survey report (the fence encroaches on the neighbor's lot) or an editorial about government power.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming territory, a right, a domain, or time. A gerund is possible but uncommon (encroaching on having any evening to yourself); no to-infinitive (✗ encroach on to take his land) and no clause. The subject is usually a thing — a fence, a program, a deadline — rather than a person acting deliberately.
entries.variants: Encroach upon is the same pattern in a higher register and is common in judicial writing. The noun keeps the preposition: an encroachment on / upon [something].
entries.pattern: encroach on / upon [land, rights, authority, time] · an encroachment on [a right] · encroach — intransitive, of vegetation or development
entries.contrast: Encroach on is gradual advance across a line; infringe on is violation of a right. A hedge encroaches on a driveway inch by inch, but a knockoff infringes on a trademark the moment it ships. Impinge on is the physics-flavored version (one thing pressing against another), intrude on is social (intrude on a private conversation), and interfere with is the most general. All four resist the direct object: ✗ encroach the property line.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and gradual, which is why the progressive suits it: sagebrush is encroaching upon what used to be grassland. The subject is typically a thing, not a deliberate agent.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object (✗ encroach the property line), like infringe on, impinge on, and intrude on.
entries.passive: restricted. The participle is the usable form — rights constantly encroached upon, land encroached on by development — while a full clause sounds labored: ?the setback is being encroached on by the new deck.
entries.see also: infringe on, infringe upon · impose on, impose upon · interfere with, interfere in · on

entries.meaning: Get away from confinement, danger, or something unpleasant.
examples: Two inmates escaped from the county facility on a Sunday morning.
She escaped from the meeting by inventing a dentist appointment.
Everyone in the front car escaped serious injury.
He spent his twenties trying to escape from the town he grew up in.
The detail had escaped everyone's notice until the audit.
The name escapes me, but I'd know the face.
entries.русский: убегать из, спасаться от — вырываться из заточения или опасности
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (escaped from having to testify) — never a to-infinitive, never a clause. But the verb also has a transitive use with no preposition at all: escape injury, escape prosecution, escape notice — and there the from would be wrong.
entries.pattern: escape from [a place, a captor, a situation] · escape [a fate, notice, detection] — no preposition · escape to [somewhere] · [something] escape [someone] — elude the memory
entries.contrast: Escape from a place, but escape a consequence. You escape from prison, a burning car, or a bad marriage — a thing you were physically or literally inside. You escape injury, blame, punishment, or someone's notice — no preposition, because you were never inside those. Both are correct; using from with the second group (✗ escaped from injury) is the error. Note the idiom it escapes me, meaning I can't recall it, which is the transitive sense turned around.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an event of getting away: two inmates escaped from the county facility. The idiom the name escapes me is stative.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with from before a place or captor, transitive with no preposition before a consequence: escape serious injury, escape notice; ✗ escaped from injury.
entries.passive: no in either frame, despite the transitivity: ✗ serious injury was escaped, ✗ the audit's notice had been escaped by the detail, ✗ the county facility was escaped from. Rewrite as avoided or went unnoticed.
entries.see also: recover from · prevent from · hide from · rescue from · save from

entries.meaning: Forgive a small offense, or release someone from an obligation.
examples: Excuse me for asking, but is any of this actually funded?
The judge excused two jurors from service.
You'll have to excuse the mess.
Nothing excuses the way he spoke to her.
She was excused from gym for the rest of the semester.
There is no excuse for sending it out unproofed.
entries.русский: прощать за (небольшую провинность) — а excuse from освобождать от обязанности
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase or a gerund (excuse me for interrupting) — never a to-infinitive (✗ excuse me for to interrupt). from takes a duty or requirement. The person excused is a direct object and takes no preposition: ✗ excuse to me.
entries.pattern: excuse [someone] for [something / verb-ing] · excuse [someone] from [a duty] · excuse [someone] · excuse [behavior] · Excuse me · there's no excuse for [something]
entries.contrast: Excuse for forgives; excuse from releases. The dean excused her for the late filing means it was forgiven; The dean excused her from the requirement means she doesn't have to do it. Both are standard, and mixing them (✗ excused from the late filing) says something else. Note that excuse takes the person directly — like forgive and thank, unlike apologize, which needs to. The noun keeps for: no excuse for that.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a performative act of forgiving or releasing: the judge excused two jurors from service.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person is the direct object with no preposition (✗ excuse to me), and for or from follows. Excuse also takes a bare thing as object: you'll have to excuse the mess.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the usual frame for the from sense: she was excused from gym for the rest of the semester, he was excused for the late filing.
entries.see also: forgive for · apologize for · blame for · punish for · thank for

entries.meaning: Make something clear to someone.
examples: Could you explain the billing cycle to me one more time?
She explained to the board why the pilot had run over budget.
He never explained himself and never had to.
Try explaining that to a nine-year-old.
The letter explains to applicants exactly what documentation is required.
Nobody could explain the discrepancy to the auditors.
entries.русский: объяснять кому-то — только explain smth to smb, не ✗ explain me smth
entries.complement: to takes the person hearing it, and the person always needs it: ✗ explain me the rules. The thing explained is a direct object, a that-clause, or a wh-clause: explain the rules, explain that the rules changed, explain how it works. A gerund is possible as the object (explain being late) but a to-infinitive is not.
entries.pattern: explain [something] to [someone] · explain to [someone] that / how / why [clause] · explain [something] · explain [oneself]
entries.contrast: Explain me something is one of the most persistent errors in English, because explain looks like tell and behaves like say. Tell, give, show, send, and offer take the person as a bare indirect object — tell me the rules — while explain, say, describe, suggest, mention, announce, report, and introduce all require to: explain the rules to me, say it to me, describe it to me. When the explanation is long, put the person first: explain to the class why the second method fails.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; progressive is normal: try explaining that to a nine-year-old.
entries.transitivity: transitive, but never ditransitive — the thing explained is the direct object and the hearer must take to: explain the rules to me, ✗ explain me the rules. The object may be a that- or wh-clause: explained to the board why the pilot ran over budget.
entries.passive: yes — the thing explained promotes: the billing cycle was explained to me twice. The hearer never does: ✗ I was explained the billing cycle, one of the most persistent errors in English.
entries.see also: introduce to · refer to · comment on · apologize to

entries.meaning: Project a known pattern beyond the evidence you actually have.
examples: It's a mistake to extrapolate from one unusually warm winter.
The team extrapolated the growth curve from eighteen months of billing data.
Nothing in the sample lets you extrapolate from the city to the state as a whole.
She extrapolated from two cases and got the policy badly wrong.
Forecasters extrapolate from the last five days of ice loss, which is why the numbers move so much.
Extrapolating from the pilot program, the district projected a shortfall of $4 million.
entries.русский: экстраполировать из — переносить известную закономерность за пределы данных
entries.register: neutral-technical — statistics, forecasting, lab work, and business planning
entries.complement: from takes a noun phrase naming the data or the case you are reasoning out of, or a gerund (extrapolating from having seen two quarters of it). No to-infinitive (✗ extrapolate from to see two quarters) and no clause. What is projected may appear as a direct object before from: extrapolate a trend from the sample.
entries.pattern: extrapolate from [data, a sample, one case] · extrapolate [a trend, a value] from [data] · extrapolate [a curve] to [a future point] · extrapolation from [the data] — the noun keeps from
entries.contrast: Extrapolate from projects past the edge of your data; interpolate fills in between points you already have. Against the reasoning verbs: deduce from claims certainty from a premise, infer from claims probability from evidence, and extrapolate from claims a continuation of a pattern — which is why it so often carries a warning: you can't extrapolate from a single quarter. Note the second preposition in the technical frame: you extrapolate from the known values to the unknown one.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of projection: forecasters extrapolate from the last five days of ice loss; progressive and participle both normal.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with from alone (it's a mistake to extrapolate from one warm winter), transitive when the projected thing is named: extrapolate a trend from the sample.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive frame: the growth curve was extrapolated from eighteen months of billing data. The prepositional passive is weaker: ?a single quarter should not be extrapolated from.
entries.see also: infer from · deduce from · derive from · follow from · from

entries.term: face up to, back out of, drop out of, walk out on
entries.meaning: Confront something unpleasant, or withdraw from a commitment — four fixed three-word verbs on the same frame.
examples: At some point he is going to have to face up to what the surgery costs.
She never faced up to being the reason the partnership dissolved.
The buyer backed out of the deal two days before closing.
Half the cohort dropped out of the program in the first semester.
He walked out on the negotiation and did not come back.
Nobody walks out on a pension that size without a plan.
They backed out of renovating and sold the place as it stood.
entries.русский: признать и принять (face up to); отступиться — back out of, drop out of, walk out on
entries.register: informal to neutral — ordinary spoken American English
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after the final preposition — face up to being broke, backed out of buying the house, dropped out of teaching altogether, walked out on a twenty-year marriage. Never a to-infinitive (✗ face up to be broke, ✗ back out of to buy it) and never a clause. Each of the four takes its own kind of object: face up to a fact or a failing, back out of an agreement, drop out of a school or a process, walk out on a person or a commitment.
entries.pattern: face up to [a fact, a mistake, a debt] · back out of [a deal, a wedding, a promise] · drop out of [school, a race, the workforce] · walk out on [a spouse, a job, a negotiation] · [any of them] + [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: These are three-part verbs, and the giveaway is that the object cannot move. With a genuine separable particle you have a choice — turn the light on or turn on the light, throw the mail out or throw out the mail — and those belong to the phrasal-verb discussion rather than to this file, because the second word is a particle, not a preposition. Here the whole string is welded together: ✗ face it up to, ✗ back the deal out of, ✗ drop school out of, ✗ walk his wife out on. The final word behaves exactly like the dependent prepositions in the rest of this file, which is why a gerund follows it and an infinitive never does. Note the two-part relatives that mean something else: face the music (no preposition), back out with no object (he backed out at the last minute), drop out alone (she dropped out in March), and walk out alone (the union walked out).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, all four; each names a deliberate move, and the progressive is normal: he's backing out of the deal, she's dropping out of the program.
entries.transitivity: intransitive three-part verbs — the object follows the final preposition and can never move: ✗ face it up to, ✗ back the deal out of, ✗ walk his wife out on. Each takes its own object type: a fact, an agreement, a school, a person.
entries.passive: restricted. Back out of and walk out on passivize in speech (the deal was backed out of two days before closing, nobody likes being walked out on); face up to and drop out of resist: ✗ the debt was faced up to, ✗ the program was dropped out of.
entries.see also: put up with · get away with · keep up with, catch up with, catch up on · live up to · look up to, look down on

entries.meaning: Be a logical consequence of something already established.
examples: Nothing in the report follows from the data they actually collected.
It follows from the first assumption that the payments cannot both be optional.
