The conclusion follows from the premises only if the sample was random.
Two corollaries follow from the theorem, and neither is obvious.
Does it follow from his silence that he agreed? It does not.
Everything else in the argument follows from that one definition.
entries.русский: следовать из — быть логическим следствием
entries.complement: from takes a noun phrase naming a premise, an assumption, or an earlier result, or a gerund (follows from assuming the rate is constant). No to-infinitive and no clause after the preposition. The subject is the conclusion, and the commonest frame puts it in a dummy it: it follows from the first two lemmas that the series converges.
entries.pattern: [a conclusion] follow from [a premise] · it follows from [X] that [clause] · it follows that [clause] · follow [a rule, a recipe, a car] — transitive, no preposition
entries.contrast: Follow from is logical consequence, not sequence. B follows A means B comes next; B follows from A means B is entailed by A, and the from is doing all the work. Keep it apart from transitive follow (follow the instructions, ✗ follow to the instructions) and from follow up on (follow up on the complaint), which means chase a matter further. The British follow on from — following on from last week's memo — is not American usage; write following or further to. Against the neighbors: result from names a real-world outcome, stem from names a cause, and follow from names an entailment.
entries.verb type: stative — logical entailment, not an event; the progressive is out: ✗ the conclusion is following from the premises.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no object (✗ follow the premises in this sense, which is a different verb), and the commonest frame is a dummy subject: it follows from the first two lemmas that the series converges.
entries.passive: no. Stative and objectless: ✗ the premises are followed from by the conclusion, ✗ that one definition is followed from. Transitive follow (the instructions were followed) is a different verb.
entries.see also: result in, result from · stem from · deduce from · infer from · from

entries.meaning: Take back mortgaged property after the borrower stops paying — or, transitively, rule something out.
examples: The bank foreclosed on the property after eleven months of missed payments.
Three houses on that block were foreclosed on in the same year.
They refinanced twice to keep the credit union from foreclosing on them.
Nobody wants to foreclose on a family with two kids in the local school.
The decision forecloses any argument that the deadline was advisory.
Filing late does not foreclose the claim entirely.
entries.русский: обращать взыскание на (заложенное имущество); исключать (возможность)
entries.register: neutral — banking, real estate, and the courts
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the property, the loan, or the borrower: foreclose on the house, on the mortgage, on the family. No gerund (✗ foreclose on missing three payments), no infinitive, and no clause. The verb also appears with no object at all (the bank moved to foreclose).
entries.pattern: foreclose on [a property, a mortgage, a borrower] · foreclose — intransitive · foreclose [an option, a possibility, an argument] — transitive, no preposition · foreclosure on [a home] — the noun keeps on
entries.contrast: The financial sense takes on; the abstract sense usually takes nothing. A lender forecloses on a house, but a ruling forecloses an argument — direct object, no preposition — and the statute forecloses that reading is the standard legal phrasing. (Foreclose on the possibility does occur, and nobody will misunderstand it, but the bare transitive is cleaner.) Note the sequence in ordinary use: a borrower defaults on the loan, the bank forecloses on the property, and the house is then disposed of at auction.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a legal process with a date: the bank foreclosed on the property after eleven months of missed payments; progressive normal: the credit union is foreclosing on them.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with on in the financial sense, and with no object at all (the bank moved to foreclose); transitive with no preposition in the abstract sense: the decision forecloses any argument that the deadline was advisory.
entries.passive: yes in both frames, and the entry uses it: three houses on that block were foreclosed on in the same year, the argument is foreclosed by the decision.
entries.see also: default on · dispose of · petition for · sue for · on

entries.meaning: Stop holding something against someone.
examples: She never quite forgave him for missing the funeral.
Forgive me for asking, but how much did that cost?
He was forgiven for the first two lapses and fired for the third.
You could be forgiven for thinking the building was abandoned.
The lender agreed to forgive half the balance.
I forgive you, but I'm not forgetting it.
entries.русский: прощать за — перестать держать обиду (человек без предлога: forgive me for)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (forgive her for missing it) — never a to-infinitive (✗ forgive her for to miss it). The person forgiven is a direct object: ✗ forgive to her. An older two-object frame survives in fixed religious language: forgive us our trespasses.
entries.pattern: forgive [someone] for [something / verb-ing] · forgive [someone] · forgive [a debt, a loan] · forgive [someone] [something] — formal, fixed · You could be forgiven for [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Like excuse and thank, forgive takes the person directly and the offense with for — ✗ forgive to someone and ✗ forgive about something are both wrong. Note the specialized financial sense: forgive a loan means cancel the obligation, and takes no preposition at all. And note the useful hedge you could be forgiven for thinking — always with a gerund — which is how American writers concede a reasonable misreading.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic as an act (I forgive you), and the resulting be forgiven is a state. Progressive is rare but possible: she's slowly forgiving him for it.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person is the direct object with no preposition (✗ forgive to her) and the offense takes for. A frozen ditransitive survives in religious language: forgive us our trespasses. The financial sense takes a thing: forgive a loan.
entries.passive: yes, and one passive is a fixed hedge: you could be forgiven for thinking the building was abandoned. Also he was forgiven for the first two lapses and fired for the third.
entries.see also: excuse for · apologize to · blame for · punish for · thank for

entries.meaning: Have an easy enough relationship with somebody.
examples: She gets along with everyone on the crew except the foreman.
The two of them have never gotten along, and the trip did not help.
He gets along with his ex better now than when they were married.
New hires who get along with the schedulers get the shifts they want.
Do you think you could get along with someone that particular for six months?
They got along without air conditioning for thirty summers.
entries.русский: ладить с — уживаться с человеком; разг.
entries.register: informal to neutral — the ordinary American way to talk about relationships at work and at home
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person or group — get along with your sister, with the new manager, with everybody. No gerund (✗ get along with working nights) and no clause; if you want a manner, use an adverb instead: they get along fine. The string is fixed and the object never moves: ✗ get her along with.
entries.pattern: get along with [a person, a group] · get along — intransitive (they get along) · get along without [something] — manage · get along — of age or time (getting along in years)
entries.contrast: Get along with is about the relationship; go along with is about agreeing. You can get along with a colleague you never go along with. The British get on with someone means the same as get along with, but in American English get on with it means only stop stalling. And note the third member of the family, get along without, which means manage in the absence of something: we got along without a car for a year.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic enough to take the progressive (they're getting along better lately), but it reports an ongoing relationship rather than an event, so it is close to stative in the habitual present: she gets along with everyone on the crew.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — a fixed string with no direct-object slot (✗ get her along with); it stands alone with a plural subject: the two of them have never gotten along.
entries.passive: no. The idiom cannot be passivized: ✗ the foreman isn't gotten along with, ✗ the schedulers are gotten along with by new hires.
entries.see also: go along with · hang out with · put up with · deal with, deal in · with

entries.meaning: Remove or discard something, or free yourself of it.
examples: We finally got rid of the couch that had been in the garage since 2009.
He can't get rid of this cough.
The new director got rid of three vice presidents in a month.
If you want to get rid of the smell, you have to pull up the pad underneath.
I'd get rid of the second paragraph entirely.
They were glad to be rid of the whole arrangement.
entries.русский: избавляться от — убирать, выбрасывать, освобождаться от чего-то
entries.register: informal to neutral — the everyday American twin of dispose of
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a thing, a person, or a problem. No gerund (✗ get rid of smoking — English says quit smoking), no infinitive, no clause. Nothing may be inserted into the string: ✗ get it rid of, ✗ get rid the couch of; the object always follows of.
entries.pattern: get rid of [something, someone] · be rid of [something] · rid [a place] of [something] — transitive, formal · good riddance — the fixed noun
entries.contrast: Get rid of is the plain version of dispose of, and it covers throwing out, selling, firing, and curing: get rid of the couch, of the car, of the manager, of a cough. The formal relatives are rid X of Y (rid the building of asbestos) and be rid of (glad to be rid of him). Note that rid here is not a movable particle but an adjective-like word inside a fixed frame, which is why the object cannot climb over it. For a habit, English switches verbs: quit smoking, give up smoking, never ✗ get rid of smoking.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a fixed idiom for removing, discarding, selling, firing, or curing: the new director got rid of three vice presidents in a month. Rid here is adjective-like inside the frame, so get is close to linking — compare the stative be rid of.
entries.transitivity: intransitive as a frame — the object always follows of and nothing may be inserted: ✗ get it rid of, ✗ get rid the couch of. The formal relative rid X of Y is genuinely transitive: rid the building of asbestos.
entries.passive: no in American English: ✗ the couch was finally gotten rid of is clumsy at best. Use dispose of, which passivizes cleanly (the servers were disposed of), or the stative be rid of: they were glad to be rid of it.
entries.see also: dispose of · divest of · deprive of · deal with, deal in · of

entries.term: get used to, get accustomed to
entries.meaning: Grow familiar with something so that it stops bothering you.
examples: It took her most of a winter to get used to the cold.
You never really get used to being on call.
Don't get used to the corner office; the lease is up in March.
He's getting accustomed to the new scheduling software, slowly.
I'm still not used to seeing his name on the door.
The horses have gotten used to the trains going by.
entries.русский: привыкать к — после to герундий: get used to working, не ✗ to work
entries.register: get used to is everyday; get accustomed to is formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (got used to driving on the left) — to is a preposition, so ✗ get used to drive on the left is an error, and so is ✗ I'm getting used to work nights. Never a clause. Note the pronunciation and spelling of used here: /just/ with an s, not /juzd/, and the d is silent in used to, which is why learners write ✗ use to.
entries.pattern: get used to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · be used to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · get accustomed to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · grow accustomed to [verb-ing] · used to [verb — a different pattern entirely]
entries.contrast: Two different used tos share a spelling and nothing else, and this is the distinction to nail down first. I used to smoke is a past habit — to is the infinitive marker, the verb is bare, and there is no be or get in front of it. I'm used to the smoke is tolerating a smoky room and I'm used to smoking means the habit no longer bothers me — in both of those to is a preposition, so the verb has to be -ing. The noun test separates them instantly: I'm used to the noise works, so that to is a preposition; ✗ I used to the noise does not, so that one is not. Get marks the process and be marks the finished state: it took a month to get used to it, and now I'm used to it. Accustomed is the formal twin with identical grammar, and the adjective forms are catalogued in the companion adjective file.
entries.verb type: linking (copular) — get joins the subject to the adjective used / accustomed, which then takes its own preposition. Get marks the process (dynamic, progressive normal: he's getting accustomed to the software); be marks the finished state: now I'm used to it.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — copular, so there is no object; to is a preposition and takes a noun phrase or -ing: ✗ get used to drive on the left, ✗ I'm getting used to work nights.
entries.passive: no — a copular frame has nothing to promote: ✗ the cold was gotten used to, ✗ being on call is gotten used to by nobody.
entries.see also: look forward to · get around to · adapt to · cope with · object to · accustomed to

entries.meaning: Spend unstructured time with somebody.
examples: He hangs out with the same four people he met in high school.
Nobody hangs out with the interns because they leave at five.
She hung out with her cousins all summer at the lake.
They hang out at the taqueria on Fourth most nights.
I don't hang out with anyone from work anymore.
My daughter would rather hang out with the dog than with the family.
entries.русский: проводить время с, тусоваться с — разг.
entries.register: informal — conversational American English, out of place in a report or a cover letter
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person or group. No gerund (✗ hang out with playing cards) and no clause; what you do together goes in a separate phrase: hang out with them playing cards. The string is fixed: ✗ hang him out with.
entries.pattern: hang out with [people] · hang out — intransitive (we just hung out) · hang out at / in [a place] · hang around with [people] — the same idea, slightly more idle
entries.contrast: Two verbs, one spelling. Hang out the laundry is a separable particle verb — you can say hang the laundry out — and it belongs with the phrasal verbs; hang out with somebody is fixed and cannot be split. The neutral-register equivalents are spend time with and see (I saw a lot of her that year), and socialize with is the word a résumé would use. In American English hang out with implies unstructured time; meet with implies an appointment.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and the progressive is its natural habitat: they're hanging out at the taqueria. Implies unstructured time, unlike meet with.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — a fixed string that cannot be split (✗ hang him out with); it also stands alone: we just hung out. The separable hang out the laundry is a different verb.
entries.passive: no. The idiom refuses the passive: ✗ the interns aren't hung out with, ✗ the dog would rather be hung out with.
entries.see also: get along with · go along with · talk to, talk with, talk about · share with · with

entries.term: hear about, hear from, hear of
entries.meaning: Receive news, learn that something exists, or get word from someone.
examples: Did you hear about the fire on Kingsbury?
I haven't heard from my brother since Thanksgiving.
I've never heard of the band, but the tickets were free.
We heard about the merger from a reporter before anyone told the staff.
You'll hear from our attorney.
She wouldn't hear of our paying for the room.
Let me know as soon as you hear from them.
entries.русский: слышать — from получить весть от кого-то, about узнать новости о, of знать о существовании
entries.complement: about takes a noun phrase, a gerund, or a wh-clause. from takes a person or organization only. of takes a noun phrase or a gerund and is largely restricted to existence and to the negative. None takes a to-infinitive. Bare hear is transitive (hear the alarm) and also takes someone do or someone doing: I heard her leave, I heard her singing. A clause takes no preposition: I heard that they sold it.
entries.pattern: hear about [news, details] · hear from [a person — receive word] · hear of [existence] · never hear of [something] · won't hear of [verb-ing] · hear [something] · hear that [clause] · hear [someone] do / doing
entries.contrast: Three prepositions, three jobs, and one of the highest-value distinctions in the language. Hear from Marcus means Marcus contacted you. Hear about Marcus means somebody told you news of him. Hear of Marcus means you know he exists — which is why I've never heard of her is a statement about your ignorance and I've never heard from her is a complaint. The fixed idiom won't hear of it means flatly refuse, and takes a gerund: she wouldn't hear of our paying. Note the business-letter formula I look forward to hearing from you — from, and the gerund.
entries.verb type: Perception hear is stative and resists the progressive (✗ I am hearing a door slam); the three prepositional frames are closer to dynamic events of getting news, and journalism does allow we're hearing from readers that…
entries.transitivity: both — bare hear is transitive (hear the alarm, hear that she's retiring, hear her leave), while hear about / from / of are intransitive with a fixed preposition: ✗ hear the layoffs about.
entries.passive: restricted. Bare transitive hear passivizes (the alarm was heard three blocks away), and hear of / from survive in fixed passives: she was never heard from again, a town nobody had ever heard of. ✗ the layoffs were heard about is not idiomatic.
entries.see also: learn about · listen to · ask about · talk about

entries.meaning: Keep yourself or something out of sight.
examples: The cat hides from anyone who isn't me.
He hid the diagnosis from his kids for almost a year.
You can't hide from a subpoena forever.
The entrance is hidden from the road by a hedge.
She hid the good chocolate from her roommates.
Two of them hid from the storm under a picnic shelter.
entries.русский: прятать(ся) от — держать себя или вещь вне поля зрения
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause (✗ hide from being seen; say hide so nobody sees you). The verb works both intransitively (hide from the police) and transitively with two arguments (hide the letter from his wife). Note the irregular forms: hide, hid, hidden.
entries.pattern: hide from [someone] · hide [something] from [someone] · hide [somewhere] · be hidden from [view, sight] · hide out · nothing to hide
entries.contrast: Hide from is the direction of concealment and cannot be reversed: He hid the diagnosis from his kids is the only order that works — ✗ hid his kids from the diagnosis says something else entirely. Compare keep something from someone, which is the everyday synonym and takes the same shape, and conceal something from someone, the formal one. Note hidden from view, a fixed phrase, and the idiomatic I have nothing to hide, which takes no preposition at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; progressive normal in both frames: two of them were hiding from the storm, he was hiding the diagnosis from his kids. Irregular: hide, hid, hidden.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when you hide yourself (the cat hides from anyone who isn't me), transitive with two arguments when you hide a thing: he hid the diagnosis from his kids. The order cannot reverse: ✗ hid his kids from the diagnosis.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive frame, and it is very common: the entrance is hidden from the road by a hedge. The intransitive frame has no passive of its own: ✗ the subpoena was hidden from meaning you hid from it.
entries.see also: escape from · protect from · prevent from · from

entries.meaning: Depend entirely on one deciding fact or condition.
examples: The whole case hinges on what the security camera recorded.
Their forecast hinges on interest rates holding through the spring.
Everything hinges on getting the permit before the season closes.
The appeal hinges on whether the notice was timely.
His argument hinges upon a definition the statute never gives.
Nothing much hinges on which of the two spellings you use.
entries.русский: целиком зависеть от — определяться одним решающим обстоятельством
entries.register: neutral — journalism, argument, and courtroom summary
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (hinges on getting the votes), or a wh-clause (hinges on whether the Senate acts, on how the judge reads the statute) — never a to-infinitive (✗ hinges on to get the votes) and never a bare that-clause: ✗ hinges on that the Senate acts. The subject is abstract — a case, an outcome, a decision, the whole thing — because people do not hinge on anything: ✗ she hinges on her lawyer.
entries.variants: Hinge upon is the same pattern one register up, at home in a brief or an editorial.
entries.pattern: [an outcome] hinge on / upon [a fact, a condition] · hinge on [verb-ing] · hinge on whether / how / what [clause] · everything hinges on [X] — the commonest frame
entries.contrast: Hinge on is narrower than depend on in two ways. Its subject must be a thing, not a person — the case hinges on the timeline, but she depends on her sister — and it names a single pivot rather than a general reliance, which is why everything hinges on one witness sounds right and ✗ everything hinges on my family does not. Turn on is its close synonym in legal writing (the appeal turns on a question of standing), and rest on is the static version: a claim rests on an assumption without pivoting on it.
entries.verb type: stative — a relation of dependence, not an event; the progressive is out: ✗ the case is hinging on the timeline.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with a fixed preposition — no object (✗ hinge the outcome), and the subject must be abstract: ✗ she hinges on her lawyer.
entries.passive: no. Stative and objectless: ✗ what the camera recorded is hinged on by the case, ✗ the permit is hinged on. Use turn on or rest on if you want the same idea; they refuse the passive too.
entries.see also: depend on · rely on · count on · result in, result from · on

entries.meaning: Want something to happen and think it might.
examples: They're hoping for a settlement before the trial date.
We hoped for rain all August and got two inches in September.
She hopes to finish the draft before the semester starts.
Everyone was hoping for a shorter meeting.
Hope for the best, plan for the other thing.
I hope the connection holds.
entries.русский: надеяться на — хотеть, чтобы что-то случилось, и считать это возможным
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase only — no gerund and no to-infinitive after the preposition (✗ hope for to win, ✗ hope for winning). To put a verb after hope, drop the preposition and use the infinitive: hope to win. A clause also takes no preposition: hope that it clears up — and note that the present tense is normal there, not will: I hope it clears up tomorrow.
entries.pattern: hope for [a noun phrase] · hope to [verb] · hope that [clause] · I hope so / I hope not · hoping for [the best] · hope against hope
entries.contrast: Hope for winning is not English. The preposition takes a noun and only a noun — hope for rain, hope for a quick decision — and the moment you want a verb you must switch frames to hope to. This is the opposite of look forward to, where the preposition demands the -ing form. The fixed pair hope for the best and hope against hope are frozen. Note also that after hope the future is usually expressed with a present tense: I hope the flight lands on time.
entries.verb type: stative in meaning — a mental attitude rather than an act — but it takes the progressive freely: they're hoping for a settlement before the trial date.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with for before a noun phrase, and transitive before a clause or an infinitive, where the preposition disappears: hope that it clears up, hope to finish the draft; ✗ hope for to win, ✗ hope for winning.
entries.passive: restricted. Impersonal formal writing allows it (a quick decision is hoped for) and the participle is fixed (the hoped-for settlement), but an agent makes it fail: ✗ a shorter meeting was hoped for by everyone. Use it is hoped that… instead.
entries.see also: wish for · long for · look forward to · dream of · plan on

entries.meaning: Place a burden, rule, or cost on somebody — or take advantage of their good nature.
examples: Congress imposed new reporting requirements on small lenders.
The court imposed a six-month deadline on both parties.
I don't want to impose on you two any longer than one night.
Sanctions were imposed on the bank within a week of the ruling.
She imposes her taste in music on everyone in the car.
The tariff imposed upon imported steel raised the cost of the whole project.
entries.русский: налагать (налог, правило) на кого-то; злоупотреблять чьей-то любезностью
entries.register: neutral to formal — taxes, sanctions, deadlines, and polite apology
entries.complement: in the transitive frame the thing imposed is the direct object and on takes the person or body that has to bear it: impose a curfew on the neighborhood. In the intransitive frame on takes a person and the verb means take unfair advantage of them: I don't want to impose on you. A gerund after on is rare, and there is no infinitive and no clause: ✗ impose on to stay another night.
entries.variants: Impose upon is the formal twin, standard in legal and academic prose (the duty imposed upon the trustee) and slightly old-fashioned in the apology sense (I fear we imposed upon your hospitality).
entries.pattern: impose [a tax, a rule, a deadline, a fine] on / upon [someone] · impose on / upon [someone] — trespass on their good nature · be imposed on [someone] · impose oneself on [a group] · an imposition on [someone] — the noun keeps on
entries.contrast: The two senses share a preposition and nothing else. The state imposed a fee on filers is authority; I hate to impose is etiquette, and in that second sense the verb has no object of its own at all. Against the neighbors: inflict on is worse (inflict a speech on the guests), foist on is sneakier (foist the bill on his brother), and encroach on is gradual rather than imposed at once. Note that with people the passive is fine — conditions were imposed on the defendant — but the thing imposed can never take to: ✗ imposed a fine to the company.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: an authority levies something (Congress imposed new requirements), or a guest trespasses on good will (I don't want to impose). Progressive is fine: they're imposing a curfew.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the authority sense, where the thing imposed is the direct object and on takes the bearer (impose a fee on filers); intransitive in the etiquette sense, where the verb has no object of its own at all (I hate to impose on you).
entries.passive: yes in both — conditions were imposed on the defendant; and the person passivizes in the etiquette sense too: she was imposed upon by every relative she had.
entries.see also: encroach on, encroach upon · impute to · devolve on, devolve upon · charge with, charge for · on

entries.meaning: Charge somebody with a motive, a fault, or a value they did not actually declare.
examples: Counsel imputed bad faith to the other side without producing a document.
The knowledge of the broker is imputed to the firm that hired him.
The IRS imputes interest to below-market family loans.
Do not impute to carelessness what a simple software bug explains.
Critics imputed motives to her that the record does not support.
Negligence was imputed to the parent company through the subsidiary.
entries.русский: вменять кому-то (мотив, вину, стоимость) — приписывать незаявленное; юр./книжн.
entries.register: formal — law, accounting, and theology. An American meets it as a participle long before he meets the verb: imputed income on a tax return, imputed knowledge in an agency case, imputed negligence in a jury instruction.
entries.complement: the thing imputed is the direct object — a motive, a statement, a value, a fault — and to takes the person or entity it is charged to. A gerund after to is rare (imputed to having signed the form), and there is no infinitive (✗ impute the delay to be careless) and no clause. The object cannot be dropped: ✗ he imputed to the agency.
entries.pattern: impute [a motive, a fault, a value] to [someone] · be imputed to [someone] · imputed income / knowledge / negligence — the participle · imputation of [bad faith] — the noun takes of
entries.contrast: Impute to assigns something discreditable or artificial; attribute to is neutral. You attribute a quotation to Twain and impute a motive to an opponent — and ascribe to sits between them, more literary than either. Credit with is the flattering member of the family (credited her with the idea), and blame on the blunt one. Note that the law uses impute for something nobody actually did or knew: the agent's knowledge is imputed to the principal means the principal is treated as knowing it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a mental-cum-declarative act of charging something to somebody, and the participle (imputed income, imputed knowledge) is where Americans meet it first.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the thing imputed is the direct object and to takes the party charged; the object cannot be dropped: ✗ he imputed to the agency.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the commoner form — the agent's knowledge is imputed to the principal, no bad faith was imputed to the trustee.
entries.see also: blame for, blame on · accuse of · impose on, impose upon · refer to · to

entries.meaning: Promise in a contract to cover somebody else's losses if a specified risk lands.
examples: The vendor agrees to indemnify the university against any third-party infringement claim.
Directors are routinely indemnified against liability for good-faith decisions.
The clause indemnifies the landlord against everything short of his own negligence.
We would not sign until the contractor agreed to indemnify us from mechanics' liens.
Nothing in the policy indemnifies the company against fines imposed by a regulator.
She was indemnified for the legal fees but not for the lost year of income.
entries.русский: гарантировать возмещение убытков от — договорное обязательство; юр.
entries.register: legal — contract drafting and insurance. An American meets it in exactly one place: the indemnification clause of a lease, a vendor agreement, or a settlement, usually in the fixed triple indemnify, defend, and hold harmless.
entries.complement: the party protected is the direct object, and against takes a noun phrase naming a loss, a claim, a liability, or a suit: indemnify the landlord against claims arising from the tenant's use. A gerund is rare, and there is no infinitive and no clause: ✗ indemnify the seller against to be sued. The protected party cannot be dropped: ✗ indemnify against all claims with nobody named is drafting malpractice, not grammar.
entries.variants: Indemnify from is equally standard in American clauses (indemnify and hold harmless from any liability), and indemnify for points at a loss already suffered rather than one that might happen: indemnified the owner for the cost of repairs. Practice varies firm to firm; all three are read the same way.
entries.pattern: indemnify [a party] against / from [claims, losses, liability] · indemnify [a party] for [an amount already lost] · indemnify, defend, and hold [a party] harmless against [X] · indemnity against [loss] — the noun keeps the preposition
entries.contrast: Indemnify against is a promise between parties; insure against is a policy you buy. A subcontractor indemnifies the general contractor against third-party claims, while the general contractor separately insures against fire. Both differ from compensate for, which is payment after the fact and takes for, and from protect from, which is the everyday word. Note that the object is the person protected, never the risk: ✗ indemnify the losses against the tenant.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and performative: signing the clause is the act. Ordinarily non-progressive in drafting (Tenant shall indemnify Landlord), not because it is stative but because contracts use shall.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the party protected is the direct object and against names the loss; the object is obligatory: ✗ indemnify against all claims with nobody named.
entries.passive: yes — the landlord is indemnified against claims arising from the tenant's use, and the participial indemnified and held harmless is standard boilerplate.
entries.see also: insure against · protect from, protect against · relieve of · liable for, liable to · against

entries.meaning: Formally charge somebody with a crime by grand jury.
examples: A federal grand jury indicted him for mail fraud in November.
Two officers were indicted for falsifying the incident report.
She was indicted on seven counts, four of them dismissed before trial.
The prosecutor declined to indict anyone for the leak.
Being indicted for a crime is not the same as being convicted of one.
The grand jury refused to indict, and the case ended there.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ɪnˈdaɪt fɚ/ — the c is silent
entries.русский: предъявлять обвинение в — через большое жюри; юр., США
entries.register: legal and news — grand juries, U.S. Attorneys, and the front page
entries.complement: the person is the direct object and for takes a noun phrase naming the offense, or a gerund naming the conduct: indicted for lying to investigators. Never a to-infinitive (✗ indicted for to lie) and never a clause: ✗ indicted for that he lied. The frame indict on takes counts or charges instead — indicted on three counts of wire fraud — and is at least as common in reporting.
entries.pattern: indict [someone] for [an offense, verb-ing] · indict [someone] on [counts, charges] · be indicted for / on [something] · return an indictment against [someone] · an indictment of [a policy] — the figurative noun takes of
entries.contrast: Four verbs run the same case and none of them shares a preposition. A prosecutor charges someone with a crime, a grand jury indicts him for it (or on counts of it), a jury convicts him of it, and a judge sentences him to something. Accuse of is the everyday word for the same act, and arraign on is the step in between. Note the figurative noun, which flips the preposition entirely: the report is an indictment of the whole program, never ✗ an indictment for.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single official act by a grand jury, punctual rather than durative.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person is the direct object and for (or on, with counts) names the offense; the object is obligatory: ✗ the grand jury indicted for wire fraud.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the normal news form — he was indicted for lying to investigators, she was indicted on three counts of wire fraud.
entries.see also: charge with, charge for · accuse of · punish for · suspect of · for

entries.meaning: Draw a probable conclusion from evidence.
examples: From the tone of the email she inferred that the offer had been withdrawn.
You can infer a great deal from what a company does not disclose.
Nothing about intent can be inferred from a single missed payment.
The jury was told not to infer guilt from the defendant's silence.
He inferred from watching two shifts that the schedule was written by seniority.
Readers are left to infer the ending from three lines of dialogue.
entries.русский: делать вывод из — заключать по имеющимся данным
entries.register: neutral to formal — argument, science, and careful writing
entries.complement: from takes a noun phrase naming the evidence, or a gerund (inferred from watching the two of them) — never a to-infinitive (✗ inferred from to watch them). What is inferred is the direct object and may be a that-clause: inferred that the deal was off. The preposition never introduces the conclusion: ✗ infer from that the deal was off is a common slip for infer from her tone that the deal was off.
entries.pattern: infer [something] from [evidence] · infer from [evidence] that [clause] · [something] may be inferred from [evidence] · an inference from [the record] — the noun keeps from
entries.contrast: The usage everyone argues about: imply and infer are opposite ends of one act. The speaker implies; the listener infers. ✗ Are you inferring that I lied? means the opposite of what the speaker intends — say implying. Within the reasoning family, deduce from claims certainty, infer from claims likelihood, and extrapolate from claims a pattern will continue. All three take from; none takes of or out of: ✗ infer of his tone.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a mental act you perform, and it takes the progressive: what exactly are you inferring from that?
entries.transitivity: transitive — what is inferred is the direct object or a that-clause (inferred that the deal was off) and from names the evidence; the conclusion cannot hide inside the preposition: ✗ infer from that the deal was off.
entries.passive: yes — nothing can be inferred from a sample that small, it was inferred from her tone that the deal was off.
entries.see also: deduce from · extrapolate from · derive from · follow from · from

entries.meaning: Intrude on a right, a freedom, or protected property.
examples: The plaintiffs say the curfew infringes on rights the state constitution guarantees.
Requiring a permit for a two-person picket infringes upon speech, the court held.
He felt the new metrics infringed on how he ran his own department.
The company was found to have infringed three of the four patents.
Nothing in the lease infringes on the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.
Streaming the whole film infringes the copyright whether or not you charge for it.
entries.русский: нарушать, посягать на — на право, свободу или охраняемую собственность
entries.register: legal to neutral — constitutional argument, intellectual property, and op-eds
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a right, a freedom, or a protected interest. A gerund is unusual (infringing on being able to speak freely is possible but clumsy), and there is no infinitive and no clause: ✗ infringe on to speak freely.
entries.variants: Infringe upon is the formal twin and is common in judicial opinions. The important variant is the bare transitive: in intellectual-property law you infringe a patent, infringe a copyright, infringe the mark — with no preposition at all, and that is the professional usage.
entries.pattern: infringe on / upon [a right, a freedom, someone's autonomy] · infringe [a patent, a copyright, a trademark] — no preposition · an infringement of [copyright] · an infringement on [rights]
entries.contrast: Rights are infringed on; patents are infringed. The ordinance infringes on the right to assemble and the knockoff infringes the design patent are both standard, and swapping them marks a writer as an outsider to the field. Against the neighbors: encroach on is gradual and often physical, violate is blunt and transitive (violate the statute), impinge on is the most abstract, and interfere with is the broadest of all. The noun splits too — infringement of copyright but an infringement on civil liberties.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an ordinance or a product encroaches on a right or a patent. Often durative and progressive: the rule is infringing on speech.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with the preposition when the object is a right (infringes on the right to assemble), transitive with no preposition in the IP sense (the knockoff infringes the design patent).
entries.passive: yes in both frames — the patent was infringed, and the prepositional passive is idiomatic too: rights that are being infringed on every day.
entries.see also: encroach on, encroach upon · interfere with, interfere in · impose on, impose upon · comply with · on

entries.meaning: Belong to something as an inseparable part of what it is.
examples: Certain powers inhere in the office and do not depend on the statute.
The dignity that inheres in the individual is not conferred by government.
Whatever value the collection has inheres in keeping it together.
Risk inheres in any procedure performed under general anesthesia.
The authority to punish contempt inheres in the court itself.
He argued that the flaw inheres in the design rather than the execution.
entries.русский: быть неотъемлемо присущим чему-то — книжн./филос.
entries.register: formal and technical — philosophy, jurisprudence, and constitutional opinions (the power inheres in the office). It is rare enough in speech that most Americans know only its adjective, inherent in.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the thing the quality belongs to — an office, a relationship, a system, a role. No gerund, no infinitive, no clause, and no passive: ✗ is inhered in. The subject is the quality, right, or power, never the possessor: ✗ the court inheres in that power.
entries.pattern: [a right, a power, a quality] inhere in [an office, a thing, a relationship] · inherent in [something] — the far commoner adjective · inhere — no other frame; the verb needs in
entries.contrast: Prefer the adjective. The risk inherent in the procedure is ordinary English; the risk inheres in the procedure is a philosopher's sentence. Against the neighbors: consist in names what something essentially is (happiness consists in useful work), reside in is where a power lives by design (sovereignty resides in the people), and vest in is the legal act of putting it there (the estate vests in the heir). Inhere in claims the quality could not be separated from the thing at all.
entries.verb type: stative — a quality belongs to a thing; nothing happens. It rejects the progressive: ✗ the power is inhering in the office. Prefer the adjective, inherent in.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the subject is the quality or power and in takes the thing it belongs to; there is no object and no other frame: ✗ the court inheres that power.
entries.passive: no — the verb is intransitive and stative, and the entry marks the prepositional passive out as impossible: ✗ the office is inhered in.
entries.see also: devolve on, devolve upon · belong to · consist of · inherent in · in

entries.meaning: Demand something firmly, or maintain something in the face of doubt.
examples: He insisted on paying for everyone, which nobody had asked him to do.
The landlord insisted on a second deposit.
She insisted that the contract be reviewed before anyone signed.
They insisted on our staying for dinner.
He insisted he had mailed it, and the postmark said otherwise.
The union insisted on binding arbitration.
entries.русский: настаивать на — твёрдо требовать или упорно утверждать; после on герундий
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (insisted on paying), or possessive plus gerund (insisted on my paying) — never a to-infinitive (✗ insist to pay, ✗ insist on to pay). Before a clause the preposition drops, and American English uses the bare subjunctive: insisted that she be told, not that she is told.
entries.pattern: insist on [noun phrase] · insist on [verb-ing] · insist on [someone's] -ing · insist that [subject] [bare verb] · insist (alone)
entries.contrast: Insist to do is a fixed error — the verb has no infinitive frame at all. The two live patterns are insist on doing and insist that X do, and the second one keeps the American mandative subjunctive: He insisted that the door be locked, She insists that he take the earlier flight — bare verb, no -s, no should. (British English often inserts should.) Note the second sense, maintain in the face of doubt: she insisted that she'd sent it, where the clause is a plain indicative, not a subjunctive.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a speech act you repeat, and it takes the progressive freely: she's insisting on paying.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object ever; the demand comes through on (insisted on paying) or through a that-clause with the bare subjunctive (insisted that she be told).
entries.passive: restricted — there is no object to promote, and the prepositional passive is stiff formal-record English at best: a written waiver was insisted on, but ✗ I was insisted on to pay.
entries.see also: object to · agree to · decide on · comply with · on

entries.meaning: Buy or provide coverage that pays out if a particular risk occurs.
examples: The house is insured against fire but not against flood.
Small clinics can rarely afford to insure against a judgment that size.
The policy insures the fleet against theft and collision.
Growers insure against a late frost the way other people buy lottery tickets in reverse.
She was insured against being sued for work done before the merger.
Nothing insures against bad luck entirely.
entries.русский: страховать от — покупать полис на случай риска (не путать с ensure, assure)
entries.register: neutral — insurance, banking, and risk talk
entries.complement: against takes a noun phrase naming a risk or peril — fire, flood, theft, loss, liability — or a gerund (insured against being sued by a former client). No to-infinitive (✗ insure against to be sued) and no clause. The party or property covered is the direct object: insure the building against flood.
entries.pattern: insure [property, a person] against [a risk] · be insured against [a risk] · insure [something] for [an amount] · insure [something] with [a carrier] · insurance against [loss] — the noun keeps against
entries.contrast: Three verbs Americans mix daily. Insure is about policies, ensure is about making certain (ensure that the door locks), and assure is about telling a person something confidently (assured her it was fine) — so ✗ insure that the door locks is the error, and it is everywhere. Within the risk family: insure against buys coverage, indemnify against is a contractual promise between two parties with no policy involved, and hedge against offsets a risk with an opposite position (hedge against inflation). Note the amount takes for, not against: insured for $400,000 against fire.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; buying or writing coverage. Keep it clear of stative ensure (make certain) and assure (tell someone).
entries.transitivity: transitive — the property or party covered is the direct object and against names the peril: insure the building against flood.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the everyday form — the building is insured against flood, we're insured for $400,000 against fire.
entries.see also: indemnify against · protect from, protect against · provide with, provide for · against

entries.meaning: Disrupt something, or get involved where you have no business.
examples: The new tower interferes with reception all along the ridge.
She was told, more than once, not to interfere in her sister's divorce.
Nothing should interfere with the vote count.
The medication can interfere with several common blood thinners.
Foreign governments interfered in the election in at least three documented ways.
Long meetings interfere with getting anything actually finished.
entries.русский: мешать чему-то (with); вмешиваться во что-то не своё (in)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (interferes with getting any real work done) — never a to-infinitive. Interfere is intransitive and never takes a bare object: ✗ interfere the signal — say interfere with the signal.
entries.pattern: interfere with [a process, a signal, a plan] · interfere in [an affair, a dispute, a country] · interfere (alone)
entries.contrast: With disrupts; in meddles. The construction interferes with the Wi-Fi is about disruption of a thing; Don't interfere in their marriage is about intruding into a situation that isn't yours. In American political writing, interfere in is the standard collocation for meddling in another country's affairs or an election, while interfere with covers evidence, a witness, a signal, or a schedule. Legal usage keeps both: tortious interference with contract, interference in the proceeding.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a disruption or an intrusion that goes on over time: the construction is interfering with the Wi-Fi.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the verb never takes a bare object: ✗ interfere the signal. Everything comes through with (disrupt a thing) or in (meddle in a situation).
entries.passive: restricted — the with frame passivizes in legal and news prose (the witness had been interfered with, the evidence was interfered with); the in frame does not: ✗ the election was interfered in.
entries.see also: prevent from · cope with · comply with · involve in · participate in

entries.meaning: Make one person known to another, or bring something in for the first time.
examples: Let me introduce you to my colleague from the Denver office.
His grandmother introduced him to opera when he was six.
The bill was introduced in March and died in committee.
Zebra mussels were introduced into the Great Lakes by ballast water.
She introduced herself to everyone in the row before the plane took off.
Nobody introduced the new hire to anyone for a week.
entries.русский: представлять кого-то кому-то; знакомить с чем-то — предлог to обязателен
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause. The person being introduced is a direct object and the person met takes to: introduce her to my parents. ✗ introduce her with my parents is an error carried over from other languages. Into is a separate pattern, used for putting something new inside a system.
entries.pattern: introduce [someone] to [someone] · introduce [someone] to [a subject, a food, a habit] · introduce [something] into [a system, a market] · introduce [a bill, a topic] · introduce [oneself]
entries.contrast: Introduce with is wrong. The two live prepositions are to and into, and they do different work: introduce her to sailing opens a person's acquaintance with something, while introduce a species into an ecosystem physically inserts it. Note that introduce belongs to the explain/describe/mention group — the person always needs to, never a bare indirect object: ✗ introduce me your friend.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of making an acquaintance or inserting something new into a system.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person or thing introduced is the direct object and to takes the person or activity met; the object is obligatory: ✗ he introduced to my parents. Never a bare indirect object: ✗ introduce me your friend.
entries.passive: yes — she was introduced to my parents at the rehearsal dinner, the species was introduced into the lake in 1954.
entries.see also: explain to · refer to · invite to

entries.meaning: Accrue to somebody's benefit — or, in the passive, be hardened to something by long exposure.
examples: This warranty shall inure to the benefit of any subsequent owner.
Any savings from the settlement inure to the members of the class.
The rights granted here inure to the benefit of the licensee's successors.
Twelve years on the night desk had inured her to bad news at three in the morning.
He is thoroughly inured to being told the idea will never work.
Nurses in that unit become inured to the alarms within a month.
entries.русский: доставаться в пользу кого-то; (в пассиве) быть закалённым к чему-то; юр./книжн.
entries.register: formal and legal, in two separate lives. In a trust, a policy, or a contract you meet the fixed phrase inure to the benefit of; in essays and obituaries you meet the participle inured to meaning hardened by exposure. Neither is conversational.
entries.complement: in the legal sense, to takes a noun phrase naming the party who gets the benefit — almost always inside to the benefit of [someone]. In the participial sense, be inured to takes a noun phrase or a gerund: inured to being ignored, inured to the cold. Never a to-infinitive in either sense: ✗ inured to be ignored, and that trap is the reason the entry is here.
entries.variants: The spelling enure survives in older and British legal drafting and means exactly the same thing; American filings use inure.
entries.pattern: [a benefit, a right] inure to the benefit of [a party] · [something] inure to [someone's advantage] · be / become inured to [hardship, verb-ing] · this Agreement shall inure to the benefit of and be binding upon the parties — the boilerplate
entries.contrast: Two senses, one spelling, and neither is the everyday word. The proceeds inure to the beneficiary means they accrue to her — the plain verbs are go to and accrue to. He is inured to criticism means he has been hardened to it — the plain phrases are used to and hardened to. The second is where the gerund rule bites: like get used to and accustomed to, inured to is followed by -ing, never by an infinitive. Do not confuse either with in your interest or with ensure.
entries.verb type: stative in the legal sense — benefits simply accrue (the proceeds inure to the beneficiary), no progressive: ✗ the proceeds are inuring to her. The other life is participial inured to, a resultant state of hardening.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in the legal sense — the subject is what accrues and to takes the party; the hardening sense lives almost entirely in be/get inured to plus a noun or gerund (inured to being ignored).
entries.passive: restricted — the accrual sense is intransitive and has no passive at all (✗ the beneficiary is inured to); the hardening sense exists chiefly as a passive participle, he is inured to criticism, the active (the work inured him to it) being rare.
entries.see also: get used to, get accustomed to · adapt to · belong to · accustomed to · to

entries.meaning: Put money, time, or effort into something you expect to pay off.
examples: They invested in index funds and left it alone for thirty years.
The district is investing in early literacy instead of testing.
Honestly, invest in a good chair before you invest in a standing desk.
She invested four years in a degree she never used and doesn't regret.
The state has invested heavily in broadband for rural counties.
He's too invested in being right to hear the argument.
entries.русский: вкладывать(ся) во что-то — деньги, время или силы в расчёте на отдачу
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (invest in retraining workers) — never a to-infinitive (✗ invest in to retrain them). A formal, unrelated pattern takes with: invest someone with authority.
entries.pattern: invest in [a company, a fund, a thing worth having] · invest [an amount] in [something] · invest in [verb-ing] · invest [someone] with [authority] — formal · be invested in [an outcome]
entries.contrast: Invest on and ✗ invest to are errors — the preposition is fixed at in. Two senses live in the same frame: the financial one (invest in bonds) and the everyday one meaning buy something worth the money (invest in a decent mattress). The passive be invested in has drifted to mean emotionally committed — she's heavily invested in the outcome — and is now more common in that sense than the literal one. Keep it apart from formal invest someone with a power or a title, which is the ceremonial sense behind investiture.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; putting money, time, or trust into something: she's investing in retraining the crew. The participle invested in has drifted into a stative sense, emotionally committed.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with in (invest in bonds, invest in a decent mattress); transitive in the ceremonial frame invest someone with authority, and with an amount as object (invested $40,000).
entries.passive: yes — the endowment is invested in municipal bonds, she's heavily invested in the outcome, he was invested with full authority.
entries.see also: contribute to · pay for · benefit from · specialize in · in

entries.meaning: Ask someone to come, or ask them to do something.
examples: They invited half the department to the housewarming.
She was invited to speak at the conference in Portland.
We invited them over for the game and they stayed until midnight.
He wasn't invited to the wedding and has mentioned it four times.
The library invites the public to comment on the renovation plan.
Invite your neighbors for dinner once and you'll know within an hour.
entries.русский: приглашать на, приглашать к — звать прийти или сделать что-то
entries.complement: to takes a noun phrase naming an event or a place — no gerund after the preposition (✗ invited us to having dinner). Invite someone to do something is a separate frame in which to is the infinitive marker, not the preposition: invited us to speak. Both are correct; what is impossible is mixing them.
entries.pattern: invite [someone] to [an event / a place] · invite [someone] to [verb] · invite [someone] for [dinner, drinks] · invite [someone] in / over / along / back · be invited to [something]
entries.contrast: One preposition, two structures, and the difference is what follows it. Invite her to the wedding (preposition + noun) against invite her to speak at the wedding (infinitive). Note the American directional particles that need no to at all: invite them over, invite him in, invite her along. Invite for names the occasion in a looser way (invited us for coffee), and invite also has a figurative transitive use meaning provoke: that kind of memo invites trouble.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act. A figurative transitive sense means provoke: that kind of memo invites trouble.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the guest is the direct object and to takes the event; the object is obligatory: ✗ she invited to the wedding.
entries.passive: yes — we were invited to the wedding, and the infinitive frame passivizes too: they were invited to speak.
entries.see also: introduce to · ask for · apply to · belong to · to

entries.meaning: Take part in something, or have something as a necessary part.
examples: Three agencies were involved in the response.
She's been involved in local politics since she was nineteen.
The renovation involves moving a load-bearing wall.
Nobody wanted to get involved in a dispute between neighbors.
He was involved in raising almost half the endowment.
The role involves a fair amount of weekend work.
entries.русский: вовлекать(ся) во что-то — участвовать в чём-то или включать как часть
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (involved in raising the money) — never a to-infinitive (✗ involved in to raise the money). But note the other frame: transitive involve meaning entail takes a gerund with no preposition at all — the job involves traveling, and ✗ the job involves to travel is a common and serious error.
entries.pattern: involve [someone] in [something] · be involved in [something / verb-ing] · [a job, a process] involve [verb-ing] — no preposition · get involved with [a person, an organization]
entries.contrast: Two patterns that look alike and are not. She's involved in the campaign (prepositional, about participation) against The campaign involves knocking on doors (transitive, about what it entails). And involved with is different again: involved in a project means working on it, while involved with a person means romantically entangled, and involved with an organization means affiliated. He got involved with her and He got involved in her case are not remotely the same sentence.
entries.verb type: both — dynamic in the participation sense (they got her involved in the campaign), and stative in the transitive entail sense, which rejects the progressive: ✗ the job is involving a lot of travel.
entries.transitivity: transitive in both — involve her in the planning; and the entail sense takes an object or a bare gerund with no preposition: the job involves traveling, ✗ the job involves to travel.
entries.passive: yes in the participation sense, where the passive is the usual form — she was involved in the campaign, he got involved with the union. The entail sense resists a by-phrase: ✗ a lot of travel is involved by the job.
entries.see also: participate in · interfere in · contribute to · concentrate on · work on

entries.term: keep up with, catch up with, catch up on
entries.meaning: Stay level with something moving, close a gap, or work through a backlog.
examples: I can't keep up with the reading in that seminar.
Wages have not kept up with rent in this county since 2015.
She walked ahead and we caught up with her at the light.
Let's catch up next week when the quarter closes.
He spent Sunday catching up on email and laundry.
The paperwork he ignored in March finally caught up with him in July.
Nobody keeps up with paying two mortgages for long.
entries.русский: не отставать от; догонять кого-то; наверстывать накопившееся
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — keep up with paying the invoices, catch up on grading. Never a to-infinitive (✗ keep up with to pay them) and never a clause. The three words are welded together and the object always follows the preposition: ✗ keep the news up with, ✗ catch my email up on.
entries.pattern: keep up with [the news, a person, inflation, the payments] · catch up with [someone ahead of you; also, meet socially] · catch up to [someone] — the physical sense, American variant · catch up on [sleep, email, the backlog] · keep up — intransitive (I couldn't keep up)
entries.contrast: One family, three jobs, and the preposition does the sorting. Keep up with means stay level with something moving — the reading, the rent, a faster walker. Catch up with means close a gap that has already opened, and it has a second, friendlier life meaning meet for coffee (let's catch up) and a third, grimmer one meaning consequences arrive (the drinking caught up with him). Catch up on takes the backlog itself as its object — sleep, laundry, three weeks of email — and never a person: ✗ catch up on my sister. Note that keep up alone is intransitive, and keep something up (keep the pressure up) is a separable particle verb that belongs with the phrasal verbs, not here.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; all three are durative and take the progressive: she's catching up on three weeks of email, he isn't keeping up with the rent.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — phrasal-prepositional, so the verb has no direct object and nothing may be inserted: ✗ keep the news up with, ✗ catch my email up on.
entries.passive: restricted — three-word units passivize badly. The payments couldn't be kept up with is possible and clumsy; ✗ the backlog has been caught up on is not idiomatic. Keep the active.
entries.see also: face up to, back out of, drop out of, walk out on · live up to · put up with · cope with · with

entries.meaning: Show amusement at someone or something.
examples: Nobody laughed at the joke and he told it twice more anyway.
They laughed at her accent for a year and then hired her.
We'll laugh about this eventually, but not this week.
He laughed at the very idea of finishing by Friday.
She laughed at being mistaken for the intern.
The whole table was laughing with him, not at him.
entries.русский: смеяться над — at насмешка над кем-то, laugh with смеяться вместе с ним
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (laughed at being called sir) — never a to-infinitive, never a clause. Laugh is intransitive: the thing amusing you always needs a preposition. ✗ laugh the joke.
entries.pattern: laugh at [someone / something] · laugh about [something, usually later] · laugh with [someone] · laugh off [criticism] · be laughed at
entries.contrast: Laugh at mocks; laugh about shares the joke; laugh with includes the person. They laughed at him is cruel and They laughed with him is not — the same event described from two sides, and the preposition is the whole difference. Laugh about is what you do afterward, when the thing has become funny (we laugh about it now). Note that laugh at can also mean dismiss as absurd: the bank laughed at his projections. The phrasal laugh off means brush aside.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a reaction you perform, freely progressive: they were laughing at him.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the thing amusing you always needs the preposition: ✗ laugh the joke. Bare laugh stands alone (everybody laughed).
entries.passive: yes — the prepositional passive is fully idiomatic: he was laughed at by the whole room, her projections were laughed at.
entries.see also: smile at · stare at · boast about · complain about · at

entries.meaning: Acquire knowledge or a skill.
examples: He spent a semester learning about watershed management.
She learned everything she knows about wiring from her mother.
You learn from a bad manager exactly what not to do.
They learned about the closure from a sign on the door.
It's never too late to learn to swim.
We only learned of the change the week it took effect.
entries.русский: узнавать о чём-то (about); учиться у кого-то или на чём-то (from)
entries.complement: about takes a noun phrase, a gerund, or a wh-clause. from takes a person, an experience, or a source. Neither takes a to-infinitive — but learn itself does, with no preposition: learn to swim. Bare learn is also transitive (learn the routine) and takes a clause (learned that the office had moved). The past is learned in American English; learnt is British.
entries.pattern: learn about [a subject] · learn from [a person / an experience] · learn to [verb] · learn [something] · learn that [clause] · learn of [something] — formal, means hear about
entries.contrast: Learn about is the subject; learn from is the source; learn to is the skill. All three can appear in one sentence: she learned about soil chemistry from her father and learned to test it herself. The formal learn of means come to hear (we learned of his death from the paper) and sounds stiff in casual speech. Note the direction trap: learn is what the student does and teach is what the instructor does — ✗ she learned me how to drive is nonstandard for taught me.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a process, not a state, and it takes the progressive: she's learning about soil chemistry. The past is learned in American English.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with about and from; transitive bare (learn the routine), plus a to-infinitive (learn to swim) and a that-clause (learned that the office had moved).
entries.passive: restricted — the bare transitive passivizes (the routine has to be learned by Friday, lessons were learned), the prepositional frames do not: ✗ the war was learned about, ✗ his father was learned from.
entries.see also: hear about · explain to · think about · refer to · consult with

entries.meaning: Pay deliberate attention to a sound.
examples: She listens to the same three albums on every long drive.
Nobody listened to the safety officer until after the accident.
Listen to him tell it and you'd think he built the thing himself.
I listened to about forty minutes of hold music.
Listen for the click; that's how you know it's seated.
You're not listening to me.
entries.русский: слушать — предлог to обязателен: listen to music, не ✗ listen music (ср. hear)
entries.complement: noun phrase, or a person plus a bare infinitive or -ing (listen to her sing, listen to the rain falling). A gerund alone is fine (listen to arguing all day), but never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause. Listen is intransitive and the object always needs to: ✗ listen music, ✗ listen me.
entries.pattern: listen to [something / someone] · listen to [someone] do / doing · listen for [a sound you're waiting for] · listen (alone) · listen up · Listen.
entries.contrast: Listen music is one of the most common errors learners make, because hear is transitive and listen is not. Hear is the passive faculty and listen to is the deliberate act: I heard the alarm (it reached me) against I listened to the whole thing (I chose to). Listen for is different again — it means wait alertly for a particular sound: listen for the buzzer. And listen to someone often means heed them: nobody listened to the engineer.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and deliberate, unlike the passive faculty hear: I listened to the whole thing against I heard the alarm.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the object always needs to: ✗ listen music, ✗ listen me. Bare listen stands alone as a command (Listen.).
entries.passive: restricted — natural with a person as object (the engineer wasn't listened to, nobody was listened to), stiff with a thing: ✗ the album was listened to twice.
entries.see also: hear about · hear of · look at · stare at · concentrate on

entries.meaning: Meet the standard that a promise, a reputation, or an expectation set.
examples: The sequel never lives up to the first film.
She has spent a decade living up to a nickname she got at nineteen.
The district failed to live up to the settlement it signed in 2019.
Few restaurants live up to that kind of advance press.
He worries about living up to what his father built.
The new hire lived up to every word in her references.
entries.русский: оправдывать (ожидания, репутацию) — соответствовать заданной планке
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a standard, a promise, a reputation, or the hype. A gerund is possible but rare (never lived up to being called a prodigy), and there is no to-infinitive (✗ live up to be a prodigy) and no clause. Nothing may be inserted: ✗ live it up to, which is a different idiom entirely.
entries.pattern: live up to [expectations, a promise, a name, the billing] · fail to live up to [something] · live up to [verb-ing] — rare · live it up — an unrelated idiom (enjoy yourself)
entries.contrast: The word order matters more here than almost anywhere else in the file. Live up to it means meet the standard; live it up means spend the weekend enjoying yourself. Against the neighbors: live up to a promise is meeting a standard someone set, comply with a rule is obeying an instruction, and keep up with something is staying level with a moving target. Live with is the resigned one — live with the consequences — and live off or live on names what supports you.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; meeting a standard over time, and progressive: the sequel isn't living up to the hype.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — phrasal-prepositional, no direct object, and nothing may be inserted: ✗ live it up to, which is a different idiom entirely.
entries.passive: restricted — a promise that was never lived up to is possible in writing but heavy; American speech keeps the active: he never lived up to it.
entries.see also: keep up with, catch up with, catch up on · make up for · comply with · look up to, look down on · to

entries.meaning: Want something badly, usually something absent or out of reach.
examples: By February everyone in the office longs for daylight.
He longed for the noise of a city and moved back within a year.
She longed to see the house one more time.
They long for a version of the town that never really existed.
You could hear him longing for an argument.
After a week of rain we were all longing for one clear morning.
entries.русский: тосковать по, страстно желать — обычно о недостижимом; книжн.
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase — a gerund is possible but unusual (longed for being left alone). To put an action after long, drop the preposition and use the infinitive: long to go home, which is the more natural form by far. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: long for [a noun phrase] · long to [verb] · be longing for [something] · a longing for [something]
entries.contrast: Register is the whole story here. Long for is heightened, close to poetry, and an American in ordinary conversation says miss, want, or can't wait for. Its neighbors line up by intensity: wish for (mild), hope for (expectant), long for and yearn for (aching), pine for (aching and slightly comic). Note that with a verb, long to go is preferred over long for going — the opposite of look forward to, where the gerund is compulsory.
entries.verb type: stative — a sustained emotional state rather than an act, though unlike most statives it takes the progressive freely in literary use: she was longing for home.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — everything comes through for; to put an action after it, drop the preposition and use the infinitive: long to go home.
entries.passive: no — the verb is intransitive and the prepositional passive is not English: ✗ home was longed for by the whole crew. Only the attributive participle survives: the longed-for reunion.
entries.see also: hope for · wish for · dream of · wait for · care about

entries.term: look at, look for, look after, look into
entries.meaning: Direct your eyes, search, tend, or investigate — the preposition decides which.
examples: Look at the third column and tell me if that number makes sense.
I've been looking for my other glove since Tuesday.
Her neighbor looks after the dog whenever she travels.
The state is looking into how the permits were issued.
We're looking at raising the fee about eight percent.
He looked through the whole drawer and found nothing.
Can you look over the contract before I sign it?
entries.русский: смотреть на; искать; присматривать за; разбираться в — предлог решает всё
entries.complement: All four take a noun phrase. look at and look into also take a gerund or a wh-clause (look at raising the fee, look into what went wrong). look for takes a noun phrase only — ✗ look for getting a refund. None of them takes a to-infinitive, and none takes a that-clause. Bare look takes an adjective, not an adverb: look tired, ✗ look tiredly.
entries.pattern: look at [something — direct your eyes, or examine] · look for [something — try to find] · look after [someone — take care of] · look into [something — investigate] · look over [something — review] · look through [something — scan or search]
entries.contrast: This is the family that makes look the most treacherous verb in the dictionary — six prepositions, six unrelated meanings, and no way to guess any of them. Look at the report is reading it; look for the report is hunting for it; look after the report is nonsense unless the report is a child; look into the report is investigating what it says; look over the report is reviewing it quickly. Three more sit in their own entries: look forward to (anticipate), look up to (admire), look down on (despise). And look up a word is a seventh thing again. When in doubt, name the meaning in plain words rather than guessing a particle.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses — reading, hunting, tending, investigating. Bare look also has a linking use taking an adjective: look tired, ✗ look tiredly.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — every one of the four requires its preposition; the verb takes no bare object: ✗ look the report.
entries.passive: yes — this family gives English its textbook prepositional passives: the complaint is being looked into, the kids were well looked after, the file was never looked at.
entries.see also: look forward to · look up to · search for · care for · take care of · concentrate on · stare at

entries.meaning: Anticipate something with pleasure.
examples: I look forward to hearing from you.
She's looking forward to three weeks with no email.
We look forward to working with your team on this.
He looks forward to the county fair the way children look forward to Christmas.
I'm looking forward to seeing the finished kitchen.
Nobody looks forward to open enrollment.
entries.русский: с нетерпением ждать — после to герундий: looking forward to hearing from you
entries.register: neutral; the standard closing of American business correspondence
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — to here is a preposition, not the infinitive marker, so the verb after it must be -ing: look forward to hearing from you, never ✗ look forward to hear from you. A wh-clause is possible (look forward to whatever comes next). Never a to-infinitive, never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: look forward to [noun phrase] · look forward to [verb-ing] · be looking forward to [something] · I look forward to hearing from you (fixed closing)
entries.contrast: This is the single most-cited gerund trap in English, and the reason is that the to looks exactly like the to of want to go. The test that settles it: substitute a plain noun. I look forward to the meeting works, so to is a preposition, so a verb after it must be -ing. The same test exposes the rest of the family — object to, be used to, get used to, be accustomed to, resort to, confess to, admit to, commit to, devote yourself to, be opposed to, all of them -ing. Register note: I look forward to is the formal closing and I'm looking forward to is the warmer one; both are correct.
entries.verb type: stative — an attitude of anticipation, not an act; it is unusual among statives in taking the progressive freely, and both forms are standard: I look forward to hearing from you, I'm looking forward to it.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object; to is a preposition, so a verb after it must be -ing: ✗ look forward to hear from you.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatically available and almost never used; your reply is looked forward to is dead commercialese, and ✗ the meeting is looked forward to by everyone is not written.
entries.see also: object to · resort to · commit to · get used to · get around to · hope for · long for · look at · accustomed to · to

entries.term: look up to, look down on
entries.meaning: Admire someone, or consider someone inferior.
examples: Every apprentice in that shop looked up to her.
He looks down on anyone who didn't go to a four-year school.
Kids look up to coaches more than coaches realize.
The town has always been looked down on by the county seat.
She looked up to her older brother until she was about fourteen.
Nobody likes being looked down on by a twenty-four-year-old consultant.
entries.русский: смотреть снизу вверх, уважать (up to); смотреть свысока, презирать (down on)
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun naming a person or group — no gerund, no clause, no infinitive. Both are fixed three-word units and neither can be split: ✗ look him up to, ✗ look down them on. The object always follows the whole phrase.
entries.pattern: look up to [someone] · look down on [someone] · be looked up to · be looked down on
entries.contrast: A matched pair of opposites, and neither one is literal. Look up to means admire; look down on means consider beneath you. Do not confuse either with look up a word (consult a reference), which is a separate phrasal verb and is separable: look it up. The British look down one's nose at is the same idea with more scorn. Note that both of these passivize freely, which is unusual for prepositional verbs: he was looked up to by everyone in the shop.
