entries.verb type: stative — standing attitudes of admiration and contempt, not events; the progressive is odd: ✗ she is looking up to her brother these days.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — both are fixed three-word units taking a person through the preposition, and neither can be split: ✗ look him up to, ✗ look down them on.
entries.passive: yes — unusually free for prepositional verbs, as the entry notes: he was looked up to by everyone in the shop, she was looked down on for years.
entries.see also: look at · look forward to · think of · approve of · disapprove of

entries.meaning: Choose a field as the main, or the secondary, focus of a college degree.
examples: She majored in mechanical engineering and minored in Portuguese.
Half the people I know who majored in philosophy ended up in software.
He double majored in history and studio art, which took five years.
You don't have to major in the subject to take the seminar.
Nobody majors in that anymore; the department closed in 2018.
A minor in statistics is worth more on the transcript than most electives.
entries.русский: специализироваться на (основной профиль); брать вторым профилем; амер. вуз
entries.register: neutral — standard American college vocabulary; British speakers say read [a subject] or do a degree in
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a field of study. No gerund (✗ major in studying biology), no infinitive, no clause. The verb has no other object: ✗ she majored biology, ✗ she majored to biology.
entries.pattern: major in [a subject] · minor in [a subject] · double major in [X] and [Y] · major in [X] with a minor in [Y] · her major is [a subject] · a major in [a subject] — the noun keeps in
entries.contrast: Major in is what a student does; specialize in is what a professional does. You major in economics in college and specialize in bankruptcy work afterward. The preposition never changes: ✗ major on chemistry is not American English, and ✗ graduate in chemistry is not either — Americans graduate with a degree in chemistry or simply graduate from a school. Note that the same in stays on the noun: a major in chemistry, a minor in Spanish.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative; a course of study you pursue: she's majoring in biology.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the field always comes through in, and the verb has no other object: ✗ she majored biology, ✗ she majored to biology.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and the prepositional passive does not exist: ✗ biology was majored in by half her class.
entries.see also: specialize in · participate in · succeed in · apply for, apply to · in

entries.meaning: Be a consideration that weighs against a conclusion or a course of action.
examples: Everything in the record militates against a finding of bad faith.
The cost of relocation militates against moving the plant at all.
Two factors militate against raising rates before the fall.
His inexperience militates against giving him the district by himself.
Nothing in the survey militates against the committee's reading of the data.
The short timeline militates against a full environmental review.
entries.русский: говорить против, свидетельствовать не в пользу — книжн.
entries.register: formal — academic writing, judicial opinions, and policy analysis. An American meets it in a law review or a peer-reviewed paper, almost never in speech.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a conclusion, a finding, an outcome, or a course of action, or a gerund (militates against raising rates). No to-infinitive (✗ militates against to raise rates) and no clause. The subject is a fact or a consideration, never a person: ✗ the senator militates against the bill — a person argues against it.
entries.pattern: [a fact, a factor] militate against [a conclusion, a course] · militate against [verb-ing] · militate in favor of [something] — the much rarer positive
entries.contrast: Militate is not mitigate, and ✗ mitigate against is the single commonest error in this corner of the language. Mitigate is transitive and means lessen: mitigate the damage, mitigating circumstances. Militate against means count as a reason against something. The two are unrelated words, and an editor will catch the swap every time. If the sentence would work with argues against or weighs against, militate is the word you want; if it would work with reduces, you want mitigate.
entries.verb type: stative — a fact or consideration counts as a reason against something; nothing is done, and the subject is never a person: ✗ the senator militates against the bill. Not the transitive mitigate: ✗ mitigate against.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the conclusion opposed always comes through against; there is no bare object: ✗ militates the conclusion.
entries.passive: no — intransitive and stative; ✗ raising rates was militated against. (Transitive mitigate, the word people mean by mistake, passivizes fine: the damage was mitigated.)
entries.see also: insure against · protect from, protect against · warn about, warn against · decide on, decide against · against

entries.meaning: Ask a court or a meeting formally for a ruling or an action.
examples: The defense moved for a directed verdict at the close of the state's case.
Counsel moved for a continuance, citing the witness's surgery.
Both parties moved for summary judgment, and the judge denied both motions.
I move for adjournment.
The plaintiff moved to strike two paragraphs of the answer.
She moved that the vote be taken by roll call.
entries.русский: ходатайствовать о — вносить формальное предложение в суде или на собрании; юр.
entries.register: formal — courtroom and parliamentary procedure. An American meets it on a docket (defendant moves for summary judgment), in a transcript, or at a meeting run under Robert's Rules.
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase naming the relief or action requested: summary judgment, a mistrial, a continuance, dismissal, adjournment. No gerund (✗ move for dismissing the case) and no clause after for. The verb's other two frames use no preposition at all: move to [verb] is a to-infinitive (moved to dismiss), and move that [clause] takes a subjunctive (I move that the meeting be adjourned).
entries.pattern: move for [relief] · move to [verb] — infinitive, not a preposition · move that [clause] — subjunctive · a motion for [relief] · a motion to [verb] — the nouns split the same way
entries.contrast: Three frames, one verb, and the preposition is only in the first. Moved for summary judgment, moved to dismiss, and moved that the case be reassigned are all correct and all mean ask formally; ✗ moved for to dismiss and ✗ moved for that the case be reassigned are not. Against the neighbors: you move for relief inside a case that already exists, you petition for something to start a proceeding, and you apply for a permit or a job. And do not confuse any of this with everyday move to Denver, where to marks direction.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and performative: saying it does it, in court or under Robert's Rules. Non-progressive in use — defendant moves for summary judgment.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in this frame — the relief comes through for; the verb's other two frames take a to-infinitive (moved to dismiss) or a subjunctive clause (moved that the meeting be adjourned), never a bare object: ✗ moved summary judgment.
entries.passive: no — ✗ summary judgment was moved for is not idiomatic; the record instead passivizes the ruling: the motion was granted, summary judgment was denied.
entries.see also: petition for · apply for, apply to · ask for, ask about · comply with · for

entries.meaning: State that you are against something.
examples: Two members objected to holding the vote without a quorum.
She objects to being called by her first name in court.
Nobody objected to the change until the invoices arrived.
He objected to my parking in front of his house, which is a public street.
The defense objected and was overruled.
I don't object to the fee; I object to finding out about it afterward.
entries.русский: возражать против — после to герундий: object to being questioned
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or possessive plus gerund (objected to my being there) — to is a preposition here, so a to-infinitive is impossible: ✗ object to be questioned, ✗ object to answer. Before a clause the preposition drops: objected that the sample was too small.
entries.pattern: object to [noun phrase] · object to [verb-ing] · object to [someone's] -ing · object that [clause] · object (alone) · I object. · objection to [something]
entries.contrast: Same trap as look forward to, and the same test defuses it: you can say object to the delay, so to is a preposition, so it must be object to being delayed. Note the difference from oppose, which is transitive and takes no preposition at all — oppose the merger, ✗ oppose to the merger — although the adjective goes back to a preposition, opposed to the merger. In register, object to is stronger and more formal than mind (I don't mind waiting) and weaker than refuse.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a speech act in the courtroom or the meeting (counsel objected), and by extension a standing position (she objects to being called ma'am).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no direct object, unlike transitive oppose: oppose the merger, ✗ oppose to the merger, against object to the merger. Before a clause the preposition drops: objected that the sample was too small.
entries.passive: restricted — fine in formal minutes and briefs (the proposal was objected to by two members, the exhibit was objected to), unnatural in speech.
entries.see also: look forward to · oppose · complain about · approve of · disapprove of · agree to · insist on

entries.meaning: Come into someone's mind.
examples: It never occurred to me that he might say no.
Did it occur to anyone to check whether the room was booked?
The solution occurred to her on the drive home.
It occurs to me that we've been arguing about two different documents.
It hadn't occurred to the committee to ask the tenants.
The thought must have occurred to him at some point.
entries.русский: приходить в голову кому-то — it never occurred to me; ср. occur происходить
entries.complement: to takes a person only. The subject is nearly always the dummy it, followed by a that-clause or a to-infinitive: it occurred to me that she was right, it never occurred to him to ask. A noun phrase subject also works: the idea occurred to her in the shower. There is no gerund pattern here at all.
entries.pattern: it occur to [someone] that [clause] · it occur to [someone] to [verb] · [an idea] occur to [someone] · it never occurred to me · occur (alone — happen)
entries.contrast: Two verbs share one spelling. Plain occur means happen and takes no preposition: the outage occurred at 3 a.m., ✗ occurred to 3 a.m. Occur to means come into someone's mind, and always names a person. American speakers use the negative far more than the positive: It never occurred to me is the everyday form. Note the spelling of the inflections — occurred, occurring, with two r's.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic but punctual, an idea arriving; it still rejects the progressive: ✗ it is occurring to me that she was right. Note the spellings occurred, occurring.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the subject is the idea (usually dummy it plus a that-clause or infinitive) and to takes the person: it never occurred to him to ask.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and the person cannot become a subject: ✗ I was occurred to, ✗ he was never occurred to.
entries.see also: remind of · think of · explain to

entries.meaning: Apply one amount against another so that the two cancel.
examples: Capital losses may be offset against capital gains in the same tax year.
The contractor sought to set off the cost of repairs against the final invoice.
Any advance is offset against the royalties the book eventually earns.
Higher volume was offset by a thinner margin on every unit.
The tenant set off three months of unmade repairs against the rent she owed.
Overtime in December was offset against the hours he had banked in the fall.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌɔfˈsɛt əɡənst/ — the verb stresses the second syllable, the noun the first (an ˈoffset)
entries.русский: зачитывать одно против другого — засчитывать в погашение; фин./юр.
entries.register: formal — accounting, tax, and contract drafting
entries.complement: the amount applied is the direct object and against takes the amount it is applied to: offset the loss against this year's gains. No gerund (✗ offset against having paid twice), no infinitive, no clause. Both slots must name quantities of the same kind — money against money, hours against hours: ✗ offset the delay against the budget.
entries.variants: Set off against is the same operation in the language of contracts and litigation, and its noun is a setoff (or set-off): the buyer asserted a setoff against the unpaid balance. Note also the commoner everyday frame offset by, where the counterweight follows a passive: the gains were offset by higher fuel costs.
entries.pattern: offset [an amount] against [another amount] · set off [a claim] against [a debt] · [something] be offset by [something else] · a setoff against [a balance] · deduct [an amount] from [a total] — the neighboring frame with from
entries.contrast: Offset against subtracts one figure from another of the same kind; deduct from removes a figure from a total. You offset capital losses against capital gains, but you deduct mileage from taxable income. Offset by is the passive counterweight frame and needs no arithmetic at all (the raise was offset by the new premium), and make up for is the plain-English version of the whole idea. In British and legal drafting set off against dominates; American filings use both, and offset is the safer everyday choice.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an arithmetical operation performed on two quantities of the same kind.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the amount applied is the direct object and against names what it is applied to: offset the loss against this year's gains; the object is obligatory: ✗ offset against the gains.
entries.passive: yes — the loss can be offset against next year's gains, and the counterweight frame is passive by nature: the raise was offset by the new premium.
entries.see also: make up for · compensate for · charge with, charge for · pay for · against

entries.meaning: Take an active part in something.
examples: Four hundred families participated in the pilot program.
He participated in drafting the original charter.
Students who participate in the survey get a gift card.
Only two states declined to participate in the settlement.
You can attend without participating in the breakout sessions.
She participated in every rehearsal and missed the performance.
entries.русский: участвовать в — принимать деятельное участие
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (participated in drafting the report) — never a to-infinitive. Participate is intransitive and cannot take a bare object: ✗ participate the study.
entries.pattern: participate in [an activity, a program, a study] · participate in [verb-ing] · participate (alone) · take part in [something] — the plainer synonym
entries.contrast: Participate to and ✗ participate at are errors; the preposition is fixed at in. Take part in means exactly the same thing in plainer English and is what Americans say out loud. Keep it apart from attend, which is transitive and takes no preposition at all — attend the meeting, ✗ attend to the meeting — so she attended the workshop (was present) and she participated in the workshop (did the exercises) are genuinely different claims.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; doing the exercises, not merely being present — compare transitive attend, which claims only presence.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the verb cannot take a bare object: ✗ participate the study. Everything comes through in.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and the prepositional passive is unidiomatic: ✗ the study was participated in by forty volunteers. Say forty volunteers took part.
entries.see also: involve in · attend · contribute to · compete with · interfere in

entries.meaning: Ask a court, an agency, or an official body formally for something.
examples: The company petitioned for Chapter 11 protection in March.
Six hundred residents petitioned for a special election.
She petitioned the court for sole custody after the second incident.
Counsel petitioned for review, and the Supreme Court declined to hear it.
The neighbors petitioned the zoning board for a variance and lost twice.
He petitioned for clemency every year for a decade.
entries.русский: подавать ходатайство о — официально просить суд или орган; юр.
entries.register: formal — courts, agencies, legislatures, and civic organizing. Americans meet the frame in the First Amendment itself: the right to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase naming what is asked for — review, custody, bankruptcy, clemency, a variance, a recount. No gerund (✗ petition for getting the fee waived) and no clause. The body petitioned is a direct object placed before for: petition the board for a hearing. A to-infinitive frame exists and is not this preposition: petitioned the council to rezone the parcel.
entries.pattern: petition for [relief, a status, a hearing] · petition [a body] for [something] · petition [a body] to [verb] — infinitive · file a petition for [something] · petition in bankruptcy
entries.contrast: Three verbs, three settings. You apply for a permit, a job, or a loan — routine, on a form. You petition for something that requires a body to exercise judgment, and the word implies a formal filing or a signed request. You move for relief inside a case already pending. Sue for is different again: it names the remedy you are demanding in litigation (sue for damages). Note that the noun keeps the preposition — a petition for review, a petition for certiorari — and that with a person the verb goes straight to the object: petition the mayor, not ✗ petition to the mayor.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and formal: a filing or a signed request, a single act.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with for alone (petitioned for review), transitive when the body petitioned is named, which takes no preposition: petition the board for a hearing, ✗ petition to the mayor.
entries.passive: restricted — the person-object promotes (the board was petitioned for a hearing), the for-object does not: ✗ review was petitioned for.
entries.see also: move for · apply for, apply to · ask for, ask about · foreclose on · for

entries.meaning: Intend to do something.
examples: We're planning on driving up Thursday night.
Don't plan on getting a seat if you show up at seven.
She plans on finishing the certificate in the spring.
Plan on about two hours with traffic.
They planned for a shortfall and got a surplus instead.
I hadn't planned on any of this.
entries.русский: рассчитывать, планировать — после on герундий: plan on staying; разг.
entries.register: neutral American; more common in the U.S. than in Britain
entries.complement: gerund or noun phrase (plan on staying, plan on rain) — never a to-infinitive after the preposition (✗ plan on to stay). The infinitive belongs to the other frame: plan to stay, with no preposition. Both are correct and mean the same thing.
entries.pattern: plan on [verb-ing] · plan on [noun phrase] · plan to [verb] · plan for [a contingency] · plan [an event] · plan on [someone] -ing
entries.contrast: Plan on doing is characteristically American; British English leans harder on plan to do. Both are standard in the U.S., with plan on slightly more casual and slightly more provisional — I plan to retire in June sounds settled, I'm planning on retiring in June sounds like it could move. Plan for is different: it means prepare for a possibility (plan for a bad winter), not intend. And plan on someone doing something means count on it: don't plan on him being early.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; forming an intention, freely progressive and slightly provisional: I'm planning on retiring in June.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with on plus a gerund or noun (plan on staying, plan on rain); transitive bare (plan the trip), and with a to-infinitive and no preposition (plan to stay).
entries.passive: restricted — the bare transitive passivizes (the route was planned by a committee), the prepositional frame does not: ✗ staying an extra night was planned on.
entries.see also: decide on · commit to · prepare for · hope for · count on · depend on

entries.meaning: Indicate something with a finger, or indicate it with evidence.
examples: He pointed at the crack in the foundation and said nothing.
Every indicator points to a soft landing, which is what they said last time too.
Don't point at people.
She pointed the flashlight at the ceiling to see the water stain.
The report points to deferred maintenance as the underlying cause.
I should point out that none of this was in the original scope.
entries.русский: показывать пальцем на (at); указывать на, свидетельствовать о (to)
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause. Point out is a separate, separable phrasal verb that does take a that-clause: point out that the numbers don't match, and point something out to someone.
entries.pattern: point at [a person, a thing] · point to [a direction, a piece of evidence] · point [something] at [something] · point out [something] · point out to [someone] that [clause] · point toward [a conclusion]
entries.contrast: At is the physical gesture; to is the argument. She pointed at the map is a finger; the data point to a slowdown is an inference. Where a person is the target, point at is faintly rude — American children are told not to point at people — while point to someone as a model is a compliment. Point out is a third thing entirely: it means draw attention to a fact, takes an object or a clause, and is separable (point it out). ✗ point on is not English in any of these senses.
entries.verb type: both — dynamic in the gesture sense (she was pointing at the map); stative in the evidential sense, which resists the progressive: ✗ the data are pointing to a slowdown is far weaker than the data point to a slowdown.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in both — ✗ point the map. The verb is transitive only when what you aim is the object: point a finger at him, point the camera at the door.
entries.passive: restricted — the gesture sense passivizes with a person (nobody likes being pointed at); the evidential sense does not: ✗ a slowdown is pointed to by the data.
entries.see also: aim at · refer to · lead to · stare at · comment on

entries.meaning: Like one thing better than another.
examples: She prefers mornings to evenings for anything requiring a brain.
I prefer driving to flying for anything under six hours.
Most of the staff prefer the older system.
He'd prefer to handle it himself, which is the whole problem.
They prefer email to phone calls, and they are correct.
I'd prefer that we settle this before the meeting.
entries.русский: предпочитать что-то чему-то — здесь to значит чем, а не к
entries.complement: In the comparison frame, to is a preposition and both sides must be the same kind of thing — two noun phrases (prefer tea to coffee) or two gerunds (prefer walking to driving). ✗ prefer to walk to drive is impossible. In the other frame, prefer takes a bare to-infinitive with no comparison (I'd prefer to walk), and would prefer takes that plus a subjunctive (I'd prefer that he not come).
entries.pattern: prefer [A] to [B] · prefer [verb-ing] to [verb-ing] · prefer to [verb] · prefer [verb-ing] · would prefer [someone] to [verb] · would prefer that [clause]
entries.contrast: The trap is that prefer uses to for two completely different jobs. I prefer coffee to tea — preposition, comparison. I prefer to drink coffee — infinitive marker, no comparison. You cannot run both at once, which is why ✗ I prefer to walk to drive collapses; say I prefer walking to driving, or switch to I'd rather walk than drive, which is the form Americans actually use. Note that than is impossible with prefer in careful writing (✗ prefer coffee than tea), even though it is common in speech.
entries.verb type: stative — a standing preference, not an act, and it rejects the progressive: ✗ I am preferring tea to coffee.
entries.transitivity: transitive — prefer tea to coffee, prefer walking to driving; both sides of the comparison must match, so ✗ prefer to walk to drive collapses. The object is obligatory: ✗ she prefers to coffee.
entries.passive: restricted — the agentless passive is standard in impersonal writing (the metric version is preferred to the older one), but the stative verb refuses a by-phrase: ✗ tea is preferred to coffee by her.
entries.see also: choose between · compare to · decide on · long for · in preference to

entries.meaning: Get ready for something in advance.
examples: The whole county spent a week preparing for the storm.
She's been preparing for the boards since March.
Nothing prepares you for how loud a newborn is.
Prepare for having to explain this twice.
They were prepared for a long negotiation and got a handshake in twenty minutes.
He's prepared to walk away if the number doesn't move.
entries.русский: готовиться к — заранее приводить себя в готовность
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase or a gerund (prepare for having to move) — never a to-infinitive after the preposition (✗ prepare for to move). Prepare also takes a bare to-infinitive with no preposition: prepare to move, be prepared to negotiate — and that frame means readiness to act, not readiness for an event.
entries.pattern: prepare for [an event] · prepare for [verb-ing] · prepare [someone] for [something] · prepare to [verb] · be prepared for [something] · be prepared to [verb]
entries.contrast: Prepared for and prepared to are not the same claim. We're prepared for a strike means we have contingencies; We're prepared to strike means we're willing to do it. Reversing them in a negotiation would be expensive. Compare get ready for, the plain synonym, and provide for, which means support financially. Note also transitive prepare: you prepare a meal, prepare a brief, prepare the ground — no preposition.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative: they've been preparing for a strike all month.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with for (prepare for a strike) or a bare to-infinitive (prepared to negotiate); transitive with no preposition (prepare a meal, prepare a brief).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive frame — the brief was prepared overnight. The prepositional frame is restricted: everything had been prepared for is possible, ✗ a strike was prepared for by management is not.
entries.see also: plan on · provide for · allow for · protect against · wait for

entries.meaning: Be the person in charge of a proceeding, a body, or a period.
examples: Judge Alvarez presided over the trial for eleven weeks.
She presided over the commission during its most productive stretch.
He presided over a merger that cost four hundred people their jobs.
The vice president presides over the Senate and votes only to break a tie.
A retired bishop presided at the funeral.
Whoever presides over that department inherits a decade of deferred maintenance.
entries.русский: председательствовать на, возглавлять — руководить заседанием, органом, эпохой
entries.register: formal — courts, boards, ceremonies, and, with a twist of irony, institutional decline
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a proceeding, a body, an era, or a process: preside over the trial, over the committee, over the collapse of the company. No gerund (✗ preside over running the meeting), no infinitive, no clause. The verb needs the preposition — ✗ preside the meeting is not English, though chair the meeting is.
entries.variants: Preside at is used for a single ceremony or sitting — preside at the wedding, at the hearing — while preside over takes the whole proceeding, body, or period. Both are standard; over is far commoner.
entries.pattern: preside over [a trial, a meeting, an agency, an era] · preside at [a ceremony, a hearing] · preside — intransitive (Judge Alvarez presided) · presiding judge / presiding officer · the president of [an organization] — the noun takes of
entries.contrast: Preside over always takes a preposition; its synonyms usually do not. Chair the committee, run the meeting, and oversee the project are all transitive, and ✗ preside the committee is the error that follows from them. The ironic use is worth knowing because it is everywhere in American commentary: he presided over the loss of half the endowment attributes no action to the subject at all, only the office he held while it happened.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative; holding the chair while something runs its course, and progressive: Judge Ellis is presiding over the trial.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the verb needs its preposition: ✗ preside the meeting, unlike transitive chair, run, and oversee.
entries.passive: yes — one of the fully natural prepositional passives: the trial was presided over by Judge Ellis, a hearing presided over by the deputy commissioner.
entries.see also: prevail over · devolve on, devolve upon · participate in · belong to · over

entries.meaning: Win out over an opponent, a rival claim, or an obstacle.
examples: The plaintiffs prevailed over three motions to dismiss before reaching trial.
Where the two provisions conflict, the later one prevails over the earlier.
Nebraska prevailed over a heavily favored opponent in double overtime.
Common sense finally prevailed over the committee's fondness for process.
She prevailed in the arbitration but spent more than she recovered.
His sister prevailed upon him to stay through the holidays.
entries.русский: одержать верх над — победить соперника, притязание или препятствие
entries.register: formal — law, sports writing, and scripture-flavored prose
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an opponent, a rival claim, or an obstacle. No gerund (✗ prevailed over being outspent), no infinitive, no clause. The verb also stands alone (the plaintiff prevailed) and takes other prepositions in other senses, listed below.
entries.variants: Prevail against is the older, more literary form and survives in fixed phrases (the gates of hell shall not prevail against it); in legal writing prevail over a competing provision is the standard. Prevail in names the arena rather than the loser: prevailed in the arbitration.
entries.pattern: prevail over / against [an opponent, a competing claim] · prevail in [a suit, an election] · prevail — intransitive (the plaintiff prevailed) · prevail on / upon [someone] to [verb] — persuade, a different pattern · the prevailing wage, the prevailing wind — be widespread
entries.contrast: Two patterns, and confusing them changes the meaning completely. Prevail over someone is defeating them; prevail on someone to do something is talking them into it — and that second frame takes a person and then a to-infinitive: prevailed on her to stay another year. A third, intransitive sense means be widespread or hold sway (the practice still prevails in rural counties, the prevailing view). In drafting, this section shall prevail over any conflicting provision is the standard way to say which clause wins.
entries.verb type: both — dynamic in the defeat sense, an achievement (the plaintiff prevailed over three co-defendants); stative in the be-widespread sense, which rejects the progressive: ✗ the practice is prevailing in rural counties, the prevailing view.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every sense — the opponent comes through over, the person you talk around through on plus a to-infinitive (prevailed on her to stay); ✗ prevailed the defendant.
entries.passive: no for prevail over — intransitive: ✗ the defendant was prevailed over. But prevail on passivizes and is idiomatic: she was prevailed upon to stay another year.
entries.see also: preside over · compete with, compete against, compete for · militate against · insist on · over

entries.meaning: Stop something from happening, or stop someone from acting.
examples: A bad hinge prevented the door from closing all the way.
Nothing prevents you from filing an amended return.
The guardrail prevented the car from going into the ravine.
She was prevented from testifying by a scheduling order.
Two inches of insulation prevents most of the heat loss.
What's preventing us from starting today?
entries.русский: не давать сделать, предотвращать — после from герундий: prevent him from leaving
entries.complement: gerund or noun phrase — never a to-infinitive (✗ prevent him to leave, one of the highest-frequency advanced errors in English). The only correct verb form after from is -ing: prevent him from leaving. Prevent also takes a plain object with no preposition: prevent an accident.
entries.pattern: prevent [someone / something] from [verb-ing] · prevent [something] · be prevented from [verb-ing] · prevent [someone] [verb-ing] — British; add from in American English
entries.contrast: Prevent someone to do something does not exist. The pattern is from plus -ing, and it is shared by a whole family: stop from, keep from, discourage from, prohibit from, ban from, bar from, deter from, hinder from, restrain from. Their positive counterparts take infinitives — allow to, permit to, enable to, encourage to — which is exactly why the error is so persistent. British English also permits prevent him leaving with no preposition; American editing puts the from back in.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; stopping something before it happens.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person or thing stopped is the direct object and from takes a gerund: prevent him from leaving, ✗ prevent him to leave. Bare transitive is also fine: prevent an accident.
entries.passive: yes — he was prevented from boarding, the leak was prevented. The passive keeps the same from plus -ing: ✗ he was prevented to board.
entries.see also: discourage from · protect from · allow for · interfere with

entries.meaning: Keep someone or something safe.
examples: A good hat protects you from more sun than sunscreen does.
The statute protects whistleblowers from retaliation.
The vaccine protects against four strains.
Nothing protects a small business against a bad landlord.
The seawall protects the district from ordinary tides and nothing more.
She protected her sources from everyone, including her editor.
entries.русский: защищать от — оберегать от опасности или вреда
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (protect against having to pay twice) — never a to-infinitive. Both prepositions take the same complements and are largely interchangeable; see the contrast for the tendency that separates them.
entries.pattern: protect [someone] from [harm] · protect [someone] against [a risk] · be protected from / against [something] · protect [something] — no preposition · protection from / against [something]
entries.contrast: From leans toward harm already present; against leans toward risk anticipated. You protect a child from the sun (it's shining now) and protect a portfolio against inflation (it might come). The overlap is enormous and no American will misunderstand either. One place against wins outright is inoculation and insurance: vaccinated against measles, insured against flood, hedge against a downturn — ✗ vaccinated from measles is wrong. Guard against takes only against, and shield from takes only from.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and often durative: the coating is protecting the deck from UV.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person or thing protected is the direct object; the object is obligatory, reflexive if need be: ✗ protect from the sun with nobody named. Both prepositions take the same complements.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the everyday form — the portfolio is protected against inflation, she was protected from the worst of it, vaccinated against measles.
entries.see also: prevent from · save from · hide from · deprive of · against

entries.meaning: Supply something, support someone, or stipulate something.
examples: The district provides every ninth grader with a laptop.
They provided coffee and donuts for the volunteers.
He provided for his mother for the last eleven years of her life.
The bylaws provide for removing a director by two-thirds vote.
The grant provides the lab with three years of funding.
Nothing in the policy provides for a refund.
entries.русский: обеспечивать — provide smb with smth = provide smth for smb; provide for также содержать
entries.complement: with takes the thing supplied and the recipient is the direct object: provide students with laptops. for takes the beneficiary, or the contingency: provide for a family, the contract provides for arbitration. A gerund works after for (provides for extending the deadline); ✗ a to-infinitive does not.
entries.pattern: provide [someone] with [something] · provide [something] for [someone] · provide for [a family] · [a document] provide for [something] · provide that [clause] — legal · provide [something]
entries.two frames say the same thing with the a: provide the crew with meals = provide meals for the crew. Mixing them (✗ provide the crew meals in formal writing, ✗ provide with meals to the crew) is the error. Then provide for on its own means support financially (he provided for four children on a machinist's wage), and in a contract it means stipulate (the lease provides for a five percent escalator). The legal provide that takes a full clause and no preposition.
entries.verb type: both — dynamic in the supply and support senses (the district is providing students with laptops, he provided for four children); stative in the drafting sense, which rejects the progressive: ✗ the lease is providing for a five percent escalator.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in provide students with laptops and provide meals; intransitive with the preposition in provide for a family and the contract provides for arbitration. Not ditransitive in careful writing: ✗ provide the crew meals.
entries.passive: yes — students were provided with laptops, meals were provided for the crew, and the drafting sense gives a clean prepositional passive: arbitration is provided for in section 12.
entries.see also: cover with · pay for · prepare for · allow for · with

entries.meaning: Impose a penalty on someone for something they did.
examples: Two students were punished for something a third one did.
He was punished for taking the complaint over his manager's head.
The rule punishes small filers for an honest mistake.
Nobody should be punished for asking a question.
Tampering is punishable by a fine of up to ten thousand dollars.
She punished him for the lie rather than the thing he lied about.
entries.русский: наказывать за — налагать взыскание за содеянное
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (punished for lying) — never a to-infinitive (✗ punished for to lie) and never a clause. The person punished is a direct object: ✗ punish to him. The penalty itself takes with or by: punishable by a fine.
entries.pattern: punish [someone] for [something / verb-ing] · be punished for [something] · punish [someone] with [a penalty] · punishable by [a sentence] · punishment for [an offense]
entries.contrast: The offense takes for; the penalty takes by or with. He was punished for the leak names what he did; punishable by five years names what happens to him. ✗ punish someone of and ✗ punish someone about are errors. The noun keeps the same split: punishment for the offense, a sentence of five years. Compare blame for (assign fault, no penalty), charge with (formal accusation), and fine someone for (a specific monetary penalty, same shape as punish).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; imposing a penalty, a single act.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person punished is the direct object, the offense takes for, and the penalty takes by or with: ✗ punish to him, ✗ punish someone of the leak.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the commoner form — he was punished for the leak, the offense is punishable by five years.
entries.see also: blame for · charge with · accuse of · forgive for · excuse for

entries.meaning: Meet the requirements for something.
examples: A family of four qualifies for assistance under about sixty thousand.
Two of the four teams qualified for the regional round.
He isn't qualified for the position and everyone in the room knew it.
She's qualified to practice in Ohio and Michigan.
Does a burst pipe qualify as an emergency repair?
Very few of the applications actually qualified for review.
entries.русский: иметь право на, подходить под условия — соответствовать требованиям
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase — no gerund in ordinary use (✗ qualify for getting aid; say qualify for aid). To put a verb after qualify, use the infinitive with no preposition: qualify to vote, qualified to practice in three states. As takes a category: qualifies as a hardship.
entries.pattern: qualify for [a benefit, a program, a round] · qualify to [verb] · qualify as [a category] · be qualified for [a job] · qualify [a statement] — hedge it
entries.contrast: Qualify for is eligibility; qualify to is capacity; qualify as is classification. She qualifies for the subsidy (income), she's qualified to teach chemistry (credential), that qualifies as an emergency (definition). All three are live and none takes the others' preposition. A fourth, transitive sense means hedge or limit: he qualified the claim in a footnote — no preposition at all, and the opposite of endorsing it.
entries.verb type: both — stative in the eligibility sense, which resists the progressive: ✗ she is qualifying for the subsidy; dynamic in the athletic sense (he qualified for the finals) and in the transitive hedge sense (he qualified the claim in a footnote).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with for and as (qualifies as a hardship) and with a bare to-infinitive (qualified to practice in three states); transitive in the hedge sense: qualify the statement.
entries.passive: no in the stative eligibility sense — ✗ the subsidy is qualified for by most applicants. Yes in the hedge sense: the claim was carefully qualified in a footnote.
entries.see also: apply for · compete for · prepare for · vote for · consist of

entries.meaning: Behave in a particular way because of something that happened.
examples: Markets reacted to the announcement before anyone had read it.
She reacted to the news better than I expected.
About one patient in a thousand reacts to the dye.
He reacted to being corrected in front of the class exactly as you'd guess.
The whole neighborhood reacted against the rezoning.
Chlorine reacts with ammonia to produce something you do not want in your bathroom.
entries.русский: реагировать на — вести себя определённым образом в ответ; после to герундий
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (reacted to being asked) — never a to-infinitive (✗ react to be asked) and never a clause. React is intransitive: ✗ react the news. In chemistry the preposition is with: sodium reacts with water.
entries.pattern: react to [something] · react to [verb-ing] · [a substance] react with [another] · react against [a trend, an upbringing] · a reaction to [something]
entries.contrast: React on is an error in the ordinary sense; the preposition is to. Three related shapes: react to responds to a stimulus, react with is the chemical sense, and react against means push back at something you were formed by (a generation reacting against the earnestness of its parents). Note the medical use — react to a drug, and the noun an allergic reaction to, both with to — and compare respond to, which is interchangeable but implies more deliberation.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and involuntary, more immediate than considered respond to; freely progressive: the market is reacting to the announcement.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the stimulus always needs a preposition: ✗ react the news. to for a stimulus, with for chemistry, against for a generation pushing back.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and the prepositional passive is not English here: ✗ the announcement was reacted to badly. Say the announcement went over badly.
entries.see also: adapt to · object to · refer to · occur to

entries.meaning: Make two things agree, make peace with someone, or accept what cannot be changed.
examples: The two brothers reconciled with each other after eleven years.
I can't reconcile his account with what the timestamps show.
Accounting reconciles the daily receipts with the deposit slips every Monday.
She eventually reconciled herself to living on half the income.
How do you reconcile a hiring freeze with opening two new offices?
They were reconciled about a month before he died.
entries.русский: мирить(ся) с; согласовывать с — а reconcile oneself to смиряться с неизбежным
entries.register: neutral — the reconcile X with Y frame is standard in accounting and in argument
entries.complement: with takes a noun phrase — a person, a set of figures, a claim — or a gerund (reconcile that with claiming to be neutral); never a to-infinitive (✗ reconcile it with to claim neutrality). The separate reflexive pattern reconcile oneself to also takes a noun phrase or a gerund (reconciled herself to losing the house) and never an infinitive (✗ reconciled himself to lose it).
entries.pattern: reconcile [X] with [Y] · be reconciled with [person] · reconcile with [person] · reconcile oneself to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · be reconciled to [noun phrase / verb-ing]
entries.contrast: With joins two things that ought to match; to resigns you to one you cannot change. She reconciled with her father is a repaired relationship; she reconciled herself to her father's decision is acceptance without repair, and the second cannot use with. In accounting both prepositions are live: reconcile the statement with the ledger is the general idiom, reconcile the statement to the ledger the bookkeeper's. Note that the intransitive the couple reconciled needs no preposition at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: repairing a relationship, squaring two sets of figures, or coming to accept something (she's slowly reconciling herself to it).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in reconcile the statement with the ledger and in the reflexive reconcile oneself to; intransitive in the couple reconciled and she reconciled with her father.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive frame — the two accounts can't be reconciled with each other, the figures were reconciled to the ledger. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ her father was reconciled with.
entries.see also: agree with · comply with · compare with · differ from · with

entries.meaning: Get better after illness or difficulty, or get something back.
examples: He's still recovering from the knee replacement.
The town never really recovered from the plant closing.
It took her a semester to recover from a bad first year.
Divers recovered the black box from about ninety feet of water.
Nobody recovers from that kind of press in one news cycle.
Recovering from being publicly wrong is a skill worth having.
entries.русский: оправляться после (болезни, беды); а recover без предлога возвращать себе
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (recovering from having the flu) — never a to-infinitive, never a clause. The transitive verb is a different pattern with no preposition: recover the data, recover damages — and there from names the source instead (recover the money from the insurer).
entries.pattern: recover from [an illness, a setback] · recover from [verb-ing] · recover [something lost] · recover [something] from [a source] · make a recovery from [something]
entries.contrast: Intransitive recover from is about getting better; transitive recover is about getting something back. She recovered from the surgery and They recovered the stolen equipment share no structure at all. Watch the ambiguity in recover from: the firm recovered from the loss means it bounced back, while the firm recovered from the insurer means it collected. Compare get over, the everyday spoken synonym of the first sense, and heal from, which is newer and common in American therapeutic usage.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a process in the intransitive sense (she's still recovering from the surgery) and a single act of retrieval in the transitive one.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with from naming the illness or setback (recover from the loss); transitive with no preposition in the get-something-back sense (recover the data, recover damages), where from names the source instead.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the stolen equipment was recovered, the fees were recovered from the insurer. No in the intransitive: ✗ the surgery was recovered from.
entries.see also: suffer from · benefit from · escape from · die of · cope with

entries.meaning: Step out of a case or a decision because you have a conflict of interest.
examples: The judge recused herself from the case because her nephew worked for the defendant.
Two board members recused themselves from voting on the contract.
He should have recused himself from the review of his own department.
The attorney general recused from the investigation last spring.
She recuses herself from anything involving her former firm.
If the conflict is disclosed early, a member can recuse and the meeting goes on.
entries.русский: брать самоотвод в — устраняться из-за конфликта интересов; юр.
entries.register: legal — an American meets this word in a judge's order, an ethics memo, or a news story about a justice stepping aside; in conversation you would say step aside or sit this one out
entries.complement: the verb normally takes a reflexive object first — recuse himself from — and from then takes a noun phrase or a gerund (recused herself from hearing the appeal); never a to-infinitive (✗ recused himself from to hear it). American journalism now also drops the reflexive (the judge recused from the case) and even the object (the justice recused), but a brief will keep himself.
entries.pattern: recuse [oneself] from [a case, a vote, a decision] · recuse [oneself] from [verb-ing] · recuse from [noun phrase] · be recused from [a panel]
entries.contrast: Four verbs, four distances. Recuse from steps out of one matter because of a conflict and keeps the job; resign from leaves the job; abstain from keeps the seat and declines to vote; withdraw from says nothing about why. A judge who recuses herself from the case is still on the bench the next morning. The outsider's version is disqualify: a party moves to disqualify the judge, the judge recuses herself. ✗ Recuse of and ✗ recuse out of are errors.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and performative: the judge's stepping aside is done by saying so.
entries.transitivity: transitive with a reflexive object in careful writing — recuse himself from the case; American journalism now also runs it intransitively (the judge recused from the case, the justice recused), but a brief keeps himself.
entries.passive: no in edited legal prose — a reflexive object gives nothing to promote: ✗ he was recused from the case, which the press nonetheless prints. Use was disqualified when you need a passive.
entries.see also: refrain from · retire from · separate from · testify to · from

entries.meaning: Mention something, consult a source, or send someone onward.
examples: She never referred to the incident again.
Refer to the chart on page nine for the full schedule.
The clinic referred him to a specialist in Cleveland.
The term refers to any structure built before the 1968 code.
Everyone at the plant refers to it as the annex, though it isn't attached to anything.
The footnote refers to a study that has since been retracted.
entries.русский: ссылаться на; обращаться к (источнику); направлять к (специалисту); обозначать
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (referred to being underpaid) — never a to-infinitive (✗ refer to be underpaid). In the send-someone-onward frame the person is a direct object: refer the patient to a specialist. Note the doubled r in referred, referring, referral.
entries.pattern: refer to [something — mention] · refer to [a source — consult] · refer [someone] to [someone else] · [a word] refer to [a thing — denote] · refer to [something] as [a name]
entries.contrast: Four senses, one preposition, and they are told apart by what surrounds it. He referred to the memo (mentioned it), refer to the appendix (consult it), her doctor referred her to a cardiologist (sent her onward), "quorum" refers to the minimum number (denotes it). The compound referred to as is the standard formula for naming: the area referred to as the Loop. ✗ refer about is not English. Compare mention, which is transitive and takes no preposition — ✗ mention about it is a common error.
entries.verb type: both — dynamic in the mention, consult, and send-onward senses (she's referring to the appendix, her doctor referred her to a cardiologist); stative in the denote sense, which rejects the progressive: ✗ 'quorum' is referring to the minimum number.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with to in the mention, consult, and denote senses; transitive in the send-onward frame: refer the patient to a specialist.
entries.passive: yes — the case was referred to the appeals panel, and the prepositional passive is a fixed naming formula: the area referred to as the Loop. The denote sense stays awkward with a by-phrase: ✗ the minimum number is referred to by 'quorum'.
entries.see also: point to · comment on · consult with · introduce to · subscribe to

entries.meaning: Deliberately hold back from doing something.
examples: Please refrain from using flash photography in the gallery.
The judge asked both attorneys to refrain from interrupting each other.
He refrained from saying what everyone in the room was thinking.
Employees should refrain from discussing the settlement publicly.
She refrained from alcohol for the whole year of her residency.
I refrained from pointing out that the same thing happened last spring.
entries.русский: воздерживаться от — сознательно не делать; после from герундий
entries.register: formal — the language of signs, announcements, and policies (please refrain from smoking); in conversation Americans say don't or lay off
entries.complement: gerund, or a noun phrase naming an activity or substance (refrain from comment, refrain from alcohol) — never a to-infinitive (✗ refrain from to smoke, ✗ refrain to comment) and never a that-clause. The one who refrains is always the subject: you cannot ✗ refrain him from talking — that verb is prevent from or keep from.
entries.pattern: refrain from [verb-ing] · refrain from [noun phrase] · please refrain from [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Four ways of not doing something. Refrain from is a deliberate, usually temporary holding back; abstain from is a standing policy — from alcohol, from meat, from a vote; desist from is what a cease-and-desist letter demands; stop takes a bare gerund and no preposition (stop talking, ✗ stop from talking). And unlike prevent from and discourage from, refrain never takes an object of its own. ✗ Refrain of is an error.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a deliberate, usually temporary holding back, more occasional than policy-like abstain from.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the one who refrains is always the subject and the verb never takes an object of its own: ✗ refrain him from talking — that verb is prevent from or keep from.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and the prepositional passive is not used: ✗ comment was refrained from by the office. Say the office declined to comment.
entries.see also: prevent from · discourage from · recuse from · object to · from

entries.meaning: Concern something, identify with someone, or connect one thing to another.
examples: Nothing in the memo relates to the layoffs.
I can relate to wanting to quit halfway through a shift.
He has trouble relating to people he didn't grow up with.
The professor related the data to an earlier study out of Michigan.
All documents relating to the merger have to be preserved.
She's related to half the families in the county.
entries.русский: касаться чего-то; понимать, сочувствовать кому-то; излагать что-то кому-то
entries.register: neutral; the empathy sense (I can relate to that) is informal and thoroughly American
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (I can relate to being the new person) — never a to-infinitive (✗ relate to be the new person). A wh-clause is fine (everything relating to what happened that night). In the transitive relate X to Y frame both slots are noun phrases.
entries.pattern: [something] relate to [something] · relate to [someone / an experience] · relate to [verb-ing] · relate [X] to [Y] · be related to [someone] · relating to [topic]
entries.contrast: Three verbs wear one spelling. This relates to the second complaint means it concerns it; I can relate to her means I identify with her — informal, and the object may be a person, a feeling, or a whole situation; he related the story to us means he told it. Family is a fourth thing again and needs the passive participle: she's related to the governor, never ✗ she relates to the governor. The participle relating to is a stock connector in contracts and subpoenas, interchangeable with concerning and in relation to.
entries.verb type: both — stative in the concern sense (this relates to the second complaint) and the identify-with sense (I can relate to her), both odd in the progressive; dynamic in the narrate sense: he related the story to us.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with to in the concern and identify senses; transitive in relate the story to us and in relate X to Y. Kinship needs the participle: she's related to the governor, ✗ she relates to the governor.
entries.passive: restricted — the narrate sense passivizes (the story was related to us by her brother) and the kinship participle is fixed (she's related to the governor), but the stative concern sense does not: ✗ the complaint is related to by this clause.
entries.see also: refer to · respond to · belong to · in relation to · to

entries.meaning: Take a duty, a burden, or a possession away from someone.
examples: The colonel was relieved of command within a week.
A settlement would relieve the company of any further obligation.
She was relieved of the paperwork so she could spend the hour with patients.
The new system relieves the front desk of having to re-key every order.
Two administrators were quietly relieved of their responsibilities in June.
Somebody in the crowd relieved him of his wallet.
entries.русский: освобождать от (обязанности, ноши) — снимать бремя с человека
entries.register: formal, and usually a euphemism — the wording of a personnel notice or a military order (relieved of command); its joking use (relieved me of forty dollars) is a joke about the euphemism
entries.complement: the person always sits between the verb and of — relieve someone of something — and of takes a noun phrase or a gerund (relieved of having to file the report); never a to-infinitive (✗ relieved of to file the report). There is no ✗ relieve of with no person named, and the passive (was relieved of his duties) is far commoner than the active.
entries.pattern: relieve [someone] of [duties / a burden / a possession] · [someone] be relieved of [noun phrase / verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Do not confuse the verb with the feeling. He was relieved of his post means he was removed from it; he was relieved at the news, relieved by the verdict, relieved to hear it means he felt relief — a different word, an adjective, with its own prepositions. Only the first is this pattern. Among neighbors, relieve someone of takes a burden away, free someone from removes a constraint, absolve someone of clears the blame, and fire says plainly what relieved of his duties is written to avoid.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; taking a burden or a post away from somebody. Do not confuse it with the adjective of feeling in relieved at the news.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person always sits between verb and preposition: relieve someone of something; the object is obligatory: ✗ relieve of the reporting requirement.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is far commoner than the active — he was relieved of his duties, she was relieved of having to file the report.
entries.see also: deprive of · rob of · rescue from · retire from · of

entries.meaning: Trust something or someone to do what is needed.
examples: The whole valley relies on one two-lane bridge.
You can rely on her to catch anything I miss.
They relied on volunteer labor for the first three seasons.
Don't rely on the automatic backup; check it once a month.
The finding relies on a sample of forty-one people.
Rural clinics rely upon federal reimbursement for most of their revenue.
entries.русский: полагаться на — доверять, что сделает нужное
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (relying on getting reimbursed) — never a to-infinitive after the preposition (✗ rely on to get reimbursed). A to-infinitive is correct after a person: rely on her to check it. A wh-clause is fine. Rely never appears without its preposition: ✗ you can rely me.
entries.pattern: rely on [someone / something] · rely on [someone] to [verb] · rely on [verb-ing] · rely on [someone's] -ing · reliance on [something]
entries.variants: rely upon — identical in meaning, more formal, common in legal and academic writing
entries.contrast: Rely to, ✗ rely in, and ✗ rely of are all errors. Within the family, rely on is the neutral written form, count on the warm spoken one, and depend on the one that also carries the be-determined-by sense that neither of the others has. Rely upon is the formal variant, standard in legal and academic prose. Note the noun: reliance on — and the legal phrase detrimental reliance, which is this same preposition frozen.
entries.verb type: stative — a standing state of dependence rather than an act, though it takes the progressive for a temporary arrangement: we're relying on you this week.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the verb never appears without its preposition: ✗ you can rely me. A to-infinitive is possible after a person: rely on her to check it.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is standard in legal and academic prose (the affidavit was relied on by the court, the cases relied upon), stiff in speech: ✗ I'm relied on by everybody.
entries.see also: depend on · count on · believe in · on

entries.meaning: Cause someone to remember something, or make you think of something else.
examples: This street reminds me of the town my mother grew up in.
Remind me about the parking pass before we leave.
She reminded him to bring the second set of keys.
Your handwriting reminds me of my grandmother's.
Remind the committee that the deadline is a statutory one.
Nothing reminds you of how old a house is like a January heating bill.
entries.русский: напоминать — of о сходстве или о факте, about о деле, о котором забыли
entries.complement: of takes a noun phrase or a gerund and covers both resemblance and recollection. about takes a noun phrase or a gerund and covers upcoming obligations. The person reminded is always a direct object: ✗ remind to me. Remind also takes a to-infinitive after the person (remind me to call) and a that-clause (remind him that it's Tuesday) — neither with a preposition.
entries.pattern: remind [someone] of [something / someone] · remind [someone] about [an obligation] · remind [someone] to [verb] · remind [someone] that [clause] · That reminds me.
entries.contrast: Four patterns, and of versus about is the one that carries meaning. You remind me of my father is resemblance — it says you are like him. Remind me about the deposit is a prompt about a task. And remind me to make the deposit is a prompt to act, using the infinitive rather than any preposition. Mixing them produces sentences that are grammatical and wrong: ✗ remind me of making the deposit says the act of depositing calls something else to mind.
entries.verb type: both — dynamic in the prompting sense (remind me about the deposit, remind me to call); stative in the resemblance sense, where nothing happens: you remind me of my father.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person reminded is always a direct object: ✗ remind to me. The verb also takes a to-infinitive after the person (remind me to call) and a that-clause (remind him that it's Tuesday), neither with a preposition.
entries.passive: yes in the prompting sense — staff were reminded of the deadline, she was reminded to sign both copies. The stative resemblance sense resists: ✗ my father is reminded of by you.
entries.see also: forget about · occur to · think of · warn about · explain to

entries.meaning: Get someone out of danger or difficulty.
examples: The crew rescued four people from the roof of a submerged car.
A neighbor rescued the dog from a storm drain.
She rescued the whole presentation from a dead projector and a lost cable.
Two hikers were rescued from the ridge after dark.
He was rescued from having to give a toast by a well-timed power outage.
The fund rescued the theater from closing.
entries.русский: спасать из, спасать от — вытаскивать из опасности или беды
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (rescued from having to speak) — never a to-infinitive, never a clause. The person or thing rescued is a direct object and the danger takes from: ✗ rescue to someone.
entries.pattern: rescue [someone] from [danger] · be rescued from [something] · rescue [someone] · a rescue from [something] · rescue [an animal] — as a noun, an adopted animal
entries.contrast: Rescue takes only from. Its neighbors keep their own: save someone from (interchangeable, broader), free someone from or of, deliver someone from (biblical or formal), bail someone out of trouble (informal, and note the particle). In American usage rescue has also become a noun for an adopted shelter animal — she's a rescue — with no preposition at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of pulling someone out of danger.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person or thing rescued is the direct object and from names the danger: ✗ rescue to someone, ✗ rescue from the fire with nobody named.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual news form — the crew was rescued from the water by a Coast Guard helicopter, she was rescued from having to speak.
entries.see also: save from · protect from · escape from · recover from

entries.meaning: Have your legal home somewhere — or, of a quality or a power, be located in something.
examples: Both parties resided in Cook County at the time of filing.
Sovereignty resides in the people, not in the office.
She resides at 400 East Sixth Street.
Custody resides with the mother until the hearing.
The real difficulty resides in the definition of "employee."
Anyone residing in the district for thirty days may register to vote.
entries.русский: проживать где-то (юр.); быть заключённым в — о свойстве или власти
entries.register: formal — a lease, a tax form, a voter-registration rule, a court opinion, or a civics sentence about where power lies; in speech Americans say live
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a place, a body, or an abstraction (the difficulty resides in the wording). A gerund is possible in the abstract sense but stilted (its value resides in being reproducible) — prefer a noun. Never a to-infinitive (✗ resides in to be reproducible) and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: reside in [a city, a state, a district] · reside at [a street address] · reside with [a person, or a body that holds authority] · [a quality / a problem] reside in [something]
entries.contrast: The three prepositions divide by scale and by kind. You reside in a county, reside at 400 East Sixth Street, and reside with your grandmother — or, for authority, with the body that holds it (final approval resides with the board), which is the same frame as rest with. Against plain live: reside is what the form asks (Where do you currently reside?) and live is what people answer. The abstract sense — the problem resides in the design — is the formal twin of lie in, and is standard in academic prose.
entries.verb type: stative — where a person lives or where a power belongs by design; it rejects the progressive: ✗ sovereignty is residing in the people, ✗ the difficulty is residing in the wording.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the place, body, or abstraction always comes through in (or at for a street address, with for authority): ✗ she resides the county.
entries.passive: no — intransitive and stative, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the county is resided in by 40,000 people, ✗ the wording is resided in.
entries.see also: rest with · belong to · vest in · consist of · in

entries.meaning: Turn to something undesirable because nothing better is available.
examples: They resorted to hauling water by hand for most of August.
Nobody wants to resort to layoffs, which is what everyone says before layoffs.
He resorted to checking the spreadsheet line by line.
The department resorted to a hiring freeze rather than cut programs.
You can usually settle it without resorting to lawyers.
As a last resort, we can push the launch to October.
entries.русский: прибегать к — обращаться к нежелательному средству; после to герундий
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — to is a preposition here, so a verb after it must be -ing: resorted to lying, never ✗ resorted to lie. Never a clause. Resort has no other verb frame at all: ✗ he resorted the lie.
entries.pattern: resort to [something] · resort to [verb-ing] · as a last resort · without resorting to [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Another member of the look forward to family, and the same test settles it: you can say resort to violence, so to is a preposition, so it is resort to shouting, not ✗ resort to shout. The word carries a built-in judgment — whatever you resort to is a fallback you would rather not have used, which is why resort to force and resort to bribery sound natural and ✗ resorted to a sensible compromise sounds odd. Compare the noun last resort, and the unrelated homonym resort meaning a vacation property.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; falling back on something you would rather not have used, which is why resort to force works and ✗ resorted to a sensible compromise sounds odd.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the verb has no other frame at all: ✗ he resorted the lie. to is a preposition, so a verb after it is -ing: resorted to lying, ✗ resorted to lie.
entries.passive: restricted — available in formal and legal prose (force was resorted to only after negotiations failed), unnatural in speech: ✗ lying was resorted to by him.
entries.see also: look forward to · object to · get around to · refer to · cope with · to

entries.meaning: Say or do something in answer to a question, a message, or a situation.
examples: Nobody responded to my email for four days.
The department responded to the complaint with a two-page denial.
Her blood pressure responded to the lower dose almost immediately.
Three engines responded to the alarm at two in the morning.
He responded to being left off the invitation by showing up anyway.
The company has yet to respond to questions about the recall.
entries.русский: отвечать на, реагировать на — на вопрос, письмо или ситуацию
entries.register: neutral, a step more formal than answer
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (responded to being passed over by quitting) — never a to-infinitive (✗ respond to be asked). A clause attaches to bare respond with no preposition at all: he responded that the file was closed. The medical and technical sense takes a plain noun: the tumor responded to radiation.
entries.pattern: respond to [a question, a letter, a crisis] · respond to [verb-ing] · respond with [an action, a counteroffer] · respond by [verb-ing] · respond that [clause]
entries.contrast: Answer takes no preposition and respond requires one — answer the question but respond to the question; ✗ answer to the question is an error, and answer to with a person means something else entirely (be accountable to). Reply to is the near-twin but is limited to messages, while respond to also covers situations, treatments, and stimuli (responded to the medication, responded to the alarm). React to is involuntary and immediate; respond to implies a considered move.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and more considered than involuntary react to: she's responding to every comment herself. The medical sense is dynamic too: the tumor responded to radiation.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the verb requires its preposition, unlike transitive answer: answer the question but respond to the question. A clause attaches to bare respond: he responded that the file was closed.
entries.passive: restricted — the letter was never responded to occurs and is clumsy; the natural passive belongs to the transitive twin, the letter was never answered.
entries.see also: react to · relate to · refer to · answer · response to · to

entries.meaning: Be supported by something, physically or logically.
examples: The entire argument rests on a single unnamed source.
The porch roof rests on four cedar posts.
Their case rests on proving he knew about the transfer.
Much rests upon the wording of the second clause.
Her gaze rested on the photograph a moment too long.
He rested his elbows on the counter and waited for an answer.
entries.русский: опираться на — держаться на чём-то физически или логически
entries.register: neutral; rest upon is formal and literary
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (the whole case rests on proving intent) — never a to-infinitive (✗ rests on to prove intent). A wh-clause also works: it rests on whether the email was sent.
entries.pattern: [an argument, a claim, an outcome] rest on [an assumption] · [a physical thing] rest on [a support] · [someone's eyes] rest on [something] · rest [something] on [something]
entries.variants: rest upon — identical in meaning, more formal and more literary; standard in appellate opinions and in descriptions of a gaze
entries.contrast: Rest on names what holds something up; rest with names who is responsible. The two never swap: the decision rests with the dean assigns the choice to a person, while the decision rests on the dean would make the dean the supporting evidence. Against depend on: rest on is static support — the argument is built on it — whereas depend on is contingency, varying with what the other thing does. Bare rest in a courtroom (the state rests) is a fixed idiom with no complement, and rest on your laurels is frozen.
entries.verb type: stative — static support, not an event; it rejects the progressive: ✗ the whole case is resting on proving intent. The subject is the thing held up, never an agent.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the support always comes through the preposition: ✗ the case rests proving intent. Bare rest in court (the state rests) is a fixed idiom with no complement.
entries.passive: no — intransitive and stative: ✗ proving intent is rested on by the whole case. Compare rest with, equally passive-proof: ✗ the dean is rested with.
entries.see also: rest with · depend on · rely on · stem from · turn on · on · upon

entries.meaning: Be the responsibility or the decision of a particular person or body.
examples: Final approval rests with the state board, not the county.
The decision rests with her, and always did.
Responsibility for the delay rests with the contractor.
Where the burden of proof rests with the plaintiff, an ambiguity favors the defense.
Whatever the doctors recommend, the choice rests with the family.
Authority to waive the fee rests with the dean's office.
entries.русский: быть на чьей-то ответственности — решение остаётся за кем-то
entries.register: formal — bylaws, contracts, editorials, and committee minutes; in speech Americans say is up to
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person or a body that holds the authority. No gerund (✗ the decision rests with deciding), no infinitive, no clause. The subject is the thing being decided — a decision, the final say, responsibility, blame.
entries.pattern: [a decision / responsibility / blame] rest with [a person or body] · the choice rests with [someone] · ultimately rest with [someone]
entries.contrast: With assigns responsibility, on assigns support — the decision rests with the board (they decide) against the decision rests on the audit (the audit is what it is built on). Lie with is the near-synonym and a shade more literary (the fault lies with the vendor); be up to is the everyday version (it's up to you); reside with is the same frame in stiffer clothes. ✗ Rest to and ✗ rest in are not this pattern.
entries.verb type: stative — a standing relation of authority, not an act; it resists the progressive (✗ the decision is resting with the board) and has no imperative (✗ rest with the dean!).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the subject is the decision and the with-phrase is obligatory: ✗ final approval rests is incomplete. There is no direct object: ✗ rest the board the decision.
entries.passive: no — intransitive and stative both block it: ✗ the board is rested with the decision, ✗ she is rested with the choice. Use the active, or switch to be vested in / be up to.
entries.see also: rest on · reside in · vest in · belong to · with

entries.meaning: Produce an outcome, or be produced by a cause.
examples: The audit resulted in four policy changes and one resignation.
Most of the delays resulted from a single misfiled permit.
Cutting the route resulted in stranding about two hundred riders.
The infection resulted from a lapse in sterilization procedure.
Higher rates usually result in fewer refinancings.
Nothing good has ever resulted from sending that email at midnight.
entries.русский: in приводить к следствию; from быть следствием причины — направление противоположно
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — resulted in closing the plant, results from having no backup — never a to-infinitive (✗ resulted in to close the plant). Never a clause. Result is intransitive and takes no object: ✗ result a delay.
entries.pattern: [a cause] result in [an effect] · [an effect] result from [a cause] · result in [verb-ing] · result from [verb-ing] · as a result of [something]
entries.contrast: The two prepositions point in opposite directions, and swapping them inverts the sentence. The storm resulted in three outages — cause first. Three outages resulted from the storm — effect first. Both are true; ✗ the storm resulted from three outages is false. Result in is the formal twin of lead to and cause; result from is the formal twin of be caused by and stem from. ✗ result to is not English in either direction.
entries.verb type: stative-relational rather than dynamic — it asserts a causal link, so it reads as a generic truth (higher rates result in fewer refinancings) and takes the progressive only grudgingly (?the cuts are resulting in delays).
entries.transitivity: intransitive in both directions; the preposition is obligatory and there is no object: ✗ result a delay, ✗ the storm resulted three outages.
