entries.passive: no — nothing to promote: ✗ four policy changes were resulted in by the audit, ✗ the storm was resulted from. The inverse is built by swapping prepositions, not by the passive: the delays resulted from a misfiled permit.
entries.see also: lead to · stem from · contribute to · die from · as a result of

entries.meaning: Stop working permanently — and the preposition names what you leave.
examples: He retired from the fire department after twenty-eight years.
She retired from competitive swimming at twenty-three.
Two of the three founders have retired from the board.
They retired to a town with one traffic light and no winter.
He retired as chief of staff and stayed on as a consultant.
The Yankees retired his number the following spring.
entries.русский: уходить на пенсию, оставлять (пост, службу, спорт)
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a job, a field, or an organization — no gerund, no clause (✗ retire from working; say retire from teaching, where teaching is a noun, or just retire). To names where you go; as names the title you held.
entries.pattern: retire from [a job, a field, an institution] · retire to [a place] · retire as [a title] · retire (alone) · be retired · retire [a number, a debt, a piece of equipment]
entries.contrast: Retire of is an error. The three live prepositions divide the sentence: she retired from the district as an assistant principal and moved to Tucson. Note the transitive senses, which take no preposition: a team retires a number, a company retires debt, an airline retires a fleet. And note the older, unrelated sense of retire meaning withdraw for the evening (he retired at ten), which survives mostly in period fiction.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a one-time change of status (he retired from the fire department in March); be retired is the resulting state, an adjective rather than a tense.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the career senses (she retired, retired from the board, retired to Tucson), transitive in the sports and finance senses (retire his number, retire the debt, retire a fleet).
entries.passive: restricted — natural in the transitive senses: his number was retired the following spring, the bonds were retired early. No passive of the career sense: ✗ the fire department was retired from.
entries.see also: escape from · recover from · separate from · from

entries.meaning: Take something from someone by force or by unfairness.
examples: Two men robbed the branch on Ellis Street at closing time.
The injury robbed him of an entire season.
She was robbed of a promotion by a reorganization nobody explained.
They robbed the till and left the safe alone.
A late frost robbed the orchard of about half its crop.
He felt robbed of the chance to make his case.
entries.русский: лишать кого-то чего-то — отнимать силой или несправедливо
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (robbed of seeing her graduate) — never a to-infinitive, never a clause. The victim or the place is the direct object and the loss takes of: robbed him of his savings, ✗ robbed his savings from him is clumsy at best.
entries.pattern: rob [someone / a place] · rob [someone] of [something] · be robbed of [something] · rob [a bank, a store] · steal [something] from [someone] — the mirror verb
entries.contrast: Rob takes the victim; steal takes the loot. They robbed the bank and they stole the money are both correct, and ✗ they robbed the money and ✗ they stole the bank are both wrong. When you want to name both, rob uses of (robbed the bank of four thousand dollars) and steal uses from (stole four thousand dollars from the bank). The figurative sense is common and always takes of: an injury robbed him of a season, robbed of the chance to say goodbye.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, an event with a victim; the figurative use (an injury robbed him of a season) is equally dynamic.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is the victim or the place, not the loot: rob the bank, ✗ rob the money. The object is obligatory (✗ two men robbed at closing time); the of-phrase is optional (they robbed the till).
entries.passive: yes, and it is the commoner form in the figurative sense — she was robbed of a promotion by a reorganization, the branch was robbed at closing time.
entries.see also: deprive of · cheat on · escape from · accuse of

entries.meaning: Openly hope that someone or something succeeds.
examples: Half the bar was rooting for the visiting team out of spite.
We're all rooting for you on Thursday.
She was quietly rooting for the amendment to fail.
He roots for whichever team his father hated.
Nobody roots for the insurance company in a movie.
I'm rooting for her to get the fellowship.
entries.русский: болеть за — открыто желать успеха; разг., амер.
entries.register: informal and American — sports, elections, and encouragement; the British equivalent is support
entries.complement: noun phrase — a team, a person, an outcome. No gerund (✗ rooting for winning), and no that-clause (✗ root that they win). An infinitive is licensed only by the person sitting between the preposition and the verb, exactly as with wait for: rooting for the underdog to win.
entries.pattern: root for [a team / a person] · root for [someone] to [verb] · be rooting for [someone]
entries.contrast: Root for is cheering from outside, with nothing at stake but sympathy. Support can mean money or votes as well as good wishes (support the team, support the bill); back puts resources behind something; cheer for is louder and more literal. Keep the separable particles apart from this fixed preposition: root out moves its object (root out corruption, root it out) and root around in means rummage — neither is this verb.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and atelic, an ongoing attitude expressed as activity; the progressive is the default form (we're all rooting for you).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — for is obligatory before the team or person (✗ root the underdog), and any infinitive is licensed by that noun, not by the verb: rooting for the underdog to win.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive does not take here: ✗ the visiting team was rooted for by half the bar, ✗ you're being rooted for. Use support or back, which are transitive and passivize freely.
entries.see also: vote for · stand up for · care about · hope for · wish for · for

entries.meaning: Keep someone or something out of danger, or set something aside.
examples: Her seatbelt saved her from far worse.
That template saved us from rewriting the same memo forty times.
Save the good tomatoes for the sandwiches.
You'd save about eleven dollars on shipping by ordering both together.
A neighbor saved the cat from the storm drain and adopted it a week later.
Calling ahead saves you a trip.
entries.русский: спасать от — а save for откладывать на, save on экономить на
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (saved us from having to reprint it) — never a to-infinitive. The thing saved is a direct object; from names the danger. Other frames take for (save it for later), on (save on shipping), and a bare object (save money, save a seat).
entries.pattern: save [someone] from [danger / verb-ing] · be saved from [something] · save [something] for [later] · save on [a cost] · save [someone] [trouble] · save up for [something]
entries.contrast: Save from is rescue; save for is postponement; save on is economy. Three prepositions, three unrelated meanings, and the sentence collapses if you swap them: save the file for Monday and save the file from Monday are not variants of each other. Note the double-object frame that skips the preposition entirely — that saved me an hour, it'll save you a trip — which is the most common form in American speech. Save up for is the money sense with a particle.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic; the rescue is an event with a result (her seatbelt saved her from far worse).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the thing saved as object, and ditransitive in the preposition-free frame Americans reach for most: that saved me an hour, it'll save you a trip.
entries.passive: yes — she was saved from far worse by her seatbelt, the cat was saved from the storm drain. The double-object frame passivizes on the person: I was saved a trip.
entries.see also: rescue from · protect from · prevent from · escape from · pay for

entries.meaning: Try to find something, or examine a place thoroughly.
examples: Volunteers searched for her along the river for three days.
Customs searched every bag on the flight.
Deputies searched the property for the missing equipment.
He spent an hour searching for a file that was open in another window.
She searched through the box and came up with two photographs.
They set out in search of somewhere with parking.
entries.русский: искать что-то — а search a place значит обыскивать место
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase naming what is missing — no gerund (✗ search for getting a signal). The transitive frame takes the place or person examined, with no preposition: search the house, search him. Both can appear together: search the house for weapons.
entries.pattern: search for [something missing] · search [a place, a person] · search [a place] for [something] · search through [a container] · in search of [something]
entries.contrast: You search a place, and you search for a thing. They searched the car means they went through it; they searched for the car means they couldn't find it. Both are correct and they describe opposite situations, which makes this one of the most consequential preposition contrasts in the whole dictionary — it is the difference between a police report and a missing-persons report. Look for is the everyday synonym of search for; search through emphasizes rummaging.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and atelic in the for frame (an activity that may fail), dynamic and telic in the transitive one (customs searched every bag).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with for naming what is missing (searched for her along the river), transitive with the place or person examined (search the house, search him), and the two can combine: searched the property for the equipment.
entries.passive: restricted — excellent in the transitive frame: every bag on the flight was searched, the property was searched for the missing equipment. No passive of the for frame: ✗ she was searched for for three days (say the search for her lasted three days).
entries.see also: look for · ask for · hope for · wait for · hide from

entries.meaning: Impose a punishment on someone who has been convicted.
examples: He was sentenced to eighteen months in federal prison.
The judge sentenced her to probation and two hundred hours of community service.
Three defendants were sentenced to time served and released that afternoon.
She was sentenced to five years for the fraud and two more for obstruction.
The court sentenced him to pay $40,000 in restitution.
Nobody in the state has been sentenced to death since 2011.
entries.русский: приговаривать к — назначать наказание осуждённому; юр.
entries.register: legal, and the standard register of court reporting; the passive (was sentenced to) is far commoner than the active
entries.complement: the person sentenced sits between the verb and to, and to takes a noun phrase naming the punishment — a term, a fine, probation, death. No gerund (✗ sentenced to serving time). A to-infinitive does appear, but only in the courtroom formula sentenced to serve 36 months, sentenced to pay restitution, where to serve is the infinitive marker and not this preposition. The test settles it: sentenced to five years takes a plain noun, so that to is the preposition.
entries.pattern: sentence [someone] to [a term / a fine / death] · [someone] be sentenced to [noun phrase] · be sentenced to [a term] for [the offense] · sentence [someone] to [verb — courtroom formula]
entries.contrast: The offense takes for and the punishment takes to, and they never swap: sentenced to three years for wire fraud. Around it stand the other stages, each with its own preposition: charge someone with an offense, convict someone of it, sentence them to a term, fine them (no preposition at all). Condemn to is now figurative or historical (condemned to death, condemned to a life of paperwork) where sentence to is the live legal verb.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, a performative act of the court, complete the moment it is uttered.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person sentenced is the direct object and is obligatory (✗ the judge sentenced to probation); the to-phrase naming the punishment is nearly obligatory too.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the default in news and legal prose: he was sentenced to eighteen months in federal prison, three defendants were sentenced to time served.
entries.see also: charge with · accuse of · punish for · testify to · sue for · to

entries.meaning: Move or keep two things apart.
examples: Separate the yolks from the whites while the eggs are cold.
A chain-link fence separates the playground from the parking lot.
What separates this camera from the cheaper one is the sensor.
He was separated from his unit for two days.
Separate the invoices into paid and unpaid.
They separated in April and reconciled by August.
entries.русский: отделять(ся) от — разъединять или держать порознь
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause. Into takes the resulting parts (separate into groups), and the intransitive separate takes no complement at all (the couple separated). Note the pronunciation split: the verb ends /eɪt/, the adjective /ət/.
entries.pattern: separate [A] from [B] · be separated from [something] · separate into [parts] · separate (intransitive) · separation from [something]
entries.contrast: Separate from divides two things; separate into divides one thing up. Separate the yolks from the whites against separate the class into four groups — different structures, and using from for the second (✗ separate the class from four groups) is nonsense. Compare divide into, which behaves like separate into, and distinguish between / distinguish from, which is about telling apart rather than pulling apart. The figurative use is common in American business prose: what separates a good manager from a bad one.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the physical senses (separate the yolks from the whites); in the descriptive use (what separates this camera from the cheaper one is the sensor) it is a stative relation, which is why the progressive sounds odd there.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with an object plus from or into (separate the invoices into paid and unpaid), intransitive with no complement at all (they separated in April).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — he was separated from his unit for two days, the playground is separated from the lot by a chain-link fence. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ they were separated in April means something else.
entries.see also: differ from · translate into · escape from · consist of

entries.meaning: Give someone part of what you have, or have something in common.
examples: She shared her notes with anyone who asked.
Would you share that with the rest of us?
The two houses share a driveway with no written agreement of any kind.
Junior partners share in the profits but not the losses.
He shares a birthday with his grandfather.
They shared one bathroom with six other tenants.
entries.русский: делиться с — отдавать часть своего или иметь что-то общее
entries.complement: with takes the person you share with; the thing shared is a direct object: share the file with the team. A gerund can be the thing shared (share being on call), but no to-infinitive and no clause. In takes something you partake of: share in the profits.
entries.pattern: share [something] with [someone] · share [something] · share in [profits, credit, blame] · share [a trait] with [someone] · have [something] in common with [someone]
entries.contrast: Share with gives a portion away; share in takes a portion of something already collective. She shared her notes with me (I got a copy) against she shared in the credit (she got a piece of it). ✗ share to someone is an error, though it has spread through social-media interfaces. Note the third sense, hold in common: the two languages share a root, which takes a direct object or with, never in.
entries.verb type: both — action when something is handed over (she shared her notes with anyone who asked), stative when something is held in common (he shares a birthday with his grandfather, the two houses share a driveway), where the progressive is odd.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the thing shared as object and with naming the recipient; intransitive with in for taking a portion (junior partners share in the profits), where no object is possible.
entries.passive: restricted — fine in the transitive giving sense: the notes were shared with the whole team. No passive of share in (✗ the profits were shared in) and none of the stative sense (✗ a driveway is shared by the two houses is possible but reads as a description, not an act).
entries.see also: provide with · consist of · belong to · compete with · with

entries.meaning: Enroll in something, or put your name down for it.
examples: Forty people signed up for the Saturday session in the first hour.
I signed up for the two-year plan and regretted it by March.
Sign your kids up for swim lessons before the list fills.
She signed up to work the overnight shift on Christmas.
He signed up for a gym membership he has never once used.
Long hours are one thing, but nobody signed up for this.
entries.русский: записываться на — регистрироваться или подписываться на что-то
entries.register: neutral to informal — everyday American English for classes, shifts, plans, and mailing lists
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase — a class, a service, a shift, a plan. A gerund is unusual and marked (?signed up for cleaning the garage); to put a verb after sign up, drop for and use the infinitive: signed up to volunteer. No that-clause.
entries.pattern: sign up for [a class, a service, a shift] · sign up to [verb — infinitive] · sign [someone] up for [something] · sign up with [an organization]
entries.contrast: The particle moves and the preposition does not. Up slides around an object — sign me up, signed the whole family up — while for never leaves its noun: ✗ sign up the class for. Then the prepositions divide the meanings: sign up for is enrolling in something, sign up with is joining an outfit (signed up with a new agency), sign for is signing a receipt (sign for the package), and sign on to is endorsing (signed on to the letter). The idiom I didn't sign up for this means this is not what I agreed to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, a single act of enrollment (forty people signed up for the Saturday session in the first hour).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with for (I signed up for the two-year plan), transitive when someone else is enrolled and the particle moves around them: sign your kids up for swim lessons, sign me up.
entries.passive: restricted — the causative frame passivizes naturally: the kids were signed up for swim lessons. The plain enrollment sense does not: ✗ the Saturday session was signed up for.
entries.see also: apply for · qualify for · participate in · commit to · for

entries.meaning: Turn a smile toward someone or something.
examples: He smiled at everyone in line and meant it, which was unsettling.
She smiled at the photograph for a long moment before putting it back.
Smile at the camera, not at me.
They smiled about it for weeks afterward.
The weather smiled on the whole weekend for once.
He smiled at being recognized after all those years.
entries.русский: улыбаться кому-то — направлять улыбку на кого-то
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (smiled at being remembered) — never a to-infinitive, never a clause. Smile is intransitive and the target always needs a preposition: ✗ smile me. A rare transitive survives in smile a thin smile.
entries.pattern: smile at [someone / something] · smile about [something] · smile on [someone] — favor · smile (alone) · a smile for [someone]
entries.contrast: At aims the smile; about names the cause; on is fortune. She smiled at the baby directs it; she smiled about the whole thing later explains it; fortune smiled on them is a fixed literary idiom meaning they got lucky. ✗ smile to someone is not idiomatic American English. Compare laugh at, which is usually hostile, with smile at, which almost never is — the same preposition, opposite social temperature.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a brief bodily act; the progressive is normal (she was smiling at the baby).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the target always needs a preposition (✗ smile me), and the verb stands alone freely (don't smile). Only the cognate object survives transitively: smile a thin smile.
entries.passive: no for at — ✗ everyone in line was smiled at, ✗ the photograph was smiled at. The one fixed exception is the fortune idiom, where the passive participle is idiomatic: the weekend was smiled on by the weather, a smiled-upon candidate.
entries.see also: laugh at · stare at · look at · point at

entries.meaning: Concentrate your work or study on one narrow field.
examples: The firm specializes in municipal bond work.
She specializes in restoring plaster ceilings, which is a smaller field than you'd think.
He specialized in pediatric cardiology after a residency in Cleveland.
That shop specializes in parts for cars nobody makes anymore.
Two of the four practices specialize in elder law.
You can't specialize in everything.
entries.русский: специализироваться на — сосредоточивать работу в узкой области
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (specializes in restoring old plaster) — never a to-infinitive (✗ specializes in to restore plaster). Specialize is intransitive: ✗ specialize immigration law. American spelling is -ize; specialise is British.
entries.pattern: specialize in [a field / verb-ing] · be specialized in — avoid; use the active · a specialist in [a field] · specialize (alone)
entries.contrast: Specialize on and ✗ specialize at are errors — the preposition is fixed at in, and so is the noun's: a specialist in labor law. Compare major in (an American college term, same shape: major in biology), concentrate on (attention rather than expertise), and be good at, which takes at and never in. Note that the passive is specialized in sounds translated; American writers use the active.
entries.verb type: stative in practice — it describes what a firm or person characteristically does (the firm specializes in municipal bond work), so the progressive is odd except for a change in progress (?they're specializing in elder law now).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — in is obligatory: ✗ specialize immigration law, ✗ specialize on bond work. The verb also stands alone: you can't specialize in everything.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote, and the entry flags the calque directly: ✗ the firm is specialized in bond work. American writers use the active, or the noun frame a specialist in labor law.
entries.see also: concentrate on · work on · invest in · participate in · in

entries.meaning: Look at something fixedly for a long time.
examples: He stared at the ceiling until about four in the morning.
Two people on the platform were openly staring at her.
She stared at the invoice as though it might revise itself.
Don't stare.
He stared into the middle distance and said he'd think about it.
The answer had been staring us in the face for a week.
entries.русский: пристально смотреть на — глядеть подолгу, не отрывая взгляда
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause. Stare is intransitive and always needs at before its target: ✗ stare the screen. The only bare use is absolute: don't stare.
entries.pattern: stare at [someone / something] · stare (alone) · stare into [space, the distance] · stare down [someone] · be staring [someone] in the face
entries.contrast: Stare at is fixed — ✗ stare to and ✗ stare on are errors. The family sorts by intensity and politeness: look at is neutral, watch is transitive with no preposition (watch the game), stare at is rude, glare at is hostile, gaze at is fond or dreamy, and glance at is brief. Only watch drops the preposition, which is why ✗ watch at the game and ✗ stare the game are both wrong.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative, an activity you can be caught in the middle of: two people on the platform were openly staring at her.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — at is obligatory before the target (✗ stare the screen), unlike watch, which is transitive (watch the game). Bare don't stare is the absolute use.
entries.passive: yes, restricted to the prepositional passive, which is genuinely idiomatic here — she was being stared at, nobody likes being stared at. Compare watch, which passivizes the ordinary way: the game was watched by millions.
entries.see also: look at · laugh at · smile at · listen to

entries.meaning: Have its origin in something.
examples: The charges stem from a 2019 procurement contract.
Most of the friction stems from a job description nobody has updated since 2011.
Her interest in soils stemmed from a summer on a research plot.
The delays stem from having only one inspector for the whole county.
The dispute stems from a boundary survey done in 1948.
Almost every complaint stems from the same two forms.
entries.русский: происходить из, восходить к — иметь своим источником
entries.register: neutral to formal — common in journalism and analysis
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (stems from having no oversight) — never a to-infinitive, never a clause. Stem in this sense is intransitive and never takes an object: ✗ stem the problem is a different verb entirely, meaning stop the flow.
entries.pattern: [a problem, a belief, a case] stem from [a cause] · stem from [verb-ing] · stem [the tide, the bleeding, the flow] — a different verb, no preposition
entries.contrast: Stem from points from effect back to cause, exactly like result from and arise from, and the opposite of result in and lead to. ✗ stem to does not exist. Watch the homonym: stem the losses means stanch them, takes a direct object, and has nothing to do with this pattern — the charges stem from the losses and the charges stemmed the losses are unrelated sentences. Journalists lean on stem from heavily because it asserts a cause without asserting blame.
entries.verb type: stative — a relation of origin, not an event; it resists the progressive (✗ the charges are stemming from a 2019 contract). The homonym stem the bleeding is a different, dynamic verb.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — no object in this sense (✗ stem the problem belongs to the other verb), and from is obligatory: ✗ the friction stems.
entries.passive: no — intransitive and stative: ✗ a 2019 contract is stemmed from. Only the unrelated homonym passivizes: the losses were stemmed by the third quarter.
entries.see also: result from · lead to · result in · die from

entries.meaning: Agree formally, on the record, that a fact may be taken as established.
examples: Both sides stipulated to the authenticity of the recordings.
The defense would not stipulate to the value of the stolen property.
Counsel, will you stipulate to the witness's qualifications?
They stipulated to liability and tried the damages question alone.
The parties stipulated to entering the medical records without a custodian.
If we stipulate to the timeline, the hearing takes an afternoon instead of a week.
entries.русский: признавать факт по соглашению сторон — юр., в процессе
entries.register: legal — an American meets stipulate to in a courtroom, a deposition transcript, or a settlement agreement; outside law the verb is used without to (the lease stipulates a thirty-day notice)
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a fact, an exhibit, or an element (stipulated to the authenticity of the recording), or a gerund (stipulated to entering the records without a custodian) — never a to-infinitive (✗ stipulated to admit the exhibit). For a full proposition, drop the preposition: stipulate that the report was authentic.
entries.pattern: stipulate to [a fact / an exhibit / an element] · stipulate to [verb-ing] · stipulate that [clause — no preposition] · stipulate [a condition] · enter into a stipulation as to [something]
entries.contrast: The two senses take opposite kinds of act. Plain transitive stipulate means require as a condition — the grant stipulates that funds be spent within a year. With to, it means agreeing with the other side that something need not be proved at all: the defense stipulated to the chain of custody, and that issue leaves the trial. Neighbors: concede and admit to give away a point in argument, agree to accepts a proposal, consent to authorizes — none of them has the technical effect of removing an element from proof.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and performative, a speech act with legal effect the moment counsel makes it (both sides stipulated to the authenticity of the recordings).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with to in the agreement sense, transitive in the requirement sense (the grant stipulates a one-year window, stipulate that funds be spent within a year).
entries.passive: restricted — natural in the requirement sense: it was stipulated that the funds be spent within a year. The to frame passivizes only in legal register and stiffly: ?the chain of custody was stipulated to; prefer the active the parties stipulated to it.
entries.see also: agree to · admit to · testify to · submit to · to

entries.meaning: Yield to something, or hand something in to someone.
examples: He refused to submit to a search without a warrant.
All bids must be submitted to the purchasing office by Friday.
She submitted to two rounds of interviews before anyone mentioned salary.
The paper was submitted to three journals and rejected by all three.
They would rather close than submit to being audited every quarter.
Members submit to the ethics rules when they join.
entries.русский: подчиняться чему-то, подвергаться; подавать что-то куда-то — два разных глагола
entries.register: formal in the yielding sense; the hand-it-in sense is everyday office and academic English
entries.complement: in the yielding sense, to takes a noun phrase or a gerund (submitted to being searched) — never a to-infinitive (✗ submit to be searched). In the hand-it-in sense the thing submitted is the direct object and to names the recipient, always a noun phrase: submit the form to HR.
entries.pattern: submit to [authority, a test, an examination] · submit to [verb-ing] · submit [something] to [someone] · be submitted to [a committee] · submit that [clause]
entries.contrast: Two verbs share one spelling, and the direct object tells them apart. He submitted to a drug test is undergoing something; he submitted the form to HR is handing it in — only the second has an object before to. Among the yielding verbs: surrender to is giving up in a contest or to the police, yield to is giving way to traffic or pressure, defer to is bowing to someone's judgment while keeping your own position. And the lawyer's we submit that the statute is clear takes a clause and no preposition at all.
entries.verb type: action in both senses — dynamic yielding (he refused to submit to a search) and dynamic handing-in (she submitted the form to HR). Neither is stative, though the yielding sense can describe a standing arrangement: members submit to the ethics rules when they join.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with to in the yielding sense (no object: ✗ submit a search), transitive in the filing sense, where the thing submitted is the object and to names the recipient.
entries.passive: restricted — the filing sense passivizes constantly and is the standard form: all bids must be submitted to the purchasing office by Friday. The yielding sense has no passive: ✗ a search was submitted to, ✗ he was submitted to.
entries.see also: subscribe to · stipulate to · comply with · object to · to

entries.meaning: Pay to receive something regularly, or accept a view.
examples: They still subscribe to the print edition on Sundays.
I don't subscribe to the theory that everything was better in 1994.
The lab subscribes to three databases nobody uses.
She subscribes to the view that meetings should have an agenda or a cancellation.
He subscribed to four streaming services and watched one.
A subscription to the journal runs about ninety dollars a year.
entries.русский: подписываться на; разделять (взгляд, мнение)
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause (✗ subscribe to getting the paper). Both senses share the frame: a publication or service, and a view or doctrine.
entries.pattern: subscribe to [a publication, a service] · subscribe to [a view, a theory] · subscribe [an amount] — formal, rare · a subscription to [something]
entries.contrast: Subscribe of and ✗ subscribe for are errors in ordinary use (subscribe for shares survives only in securities language). The second sense is the useful one for writers: I don't subscribe to that theory means I don't accept it, and it is a shade more formal and more distancing than I don't believe it. The noun keeps to: a subscription to the Times. Compare sign up for, the everyday American phrasal equivalent of the service sense.
entries.verb type: stative in both senses — holding a subscription and holding a view are states, not acts (✗ I'm subscribing to that theory); the inceptive act is sign up for or subscribed in the simple past.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — to is obligatory: ✗ subscribe the print edition, ✗ subscribe of that view. The bare transitive subscribe an amount survives only in old securities language.
entries.passive: no ordinary passive — ✗ the print edition is subscribed to by them, ✗ three databases are subscribed to. Only the postmodifying participle survives in formal prose: a view widely subscribed to among economists.
entries.see also: belong to · agree with · believe in · refer to · apply for

entries.meaning: Put one thing in the place of another.
examples: Substitute buttermilk for the whole milk and add a little baking soda.
You can substitute almond flour for about a third of the wheat flour.
She substituted for the regular teacher three days a week.
There's no substitute for actually reading the contract.
The committee substituted a milder resolution for the one on the floor.
Replace the gasket with the one in the kit — same job, opposite wording.
entries.русский: заменять собой — ставить одно вместо другого
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause. The new item is the direct object and the old one takes for: substitute margarine for butter means use margarine instead of butter. The intransitive frame reverses the feel: substitute for someone means fill in for them.
entries.pattern: substitute [new] for [old] · substitute for [someone] — fill in · be substituted for [something] · a substitute for [something] · replace [old] with [new] — the mirror verb
entries.contrast: This is the most commonly reversed pattern in the dictionary. Substitute X for Y puts X in and takes Y out. Replace X with Y takes X out and puts Y in. So substitute honey for sugar and replace sugar with honey describe the same recipe, and getting either backwards inverts it. Because so many people reverse it, substitute X with Y has spread in speech; it is still widely criticized in edited American prose, and the safe move is to use replace ... with whenever you want the with-frame.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both frames: swapping one thing for another (substitute buttermilk for the whole milk) and filling in for a person (she substituted for the regular teacher).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the new item as object and the old one under for, intransitive in the fill-in sense, where for takes the person replaced.
entries.passive: restricted — the swap frame passivizes: buttermilk can be substituted for the whole milk, a milder resolution was substituted for the one on the floor. The fill-in sense does not: ✗ the regular teacher was substituted for.
entries.see also: prefer to · compare with · provide with · separate from

entries.meaning: Manage to do something, or take over someone's position.
examples: They succeeded in raising almost twice the target.
He never quite succeeded in explaining why the numbers changed.
Two of the eight succeeded in passing on the first attempt.
The campaign succeeded in registering four thousand new voters.
She succeeded him as chair in the spring.
Nobody succeeds in that job without a very good deputy.
entries.русский: суметь, добиться — после in герундий; а succeed smb сменить на посту
entries.complement: gerund or noun phrase — succeeded in raising the money — never a to-infinitive (✗ succeeded to raise the money, which is a different and mostly obsolete pattern about inheriting a throne). Never a clause.
entries.pattern: succeed in [verb-ing] · succeed in [a field, an effort] · succeed [someone] — follow in office, no preposition · succeed to [a title, a throne] — formal, archaic · succeed (alone)
entries.contrast: Succeed to do something is wrong. The verb has no infinitive frame: use succeed in doing, or switch to manage to do, which is the ordinary American way of saying it. The bare transitive is a different verb altogether — she succeeded him as chair means she took over the job — and the archaic succeed to the throne is the only surviving to pattern. Compare fail, which behaves in the opposite way and takes the infinitive: failed to raise the money.
entries.verb type: action — an achievement verb, dynamic and telic; the progressive is limited to the ongoing struggle (they're succeeding in raising the money, marked).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in this pattern (✗ succeed the money; in plus a gerund is the frame, and ✗ succeed to raise the money is wrong), transitive in the unrelated sense of following in office: she succeeded him as chair.
entries.passive: restricted — the office sense passivizes normally: he was succeeded by his deputy. The in frame has no passive: ✗ raising the money was succeeded in.
entries.see also: cope with · result in · qualify for · specialize in

entries.meaning: Bring a lawsuit seeking something, or on a particular ground.
examples: The contractor sued for the balance of the contract plus interest.
She sued the hospital for negligence and settled a year later.
Two shareholders are suing for $4 million in damages.
He sued the magazine for running the photograph without permission.
They filed to sue for divorce in a state neither had lived in.
Cut off from resupply, the garrison sued for peace.
entries.русский: подавать в суд, требуя чего-то — for называет иск или сумму; юр.
entries.register: neutral, legal-adjacent; sue for peace is a frozen diplomatic idiom
entries.complement: noun phrase naming either the relief sought (sue for damages, sue for $2 million, sue for divorce) or the ground (sue for breach of contract, sue for negligence). A gerund works for the ground (sued the paper for printing the photo) but never for the relief, and there is no to-infinitive (✗ sued for to recover the deposit).
entries.pattern: sue [someone] for [damages / an amount] · sue [someone] for [a wrong] · sue for [verb-ing] · sue over [an episode] · sue [someone] in [a court]
entries.contrast: For does double duty and only context separates the two jobs: sued for defamation names the claim, sued for $3 million names the money. Sue over names the episode that prompted the suit (sued over the layoffs) and is the journalist's preposition. Around it: a prosecutor charges someone with a crime, a private party sues, and prosecute takes no preposition. Sue for peace is fixed — an army sues for peace, and nobody sues for a truce.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, the act of filing; be suing is normal for a case in progress (two shareholders are suing for $4 million).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the defendant as object (she sued the hospital for negligence), intransitive when only the relief or ground is named (the contractor sued for the balance).
entries.passive: restricted — excellent when the defendant is the object: the hospital was sued for negligence, the magazine was sued for running the photograph. The relief phrase cannot be promoted: ✗ $4 million is being sued for.
entries.see also: charge with · accuse of · sentence to · testify to · apply for · for

entries.meaning: Be affected by an illness, a flaw, or a hardship.
examples: About one adult in eight suffers from some form of chronic pain.
The building suffers from a roof that was never right to begin with.
The report suffers from relying on a single source.
He suffered a stroke in March and was back at the shop by June.
Small towns along that corridor have suffered from forty years of decline.
The whole argument suffers from not defining its terms.
entries.русский: страдать от — быть подверженным болезни, недостатку или тяготе
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (suffers from having no natural light) — never a to-infinitive, never a clause. The transitive frame takes a single event with no preposition: suffer a stroke, suffer a defeat — and from would be wrong there.
entries.pattern: [someone] suffer from [a chronic condition] · [something] suffer from [a flaw] · suffer [an injury, a loss, a defeat] · suffer (alone) · suffer for [one's art]
entries.contrast: Suffer from is ongoing; bare suffer is a single event. He suffers from migraines is a condition he lives with; he suffered a concussion happened once, and ✗ suffered from a concussion on Tuesday is odd. The pattern extends past medicine: the argument suffers from a missing premise, the neighborhood suffers from decades of disinvestment. Note that careful American writing increasingly avoids suffers from for disabilities in favor of has, on the grounds that suffer editorializes.
entries.verb type: stative in the from frame — a condition lived with, though it takes the progressive for temporary ones (he's suffering from the flu). The bare transitive is action: he suffered a stroke in March is a single event.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with from naming an ongoing condition or flaw (the report suffers from relying on a single source), transitive with a single event and no preposition (suffer a defeat, suffer a loss).
entries.passive: restricted — no passive at all for suffer from: ✗ chronic pain is suffered from by one adult in eight. The transitive object is not a true patient, so its passive is confined to formal financial and military prose: heavy losses were suffered in the third quarter, but ✗ a stroke was suffered by him.
entries.see also: recover from · benefit from · die of · cope with · complain about

entries.meaning: Believe, without proof, that someone has done something.
examples: Investigators suspected him of moving money through the parts business.
She was suspected of leaking the schedule and never asked about it directly.
I suspect the thermostat, not the furnace.
Two employees were suspected of falsifying the counts.
He suspected that the offer would be withdrawn by Monday.
Nobody suspected the quietest person in the office of anything.
entries.русский: подозревать в — считать виновным без доказательств
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (suspected him of skimming) — never a to-infinitive after of (✗ suspected him of to skim) and never a that-clause after the preposition. The active ✗ suspected him to be skimming is unidiomatic too; the only live infinitive frame is the formal passive the fire is suspected to have been deliberate, and even there suspected of being is the commoner form. Suspect does take a that-clause with no preposition: I suspect that she already knew. Note the stress shift: the verb is /səˈspɛkt/, the noun /ˈsʌspɛkt/.
entries.pattern: suspect [someone] of [something / verb-ing] · be suspected of [something] · suspect that [clause] · suspect [something] · a suspect in [a case]
entries.contrast: Suspect of is the private version of accuse of. Suspicion is held; accusation is voiced; a charge is filed — suspected of, accused of, charged with, and the preposition changes only at the last step. ✗ suspect someone for something is an error. Note the noun frame, which uses a different preposition again: a suspect in the robbery, never ✗ a suspect of the robbery.
entries.verb type: stative — a mental state, not an act; the progressive is marked (?I'm suspecting the thermostat), where investigate and accuse are the dynamic neighbors.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person suspected is the direct object and the of-phrase names the wrongdoing: suspected him of moving money. The object is obligatory: ✗ investigators suspected of skimming.
entries.passive: yes — the exception among stative verbs, and the passive is the commoner form: she was suspected of leaking the schedule, two employees were suspected of falsifying the counts.
entries.see also: accuse of · charge with · blame for · confess to · admit to

entries.meaning: Look after someone, or deal with a task.
examples: Her neighbor takes care of the plants whenever she travels.
I'll take care of the deposit on my way in.
Somebody needs to take care of getting the permit amended.
He took care of his father for the last three years of his life.
The warranty takes care of everything except the labor.
Take care to keep the original; they'll ask for it.
entries.русский: заботиться о; заниматься (делом) — после of герундий
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (take care of getting it notarized) — never a to-infinitive after of (✗ take care of to get it notarized). A separate frame, take care to do something, uses the infinitive and means be careful to: take care to date it. The two are not interchangeable.
entries.pattern: take care of [someone] · take care of [a task / verb-ing] · take care to [verb] · take care (farewell) · be taken care of
entries.contrast: Take care of it handles it; take care to do it is cautious about it. Take care of the paperwork means do it; take care to sign the paperwork means don't forget the signature. The idiom covers both people and jobs, which care for does not — care for is only about people and only about tending. Note the euphemism, alive and well in American crime fiction: we'll take care of him. And Take care on its own is a goodbye.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both readings, tending (her neighbor takes care of the plants) and handling (I'll take care of the deposit). Distinguish take care to do, which is a different frame.
entries.transitivity: transitive as a unit — the whole idiom take care of governs the object, and care is a frozen noun that takes no article or plural (✗ take a care of it).
entries.passive: yes — the prepositional idiom passivizes cleanly, and the entry lists it: the plants are taken care of while she travels, everything except the labor is taken care of by the warranty.
entries.see also: care for · care about · look after · cope with

entries.meaning: Rank ahead of something else when the two conflict.
examples: Patient safety takes precedence over the schedule, every time.
A federal statute takes precedence over a conflicting state rule.
In this house, homework takes precedence over screens.
The earlier filing takes precedence over the amended one.
Nothing takes precedence over getting the water back on.
Where two provisions conflict, the more specific one takes precedence.
entries.русский: иметь приоритет перед — стоять выше при столкновении интересов
entries.register: formal — statutes, contracts, policies, and workplace prose
entries.type: verb + noun + preposition — a fixed idiom rather than a simple verb + preposition
entries.complement: over takes a noun phrase or a gerund (safety takes precedence over meeting the deadline) — never a to-infinitive (✗ takes precedence over to meet the deadline) and never a clause. The noun is frozen: no article (✗ take a precedence over), no plural, and no modifier beyond clear or absolute. The complement can be dropped when the other claim is understood: the more specific provision takes precedence.
entries.pattern: [X] take precedence over [Y] · [X] take precedence · take absolute precedence over [Y] · in order of precedence
entries.contrast: Over is the only preposition here — ✗ take precedence to, and take precedence of is archaic British. The idiom ranks two real claims: the earlier lien takes precedence over the later one, and both exist. Its neighbors do other things: supersede replaces one instrument with another and takes no preposition (this agreement supersedes all prior agreements), override cancels (the federal rule overrides the state rule), outweigh compares weight rather than rank. Note the spelling trap: precedence is rank, precedent is a prior case — you set a precedent but take precedence.
entries.verb type: stative — a relation of rank between two claims that both exist; the progressive is odd (✗ safety is taking precedence over the schedule) and so is the imperative.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in effect — precedence is a frozen noun, not a promotable object (no article, no plural, no modifier beyond clear or absolute), and the over-phrase is droppable when the rival claim is understood: the more specific provision takes precedence.
entries.passive: no — neither piece can be promoted: ✗ precedence is taken over the schedule, ✗ the schedule is taken precedence over. Use supersede or override, which are transitive and passivize: the state rule is overridden by the federal one.
entries.see also: comply with · rest with · over · subject to

entries.term: talk to, talk with, talk about
entries.meaning: Speak with someone, or speak about something.
examples: I need to talk to you about Thursday.
She talked with each family individually before the hearing.
They talked about moving for two years and then did it in a weekend.
He talked me out of buying it, which he was right about.
Let's talk over the numbers before we send anything.
Nobody wants to talk about the parking, and the parking is the whole problem.
Talk to your doctor before you change the dose.
entries.русский: говорить — to/with с кем-то (with на равных), about о чём-то
entries.complement: to and with take a person. about takes a noun phrase, a gerund, or a wh-clause (talked about moving, talked about where to live). None takes a to-infinitive. Talk is intransitive in all of these — the exceptions are the fixed transitive uses talk sense, talk shop, talk business, and talk someone into / out of something.
entries.pattern: talk to [someone] · talk with [someone] · talk about [a topic] · talk to [someone] about [a topic] · talk of [something] — literary · talk over [a decision] · talk [someone] into / out of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Talk with is far more common in American English than in British English, and Americans reach for it when the exchange is mutual — I talked with the family for an hour implies both sides spoke. Talk to is the default and can tilt one-directional, which is why I'm going to talk to him often means a reprimand is coming and I'm going to talk with him rarely does. Neither is wrong; the difference is tone. Talk about names the subject, talk over means discuss thoroughly to a decision, and the literary talk of is now mostly a fixed phrase (the talk of the town). Note that ✗ discuss about is an error — discuss takes a direct object.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and atelic, an activity; the progressive is completely at home (I'm going to talk with him, they were talking about moving).
entries.transitivity: intransitive in all three frames — the preposition is obligatory before a person or a topic (✗ talk him, ✗ talk the budget). The only transitive uses are fixed: talk sense, talk shop, talk business.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is idiomatic when a person is affected: he was talked to about it, she's been talked about all spring. It is weak with topics: ?moving was talked about, where discussed is the natural transitive substitute.
entries.see also: discuss · argue with · complain to · explain to · think about · hear from

entries.meaning: State something formally as a witness — or, of a thing, be evidence of something.
examples: Two employees testified to the accuracy of the time sheets.
He testified to having been in the building that night.
The condition of the roof testifies to years of deferred maintenance.
She testified before the committee for two hours without notes.
Neighbors testified to the family's character at sentencing.
The turnout testifies to how badly people wanted this.
entries.русский: давать показания о; служить свидетельством чего-то; юр.
entries.register: legal in the literal sense — a deposition, a hearing, a trial; the figurative sense (the ruins testify to a wealthy past) belongs to formal written English
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (testified to having seen him leave), or a wh-clause (testifies to how much has changed) — never a to-infinitive (✗ testified to have seen him). A full proposition drops the preposition: testified that he had seen him leave.
entries.pattern: testify to [a fact / a quality] · testify to [verb-ing] · testify that [clause] · testify against / for [a party] · testify about [a topic] · testify before [a body] · testify in [a proceeding]
entries.contrast: Each preposition takes a different piece of the courtroom. To takes the fact you vouch for, about the subject matter, against and for the side, before the body you appear in front of, in the case: she testified before the committee, for the government, about the contracts, to the authenticity of the ledgers. Among the vouching verbs, attest to is the near-twin in formal writing and on signed documents, vouch for is the personal and spoken version, swear to stresses the oath, and bear witness to is the literary one.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and performative, a speech act made under oath; in the figurative use (the turnout testifies to how much has changed) it shades stative.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the preposition is obligatory (✗ testify the authenticity of the ledgers); for a full proposition the preposition drops and a that-clause follows: testified that he had seen him leave.
entries.passive: no ordinary passive — ✗ the authenticity of the ledgers was testified to by her. Only the legal postmodifier survives: the matters testified to by the witness. Prefer the active or switch to attest.
entries.see also: vouch for · stipulate to · sentence to · recuse from · to

entries.meaning: Express gratitude for something.
examples: Thank you for covering my shift.
She thanked every volunteer for showing up in that weather.
Thanks for the ride — I owe you one.
He never thanked anyone for anything, which people noticed.
Thanks to a rescheduled flight, we got an extra day.
I'm thankful for a landlord who answers the phone.
entries.русский: благодарить за — человек без предлога: thank you for the ride
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (thanked her for coming) — never a to-infinitive (✗ thank you for to come). Never a clause. The person thanked is a direct object and never takes a preposition: ✗ thank to you.
entries.pattern: thank [someone] for [something / verb-ing] · Thank you for [verb-ing] · thanks to [someone] — because of · be thankful for [something] · no thanks to [someone]
entries.contrast: Thanks to is not the plural of thank for. Thank you for the ride is gratitude; Thanks to the ride, I made it means because of it — and thanks to is often sarcastic (thanks to him, we started forty minutes late). ✗ Thank to you is an error in every sense. Note that thank, like forgive and excuse, takes the person directly, while apologize needs to — a distinction that catches learners of every background.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and performative; thank you is the act itself, not a report of one.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person is a bare direct object and is obligatory (✗ thank to you, ✗ she thanked for coming); the for-phrase naming the favor is optional.
entries.passive: yes — she was thanked for her service at the last meeting, nobody was ever thanked for the extra hours. Note that thanks to the ride, I made it is a different construction entirely and has no active counterpart.
entries.see also: apologize to · congratulate on · forgive for · excuse for · pay for

entries.meaning: Consider something, or have something come to mind.
examples: I've been thinking about the offer all week.
I can't think of her married name to save my life.
Who thought of putting the printer in the stairwell?
What did you think of the second half?
They're thinking about selling and moving closer to the grandkids.
She thinks highly of him, which is more than he deserves.
He never thought to check whether the office was open.
entries.русский: думать — about обдумывать, of вспоминать или приходить на ум
entries.complement: Both take a noun phrase, a gerund (thinking about moving, thought of selling), or a wh-clause. Neither takes a to-infinitive (✗ think about to move) and neither takes a that-clause — for a clause, drop the preposition: think that it's a mistake. Bare think also takes an adjective complement in fixed frames: think it unwise.
entries.pattern: think about [something / verb-ing] · think of [something / verb-ing] · think of [a name, an idea] — recall or invent · think [something] of [someone] — hold an opinion · think that [clause] · think it over · think highly of [someone]
entries.contrast: Think about is the process; think of is the flash. I've been thinking about it all week is deliberation; I can't think of her name is retrieval; who thought of that? is invention. They overlap freely for plans (thinking about / of moving), but they part ways completely in the opinion frames: What do you think of it? asks for a verdict, and think highly of, think little of, and think the world of take only of. ✗ Think to do something is not English except in the narrow he never thought to ask, meaning it didn't occur to him.
entries.verb type: both — action when it means deliberate or retrieve (I've been thinking about it all week), stative when it means hold an opinion (I think highly of her, ✗ I am thinking highly of her).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with about / of plus a noun, gerund, or wh-clause; transitive when the preposition drops before a clause (think that it's a mistake) or in the fixed think it unwise.
entries.passive: restricted — no ordinary passive: ✗ the offer was thought about by everyone. But fixed evaluative passives with of are fully idiomatic: she is well thought of in the department, it was thought of as a formality.
entries.see also: worry about · care about · forget about · occur to · dream of · talk about

entries.meaning: Mention a subject briefly in passing.
examples: The report touches on staffing but never gives a number.
She touched on the lawsuit for about thirty seconds and moved on.
His remarks touched upon the constitutional question without resolving it.
Nobody at the meeting touched on what happens if the grant lapses.
The chapter touches on being raised by grandparents.
Her politeness touched on the theatrical.
entries.русский: затрагивать (тему) — упоминать вскользь
entries.register: neutral; touch upon is formal and academic
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (touched on selling the building), or a wh-clause (touched on why the numbers moved) — never a to-infinitive (✗ touched on to sell the building).
entries.pattern: touch on [a topic] · touch briefly on [a topic] · touch on [verb-ing] · touch on [wh-clause]
entries.variants: touch upon — identical in meaning, more formal; standard in academic and legal prose
entries.contrast: This on is fixed, not a movable particle: ✗ touch the subject on. And plain transitive touch is physical and takes no preposition, so he touched the subject and he touched on the subject are different sentences entirely. What varies among the neighbors is depth: touch on is a passing mention, get into and go into are thorough, cover is complete, dwell on stays too long. In a second sense touch on means come close to a quality (a politeness touching on contempt), where the neighbor is verge on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, a brief mention within a longer act of speaking; the second sense (a politeness touching on contempt) is stative and describes a quality.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — on is a fixed preposition, not a movable particle (✗ touch the subject on), and it is obligatory: bare transitive he touched the subject is a physical act and a different sentence.
entries.passive: yes — the prepositional passive is natural and common in this idiom: the pension question was touched on only briefly, several issues were touched on and none resolved.
entries.see also: comment on · refer to · talk about · about · on

entries.meaning: Put something into another language, or turn into another form.
examples: The book was translated into eleven languages before it sold well in English.
She translates technical manuals from German into English.
None of that translates into actual policy.
The idiom translates roughly as "don't borrow trouble."
A four percent bump in traffic translated into almost nothing on the bottom line.
His stage presence never quite translated into film.
entries.русский: переводить на (язык); выливаться во что-то — предлог into, не ✗ to
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the target language or result — no gerund, no clause. The source takes from: translated from the Portuguese. The figurative sense takes the same into and a noun phrase: translates into savings.
entries.pattern: translate [something] into [a language] · translate [something] from [a language] into [another] · [something] translate into [a result] · translate as [a rendering] · be translated by [a translator]
entries.contrast: Into names the target, from the source, and neither can be swapped for to: ✗ translated to Spanish is an error in careful writing, though it is heard. Note the very common figurative use in American business and sports writing — higher volume translates into lower margins, speed doesn't always translate into wins — which is a full-fledged sense of the verb, not a metaphor anyone notices anymore. Translate as introduces the rendering itself: the phrase translates roughly as "leave it alone."
entries.verb type: both — action in the language sense (translated from the Portuguese), stative-relational in the figurative one (higher volume translates into lower margins), where the progressive is odd and the claim is a generalization.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the language sense (translate the novel into Spanish), intransitive in the figurative one (speed doesn't always translate into wins) and in the middle voice (the phrase translates roughly as leave it alone).
entries.passive: restricted — routine in the language sense: the novel was translated into eleven languages, the report was translated from the Portuguese. None in the figurative sense: ✗ lower margins are translated into by higher volume.
entries.see also: result in · lead to · refer to · adapt to · into

entries.meaning: Depend on one decisive point, or suddenly attack someone.
examples: The whole appeal turns on a single sentence in the contract.
It turns on whether she knew the account was overdrawn.
The dog turned on its handler without warning.
Half the neighborhood turned on him after the vote.
Everything turns on getting the inspection done this week.
Elections in that district turn on turnout, not persuasion.
entries.русский: зависеть от (решающего обстоятельства); наброситься на кого-то
entries.register: the turn on a question sense is formal and analytic, at home in legal and editorial writing; the turn on someone sense is neutral
entries.type: verb + preposition — in the two senses below only
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (it all turns on proving intent), or a wh-clause (it turns on whether the email was sent) — never a to-infinitive (✗ turns on to prove intent).
entries.pattern: [a case, an argument, an outcome] turn on [a fact or a question] · [a person or animal] turn on [someone] · turn on [verb-ing] · turn on [wh-clause]
entries.contrast: Two different constructions share these two words, and the test is whether the object can move. Turn on the light → turn the light on → turn it on: the object slides, so on is a particle, the pair is a phrasal verb, and it belongs in the discussion of phrasal verbs rather than in this file. The case turns on one question → ✗ turns one question on: the object cannot move, so on is a fixed preposition and the pattern belongs here. The same test separates two more: turned on him means attacked him, turned him on means aroused him — word order carries the whole difference. In the analytic sense the near-synonyms are hinge on, depend on, and rest on, of which turn on is the most legal.
entries.verb type: stative in this pattern — the case turns on one question states a dependency, not an act, and the progressive is marked. This is the hinge sense; the switch sense (turn on the light) is a dynamic phrasal verb with a movable particle and a different pattern.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the test is that the object cannot move: the case turns on one question but ✗ turns one question on, which is exactly what marks on as a preposition here rather than a particle.
entries.passive: no in the hinge sense — ✗ one question is turned on by the case. The switch sense passivizes freely (the lights were turned on at six), and the attack sense too (he was turned on by the people he trusted) — three constructions, one spelling.
entries.see also: depend on · rest on · rely on · turn to · on

entries.meaning: Go to someone or something for help, or take something up.
examples: When the second round of layoffs hit, she turned to her sister.
He turned to teaching after fifteen years in restaurants.
The conversation turned to money about ten minutes in.
Turn to page 214 and read the second paragraph aloud.
A lot of people in that plant turned to painkillers.
Who do you turn to when the person you'd normally ask is the problem?
entries.русский: обращаться к (за помощью); приниматься за что-то
entries.complement: noun phrase — a person, an occupation, a substance, a page, a topic — or a gerund (turned to selling insurance). Never a to-infinitive in this pattern: he turned to write is a different sentence, in which to write is a purpose infinitive and he physically turned around.
entries.pattern: turn to [someone] for [help] · turn to [an occupation, a habit, a substance] · turn to [verb-ing] · [a conversation] turn to [a topic] · turn to [page 214]
entries.contrast: Turn to someone seeks help; turn on someone attacks them — one letter, opposite meanings. Around them: turn into is transformation (turned into a decent manager), turn against is a change of allegiance (the party turned against him), and turn down is a separable particle (turned the offer down, turned it down), which is why it is a phrasal verb and this is not. Watch the purpose-infinitive trap: he turned to writing made writing his work, he turned to write only says he swiveled in his chair.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, an act of recourse (he turned to selling insurance, she turned to her sister for help).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — to is obligatory (✗ turn her sister for help). Watch the purpose infinitive: he turned to write is a different sentence in which he swiveled around.
entries.passive: no in ordinary use — ✗ her sister was turned to for help is stiff at best; the prepositional passive survives mainly as a postmodifier (the person most often turned to in a crisis). Use consult or ask, which are transitive.
entries.see also: turn on · resort to · refer to · rely on · to

entries.meaning: Change in step with something else.
examples: The dosage varies with body weight.
Turnout varies with the weather more than anyone likes to admit.
Shipping cost varies with distance and by carrier.
Interest on the note varies with the prime rate.
Yields vary with soil temperature at planting.
How long an appeal takes varies with the circuit.
entries.русский: меняться в зависимости от — изменяться вместе с чем-то
entries.register: neutral; heavily used in technical, scientific, and consumer writing (results may vary)
entries.complement: noun phrase naming what the thing moves in step with — a season, a temperature, an income. No gerund (✗ varies with raising the temperature; say varies with temperature), no infinitive, no clause.
entries.pattern: [X] vary with [Y] · vary by [a category] · vary from [X] to [Y] · vary in [a dimension] · vary from [a norm]
entries.contrast: Five prepositions carve five different claims. With names what it moves in step with (demand varies with the weather); by names the categories it differs across (prices vary by state); in names the dimension of difference (the panels vary in thickness); from … to gives the range (varies from ten to forty minutes); and vary from alone means depart from a standard (varies from the specification). Against neighbors, depend on claims determination rather than covariation, correlate with is the statistical and symmetric version, and fluctuate takes no complement at all.
entries.verb type: stative-relational — it asserts covariation, not an event (demand varies with the weather); the progressive appears only for observed fluctuation (the readings are varying).
entries.transitivity: intransitive in this pattern — no object (✗ vary the demand with the weather changes verbs). The separate transitive vary means deliberately alter: vary the routine.
entries.passive: no — intransitive and stative: ✗ the weather is varied with by demand. Only the deliberate transitive passivizes: the routine was varied to keep them alert.
entries.see also: depend on · differ from · result from · with

entries.meaning: Place a power, a right, or a title formally in someone's hands.
examples: All legislative powers herein granted are vested in a Congress of the United States.
Title to the property vested in the trust on the date of the transfer.
The charter vests final authority in the board of trustees.
Discretion to waive the penalty is vested in the commissioner.
The statute vests the agency with rulemaking power.
On his death, the remainder vested in his two daughters.
entries.русский: закреплять (власть, право, титул) за кем-то — юр./офиц.
entries.register: legal — constitutions, trusts, corporate charters, and equity grants; an American meets it in the phrase all legislative powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress, not in conversation
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the person or body that receives the power, the title, or the right. No gerund (✗ vested in managing the fund), no infinitive, no clause. The passive is the standard form: authority is vested in the board.
entries.pattern: [a power / a right / title] be vested in [someone] · vest [a power] in [someone] · vest [someone] with [a power] · [a right] vest — intransitive
entries.two frames say the same thing with the a: vest authority in the board and vest the board with authority, exactly like provide X to Y against provide Y with X. Watch the intransitive: in the options vest in four years, in is the ordinary time preposition and nothing is receiving anything — that sentence answers when, not who, and is not this pattern. Among neighbors, confer on grants, devolve on is power passing downward or by default, and reside in and rest with say where authority already sits rather than how it got there. Do not read across to invest in, which in ordinary American English means putting money into something.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic in origin, a legal act of conferring; the resulting authority is vested in the board reads as a standing state, which is why the passive dominates.
entries.transitivity: transitive — two frames with the arguments swapped: vest authority in the board and vest the board with authority. The intransitive the options vest in four years is the ordinary time preposition and not this pattern.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the standard form: authority to approve waivers is vested in the dean's office, the power was vested in a single commissioner. The active is comparatively rare outside statutes.
entries.see also: rest with · reside in · invest in · belong to · in

entries.meaning: Express a choice in an election or a formal decision.
examples: She voted for the bond measure and against everything else on the ballot.
Two members voted against the settlement and one abstained.
The board votes on the budget at the March meeting.
They voted to adjourn before anyone could raise it again.
He's never once voted in a primary.
The district voted him out after a single term.
entries.русский: голосовать за (for) или против (against)
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a candidate or measure — no gerund (✗ vote for raising the fee; say vote to raise the fee or vote for the increase). Vote also takes a bare to-infinitive with no preposition (voted to adjourn) and a that-clause in formal minutes (voted that the matter be tabled).
entries.pattern: vote for [a candidate, a measure] · vote against [something] · vote on [a question] · vote to [verb] · vote in [an election] · vote [someone] in / out
entries.contrast: Four prepositions and an infinitive, each with its own job. Vote for and vote against take sides; vote on names the question being decided, not the side (the council votes on the ordinance Tuesday); vote in names the election; and vote to do names the action decided. ✗ vote to a candidate is an error. Note the American particles: vote someone in, vote someone out, vote down a measure — all separable and all preposition-free.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, a single countable act (every commissioner voted against the rezoning).
entries.transitivity: intransitive in this pattern — the preposition is obligatory before a candidate or measure (✗ vote the levy), though vote also takes a bare to-infinitive (voted to adjourn) and a formal that-clause (voted that the matter be tabled).
entries.passive: restricted — ✗ the bill was voted for by the council is not idiomatic. The preposition-free particle frames do passivize: the measure was voted down, two incumbents were voted out. For the prepositional sense use approve or reject.
entries.see also: decide on · agree on · choose between · qualify for · object to

entries.meaning: Say from your own knowledge that someone or something can be trusted.
examples: I've known her twenty years and I'll vouch for her.
Nobody at the agency would vouch for the numbers in the draft.
I can vouch for the coffee; I can't vouch for the parking.
Two colleagues vouched for his whereabouts that evening.
The notary vouched for the identity of both signers.
He vouched for the contractor, and then spent a year regretting it.
entries.русский: ручаться за — подтверждать надёжность по личному знанию
entries.register: neutral — everyday spoken English for people, and ordinary formal English for facts
entries.complement: noun phrase — a person, a fact, a quality (vouch for the accuracy of the transcript). A gerund is grammatical but stiff (vouch for his having been there; most speakers say vouch for that), and there is no to-infinitive (✗ vouch for to be accurate). The preposition is obligatory: ✗ vouch someone. A that-clause is marginal — say I can vouch for the fact that… or switch to attest or swear.
entries.pattern: vouch for [a person] · vouch for [a fact / a quality] · can't vouch for [something]
entries.contrast: Vouch for puts your own credit behind someone or something. Testify to does the same under oath, attest to does it in writing and often with a signature, and guarantee promises a result and takes no preposition at all (guarantee the work, ✗ guarantee for the work). Answer for is what comes afterward, when the thing you vouched for goes wrong.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and performative, putting your own credit behind someone; I can vouch for that is the modal use of the same act.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — for is obligatory: ✗ vouch someone, ✗ vouch the accuracy of the transcript. Compare guarantee, which is transitive and takes no preposition.
entries.passive: yes, restricted to the prepositional passive, which is fully idiomatic here — he was vouched for by two colleagues, every applicant has to be vouched for.
entries.see also: testify to · stand up for · count on · rely on · for

entries.meaning: Stay where you are, or delay acting, until something happens.
examples: We waited for almost an hour and nobody ever came out.
She's waiting for the inspector to sign off.
He waited on tables at a diner on Route 9 for six years.
They're still waiting on approval from the county.
Don't wait for perfect; send the draft.
I can't wait to see the finished porch.
The committee awaits the final report.
entries.русский: ждать (for); обслуживать (on); wait on в значении ждать — разг., амер.
entries.register: wait for is neutral; wait on meaning await is informal and regional in American English
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase, or a person plus a to-infinitive (wait for her to finish — this is the one place an infinitive is correct in this pattern). A gerund after for is impossible: ✗ wait for finishing. On takes a person: wait on tables in the serving sense. Await is transitive and takes no preposition at all.
entries.pattern: wait for [someone / something] · wait for [someone] to [verb] · wait to [verb] · wait on [a customer, a table] — serve · wait on [something] — informal for wait for · await [something] — formal, no preposition · can't wait to [verb]
entries.contrast: Wait on has two lives in American English. The standard sense is serving: she waited on tables through college, the clerk will wait on you next. The other — I'm waiting on the bus meaning waiting for it — began as Southern and Midland American usage, has spread nationally in speech and in business writing (waiting on approval), and is still flagged in formal edited prose, where wait for is safe. Note await, which takes a direct object and no preposition: await further instructions, ✗ await for instructions. And wait for someone to do something is one of the very few prepositional patterns that takes an infinitive, licensed by the person in between.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and atelic, an activity that fills time; the progressive is its natural home (I'm waiting for the inspector, she was waiting on tables).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — the preposition is obligatory (✗ wait the bus), which is what separates it from await, transitive and preposition-free: await further instructions, ✗ await for instructions.
entries.passive: restricted — the serving sense passivizes naturally: the customers were waited on promptly, you'll be waited on next. The waiting sense does not: ✗ the bus was waited for, ✗ approval is being waited on.
entries.see also: look forward to · hope for · count on · search for · depend on

entries.meaning: Tell someone about a danger, or tell them not to do something.
examples: The ranger warned us about the washout on the lower trail.
