Her attorney warned her against saying anything on the record.
The label warns of a risk that affects about one user in fifty thousand.
He warned everyone to leave before the tide turned.
Two inspectors had warned about the wiring the previous spring.
The forecast warns of freezing rain after midnight.
entries.русский: предупреждать — about об опасности, against чтобы чего-то не делали
entries.complement: about and of take a noun phrase naming a danger — of is the more formal of the two. against takes a noun phrase or a gerund and means advise not to (warned against signing anything) — never a to-infinitive after against. Warn separately takes a person plus a to-infinitive (warned her to leave, warned him not to sign) and a that-clause (warned that the road was flooded), neither with a preposition.
entries.pattern: warn [someone] about [a danger] · warn [someone] of [a danger] — formal · warn [someone] against [something / verb-ing] · warn [someone] to / not to [verb] · warn that [clause] · warn [someone] off
entries.contrast: About and of describe the danger; against prescribes avoiding it. He warned us about the ice tells you the ice is there; he warned us against driving tells you not to. The two often coexist: warned residents about the surge and against staying. Note that warn takes the person directly — ✗ warn to someone — and that the negative infinitive is warned her not to sign, never ✗ warned her to not sign in careful prose. The noun keeps about / of: a warning about the ice, a warning of severe weather.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and performative, a speech act; about and of describe a danger, against prescribes avoiding it.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person warned is a bare direct object (✗ warn to someone), and the verb also takes a person plus a to-infinitive (warned her not to sign) or a that-clause (warned that the road was flooded), both preposition-free.
entries.passive: yes — residents were warned about the surge, she was warned against signing anything, drivers were warned that the road was flooded. The passive is at least as common as the active in news copy.
entries.see also: remind of · discourage from · protect from · explain to

entries.meaning: Want something, often something unlikely.
examples: Everyone in the district was wishing for one more snow day.
Be careful what you wish for.
She wished for a quiet Christmas and got four houseguests.
I wish to register a complaint about the fee schedule.
I wish I had asked more questions before signing.
They wished him well and never called again.
entries.русский: желать чего-то — хотеть, часто маловероятного
entries.complement: for takes a noun phrase — no gerund and no to-infinitive after the preposition (✗ wish for going, ✗ wish for to go). Wish separately takes a bare to-infinitive (wish to speak with the manager — formal) and a past-tense clause for unreal situations: I wish I had more time, I wish she were here — note the subjunctive were.
entries.pattern: wish for [a noun phrase] · wish to [verb] — formal · wish [someone] [something] · wish [clause with past tense] · wish [someone] well · as you wish
entries.contrast: The three frames are not interchangeable. Wish for a raise is longing; wish to speak is a formal way of saying want; I wish I had a raise is counterfactual, and the past tense is doing the work rather than any preposition. ✗ I wish that I have more time is wrong — it must be had. The double-object frame is fixed and preposition-free: wish you luck, wish him well, wish them a good trip. And note the proverb, which is the pattern's most quoted use: be careful what you wish for.
entries.verb type: stative — a mental state of longing, not an act; the progressive is marked (?I'm wishing for a raise) outside seasonal formulas.
entries.transitivity: intransitive with for (✗ wish for going, ✗ wish for to go). Separately transitive with a bare infinitive (wish to speak with the manager) or a counterfactual past clause (I wish she were here), and ditransitive in the fixed frames wish you luck, wish him well.
entries.passive: no — stative and intransitive here: ✗ a raise was wished for by everyone. Only the attributive participle survives: the long wished-for reunion. The double-object frame does passivize: they were wished a good trip.
entries.see also: hope for · long for · dream of · ask for

entries.term: work on, work for, work with
entries.meaning: Do a job, or apply effort to something.
examples: She's been working on the same manuscript for six years.
He works for a firm that does nothing but municipal water.
I've worked with her on two projects and would again.
They're working on getting the variance before the weather turns.
She works in public health and at a clinic three days a week.
Marriage takes work, and he was willing to work at it.
entries.русский: работать — on над чем-то, for на кого-то, with с кем-то
entries.complement: on takes a noun phrase or a gerund (working on getting the permit) — never a to-infinitive. for takes an employer, a client, or a cause. with takes a colleague, a client, or a material. at takes a place of work or an effort; in takes a field or an industry. None of them takes a clause.
entries.pattern: work on [a project / verb-ing] · work for [an employer / a cause] · work with [a person / a material] · work at [a place / something requiring effort] · work in [a field, an industry] · work as [a role] · work out [a solution]
entries.contrast: Six prepositions, and each answers a different question. Work on = what you are building or improving (working on the second draft). Work for = who pays you (works for the county). Work with = who or what is alongside you (works with kids, works with mahogany). Work at = where, or how hard (works at the hospital, has to work at it). Work in = which field (works in public health). Work as = which role (works as a paralegal). Note that work with a person and work for a person are very different claims about a hierarchy, and people are sensitive about which one you use.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and atelic in every frame; the progressive is standard (she's working on the second draft, he's been working for the county since 2011).
entries.transitivity: intransitive — each preposition is obligatory (✗ work the second draft in this sense, ✗ work the county). The unrelated transitives work the room, work the counter, work the dough are a different pattern.
entries.passive: restricted — work on takes the prepositional passive well: the second draft is being worked on, the roof has been worked on twice. The others do not: ✗ the county is worked for by her, ✗ the kids are worked with.
entries.see also: concentrate on · specialize in · consult with · apply for · participate in · with

entries.meaning: Feel anxious about something.
examples: She worries about her mother driving at night.
Nobody at that level worries about the parking.
He's worried about missing the connection in Atlanta.
I'm worried by how quickly the estimate changed.
They worried that the inspection would turn up something expensive.
Don't worry about the dishes; I'll get them.
entries.русский: беспокоиться о — тревожиться из-за чего-то
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (worried about missing the flight), or wh-clause — never a to-infinitive (✗ worry about to miss it). Worry also takes a that-clause with no preposition: worried that the check would bounce. Reflexive worry yourself and transitive it worries me need no preposition either.
entries.pattern: worry about [something / verb-ing / wh-clause] · be worried about [something] · be worried by [something] · worry that [clause] · [something] worry [someone] · Don't worry about it.
entries.contrast: Worried about is your state; worried by is the thing's effect on you. I'm worried about the numbers describes ongoing anxiety you carry; I'm worried by the numbers names the numbers as what disturbed you, and is closer to troubled by or alarmed by. Both are correct and about is far more common. Worry for is the marginal third member — it survives in I worry for her, which sounds concerned on someone's behalf rather than anxious, and it will not substitute for about anywhere else: ✗ I worry for the deadline. ✗ Worry of is not English at all. The fixed dismissal is don't worry about it.
entries.verb type: both — stative in I'm worried about the numbers, where worried is an adjective describing a state; action in the habitual she worries about her mother driving at night, and in the causative it worries me.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with about plus a noun, gerund, or wh-clause, and with a preposition-free that-clause (worried that the check would bounce); transitive when the trouble is the subject: the estimate worries me, don't worry yourself.
entries.passive: yes for the causative — I'm worried by how quickly the estimate changed, closer to troubled by. But be worried about is an adjectival state, not a passive: it has no active counterpart ✗ the numbers worry me about.
entries.see also: care about · think about · complain about · hope for · forget about

entries.meaning: Reply to something, or be accountable to someone.
examples: Nobody answered my question, so I asked it again.
Answer the phone; it's been ringing all morning.
She answered every email the same day, which nobody asked her to do.
The inspector general answers to Congress, not to the agency.
Somebody is going to have to answer for the missing invoices.
The answer to the third question is on the back page.
entries.русский: отвечать на что-то — прямое дополнение без предлога: answer the question
entries.complement: a direct object naming the question, the phone, the door, or the person — no preposition in that sense: ✗ answer to the question, ✗ answer to my email. The genuine answer to means be accountable to a person, and answer for means take responsibility for a thing — both are real, and both mean something else.
entries.pattern: answer [a question, the phone, the door, a letter] · answer [someone] · answer to [a boss, a board] — be accountable · answer for [one's conduct] · answer back · the answer to [a question] — the noun takes to
entries.contrast: Answer to the question is wrong for replying, and right for something else. He answered the question is a reply; He answers to the board is a reporting line; He'll answer for that decision is accountability. Meanwhile the noun takes to — the answer to question 4 — which is exactly why the verb attracts it. Also correct: reply to and respond to both take the preposition, so reply to my email and respond to my email are right while ✗ answer to my email is not.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic (nobody answered my question). The answer to sense — be accountable — is stative: the inspector general answers to Congress, a standing reporting line rather than an act.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with no preposition in the reply sense (answer the question, answer the phone, ✗ answer to my email), intransitive when the object is understood (nobody answered), and intransitive with to / for in the accountability senses.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — every email was answered the same day, my question was never answered. No passive of the accountability senses: ✗ Congress is answered to by the inspector general.
entries.see also: react to · explain to · refer to

entries.meaning: Come near to something, or begin to deal with it.
examples: Two deputies approached the vehicle from opposite sides.
Enrollment is approaching nine hundred for the first time since 2009.
She approached the problem the way an engineer would.
He approached the dean about a leave and was told to put it in writing.
The storm approached faster than the forecast had allowed for.
Her approach to teaching writing has almost no rules in it.
entries.русский: подходить к; приступать к — без предлога: approach the house
entries.complement: a direct object naming a place, a person, a number, or a problem — no preposition: ✗ approach to the intersection, ✗ approach to the problem as a verb. The noun takes to (a new approach to the problem), and that is where the error comes from.
entries.pattern: approach [a place, a person, a figure, a problem] · approach [someone] about [a matter] · an approach to [a problem] — the noun · approach (intransitive): winter is approaching
entries.contrast: The noun takes to; the verb takes nothing. Her approach to the problem was unusual is correct, and ✗ she approached to the problem is not. The only preposition the verb takes is about, naming the matter raised with a person: he approached her about the vacancy. Note the numeric use, which is common in American reporting — costs approaching two million dollars — and the intransitive one, which needs no object at all: as the deadline approached.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and atelic when it means draw near (the storm approached faster than the forecast allowed for), which is why the progressive is so common: enrollment is approaching nine hundred.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a bare object (approach the vehicle, approach the problem, ✗ approach to the problem), intransitive with no object at all (as the deadline approached). Only about attaches: approached her about the vacancy.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the vehicle was approached from opposite sides, he was approached about the vacancy and told to put it in writing. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ it was approached by winter.
entries.see also: arrive at · reach · enter · react to · ask about

entries.meaning: Be present at something.
examples: About forty people attended the hearing and nine spoke.
He attended three different high schools in four years.
She couldn't attend the funeral and has never forgiven the airline.
The nurse attended to him before anyone had filled out a form.
Attendance at the workshop is optional but counted.
Please attend to the roof before the freeze.
entries.русский: посещать, присутствовать на — без предлога: attend the meeting
entries.complement: a direct object naming an event, an institution, or a service — no preposition: ✗ attend to the meeting, ✗ attend at the conference. The genuine attend to means deal with or take care of, and attend on means wait on — both are real and neither means being present.
entries.pattern: attend [a meeting, a school, a funeral] · attend to [a matter, a patient] — deal with · attend on / upon [someone] — formal, wait on · attendance at [an event] — the noun takes at
entries.contrast: Attend the meeting is being there; attend to the meeting is handling the arrangements — and one of those is almost never what a learner means. The noun goes its own way again: attendance at the meeting, an attendee at the conference. Compare participate in, which asserts more than presence, and be present at, which asserts exactly presence. In American English attend is also the standard verb for enrollment: she attended Oberlin, no preposition.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the school sense is habitual and reads almost as a state (he attended three different high schools), but it still takes the progressive: she's attending Oberlin.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a bare object for presence (attend the hearing, ✗ attend to the meeting in that sense, ✗ attend at the conference), intransitive with to for dealing with something (the nurse attended to him) and with on / upon for waiting on someone.
entries.passive: restricted — the presence sense passivizes only with a modifier or a by-phrase: the hearing was attended by about forty people, the workshop was well attended, but bare ✗ the hearing was attended is incomplete. Attend to has no passive: ✗ the roof was attended to is possible but stiff.
entries.see also: participate in · arrive at · listen to · take care of · reach

entries.meaning: Get in touch with someone.
examples: Contact the registrar's office before the deadline, not after.
She contacted three references and heard back from one.
Call me when you land.
He emailed everyone on the list twice in one afternoon.
Write me when you get settled.
They've been in contact with the family since Tuesday.
entries.русский: связываться с — без предлога: contact me, не ✗ contact with me
entries.complement: a direct object naming the person or office — no preposition: ✗ contact with the office, ✗ contact to me. The same is true of call, phone, email, text, and write with a person: ✗ phone to her, ✗ email to me. The noun takes with (in contact with the family), which is where the error starts.
entries.pattern: contact [someone] · call / phone / email / text [someone] · write [someone] — American; British adds to · be in contact with [someone] · get in touch with [someone] · reach out to [someone]
entries.contrast: Contact with someone is a noun phrase, not a verb phrase. I contacted her is right; ✗ I contacted with her is not. The whole group behaves the same way: call me, email me, text me, phone the clinic — all bare objects. The one genuine American-British split is write: Americans say write me when you get there, and British English requires write to me. Both are correct in their own varieties, and write to is safe everywhere. When you want a preposition, use the noun frames: in contact with, in touch with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, a single completed act of reaching someone (she contacted three references).
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory: ✗ I contacted yesterday, ✗ I contacted with her. The whole family behaves this way — call me, email me, text me, phone the clinic — and American write me joins them, where British English requires write to me.
entries.passive: yes — three references were contacted and one wrote back, the family has been contacted. The noun frame supplies the preposition instead: they've been in contact with the family since Tuesday.
entries.see also: reach · explain to · consult with · talk to · hear from

entries.meaning: Talk something over with someone.
examples: We discussed the budget for two hours and settled nothing.
They discussed selling the building and voted to refinance instead.
Let's discuss it with the whole team on Monday.
The board never discussed how the shortfall would be covered.
She discussed her options with an attorney before responding.
Nothing in that email is worth discussing.
entries.русский: обсуждать что-то — без предлога: discuss the plan, не ✗ discuss about
entries.complement: a direct object, a gerund (discussed selling the building), or a wh-clause (discussed how to pay for it) — and no preposition before any of them: ✗ discuss about the budget, ✗ discuss on the budget, ✗ discuss of the budget. There is no that-clause: ✗ discuss that we should move.
entries.pattern: discuss [a topic] · discuss [verb-ing] · discuss [wh-clause] · discuss [something] with [someone] · a discussion about / of [something] — the noun does take a preposition
entries.contrast: Discuss about is the single most common preposition error in English, and it comes from the noun: a discussion about the merger is perfectly correct, so the preposition leaks back into the verb where it has no business. The only preposition discuss takes is with, and it names the other person, not the topic: discuss the merger with counsel. If you want a preposition on the topic, change the verb — talk about it, speak about it, comment on it, or have a discussion about it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and atelic, an activity that occupies time (we discussed the budget for two hours and settled nothing).
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory and preposition-free: ✗ discuss about the budget, ✗ discuss on the budget, ✗ we discussed for two hours. The only preposition is with, naming the other person, never the topic.
entries.passive: yes — the budget was discussed for two hours, how the shortfall would be covered was never discussed. The noun keeps its preposition: a discussion about the merger.
entries.see also: talk about · comment on · consult with · argue about

entries.meaning: Give special importance to something.
examples: The memo emphasized the deadline three separate times.
She emphasized that nothing had been decided yet.
The program emphasizes fieldwork over coursework.
He stressed the difference between a recommendation and a requirement.
The curriculum places heavy emphasis on writing.
I want to emphasize how narrow the finding actually is.
entries.русский: подчёркивать, акцентировать — без предлога, не ✗ emphasize on
entries.complement: a direct object or a that-clause — no preposition: ✗ emphasize on the deadline, ✗ emphasize about safety. The noun takes on (emphasis on safety) and the phrasal frame is place / put emphasis on, which is where the error comes from. Stress behaves identically: stress the deadline, ✗ stress on the deadline.
entries.pattern: emphasize [something] · emphasize that [clause] · stress [something] · stress that [clause] · place / put emphasis on [something] · with an emphasis on [something]
entries.contrast: Emphasize on is wrong, and an emphasis on is right, which is the whole trap in one sentence. The same split governs stress (verb, no preposition; noun, on), highlight, underscore, and underline, all transitive. If you want the preposition, use the noun: the training places heavy emphasis on de-escalation. Note that emphasize also takes a clause directly — she emphasized that attendance was voluntary — with no on anywhere in sight.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and performative, a speech act (the memo emphasized the deadline three separate times).
entries.transitivity: transitive, object or that-clause obligatory and always preposition-free: ✗ emphasize on the deadline, ✗ emphasize about safety. Stress, highlight, underscore, and underline all behave identically.
entries.passive: yes — the deadline was emphasized three separate times, it was emphasized that attendance was voluntary. The preposition belongs to the noun: heavy emphasis is placed on writing.
entries.see also: concentrate on · point to · comment on · insist on · explain to

entries.meaning: Go into a place, or become party to an agreement.
examples: He entered the building through the loading dock.
Three hundred people entered the contest and two read the rules.
The company entered into a consent decree rather than go to trial.
She entered her thirties without any of the alarm she'd been promised.
Enter the confirmation number into the second field.
The negotiations the union entered into lasted eleven weeks.
entries.русский: входить в — без предлога: enter the room; enter into о договоре
entries.complement: a direct object naming a place, a state, or a stage — no preposition in the literal sense: ✗ enter into the room, ✗ enter to the building. The figurative enter into is a genuine and separate pattern for agreements and processes: enter into a contract, enter into negotiations.
entries.pattern: enter [a room, a building, a country] · enter [a contest, a phase, one's thirties] · enter into [an agreement, negotiations, a discussion] · enter [data] into [a system] · enter (intransitive, stage direction)
entries.contrast: Enter into the room is wrong; enter the room is right. The confusion is fed by the fact that enter into is correct for abstractions — you enter into a contract, an alliance, a partnership, or a debate. The rule of thumb: if you could physically walk in, drop the preposition. Note also enter meaning key in, which takes into or in: enter the figures into the spreadsheet. And the intransitive stage direction Enter Hamlet is the fossil that gives the verb its theatrical feel.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic in every sense: crossing a threshold, joining a contest, signing an agreement, keying in data.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive and preposition-free in the literal sense (enter the building, ✗ enter into the room), intransitive in the stage direction (Enter Hamlet). Enter into is a separate frame for abstractions (enter into a contract), and enter X into Y for data.
entries.passive: yes — the building was entered through the loading dock, the figures were entered into the second field. The abstraction frame gives a genuine prepositional passive, common in legal prose: the consent decree was entered into rather than tried.
entries.see also: arrive at · reach · approach · participate in · into

entries.meaning: Not have something that is needed or expected.
examples: The plan lacks any mechanism for enforcement.
She has never lacked confidence.
The building lacks a second exit, which is why it can't be permitted.
What the argument lacks is a single piece of evidence.
It's a careful report, though lacking in imagination.
The case was dropped for lack of evidence.
entries.русский: не иметь, недоставать — без предлога: lacks detail, не ✗ lacks of detail
entries.complement: a direct object naming what is missing — no preposition: ✗ lack of experience as a verb, ✗ lack in experience. The noun takes of (a lack of experience) and the adjective takes in (lacking in experience), and those two are the source of every error made with the verb.
entries.pattern: lack [something] · be lacking · be lacking in [a quality] · a lack of [something] · for lack of [something]
entries.contrast: Three parts of speech, three different constructions, and only one of them takes of. The proposal lacks detail (verb, bare object), the proposal shows a lack of detail (noun, of), the proposal is lacking in detail (participial adjective, in). ✗ The proposal lacks of detail mixes the first two and is wrong. Note that lack is stative and resists the progressive: ✗ is lacking experience is odd where lacks experience is right, though is lacking on its own (meaning absent) is fine: what's lacking is a budget.
entries.verb type: stative — the entry says so outright: it names an absence, not an act, and it resists the progressive (✗ the plan is lacking a mechanism where the plan lacks a mechanism is right). Bare be lacking meaning absent is fine: what's lacking is a budget.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with a bare object that is obligatory and takes no preposition: ✗ the proposal lacks of detail, ✗ the plan lacks in enforcement. The noun takes of (a lack of detail) and the participial adjective takes in (lacking in detail).
entries.passive: no — one of the classic stative refusals: ✗ a mechanism for enforcement is lacked by the plan, ✗ confidence has never been lacked by her. Use the plan lacks it, or turn it around: a second exit is missing.
entries.see also: consist of · deprive of · suffer from · provide with · for lack of

entries.meaning: Become someone's husband or wife.
examples: She married a man she met in a bus station in Lincoln.
They got married in a courthouse and had the party a year later.
He's been married to the same woman for thirty-four years.
Her sister married young and stayed married.
The couple were married by a friend who got ordained online.
They're married with three kids and a dog nobody planned on.
entries.русский: жениться на, выходить замуж за — без предлога: marry her, не ✗ marry with
entries.complement: a direct object naming the person — no preposition: ✗ marry with her, ✗ marry to him. The adjectival frame is where the preposition lives, and it is to, never with: married to a surgeon, ✗ married with a surgeon. Get married to follows the same rule.
entries.pattern: marry [someone] · marry (intransitive) · get married · get married to [someone] · be married to [someone] · marry [a couple] — what the officiant does · married with children — a different with entirely
entries.contrast: Married with her is one of the most persistent errors in English, because Spanish casarse con and French se marier avec both use the equivalent of with. English uses no preposition for the verb and to for the state: He married her in 1998 and He's been married to her since 1998. The one place with is correct is a completely different structure — married with two kids means married and having two kids, where with attaches to the children, not the spouse. Note also the officiant's transitive use: a justice of the peace married them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, a single event (she married a man she met in a bus station). Be married to is the resulting state and is adjectival, not a tense of the verb.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the spouse as a bare object (marry her, ✗ marry with her, ✗ marry to him), transitive with the couple as object when the officiant is the subject (a justice of the peace married them), and intransitive (her sister married young).
entries.passive: restricted — the officiant frame passivizes and is the live passive: the couple were married by a friend who got ordained online. The state is not a passive at all: he's been married to her since 1998 has no active ✗ she marries him.
entries.see also: introduce to · belong to · separate from · share with · to

entries.meaning: Be against something, and act against it.
examples: Every county commissioner opposed the rezoning.
She opposes raising the retirement age.
The union is opposed to reopening the contract midterm.
He opposed the nomination for reasons he never explained.
Two of the three trustees are opposed to the sale.
They want a flat fee as opposed to an hourly rate.
entries.русский: выступать против, противостоять — без предлога, не ✗ oppose to
entries.complement: a direct object naming what you are against — no preposition: ✗ oppose to the merger, ✗ oppose against the bill. A gerund can be that object, still with no preposition: opposed extending the deadline. The preposition appears only once the verb has become the adjective opposed, and then it is to plus a noun or a gerund: opposed to the merger, opposed to extending the deadline, never ✗ opposed to extend the deadline.
entries.pattern: oppose [a plan, a bill, a nominee] · oppose [verb-ing] · be opposed to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · as opposed to [noun phrase] — a fixed comparative phrase
entries.contrast: Oppose to is wrong and opposed to is right — one letter apart, and the difference is a part of speech. The verb is transitive like support, its opposite: she supports the levy, she opposes the levy, neither with a preposition. Once you reach for be, you have switched to the adjective and the to becomes obligatory — and it is a preposition, so a verb after it takes -ing, which puts opposed to in the look forward to family. Compare object to, which is a verb that does take to, so object to the merger and oppose the merger say the same thing with opposite structures. Note the fixed phrase as opposed to, which means rather than and behaves as a complex preposition of its own.
entries.verb type: both — mostly stative, naming a position held (every county commissioner opposed the rezoning), and action where it means actively fight something (they're opposing the permit at every hearing).
entries.transitivity: transitive, with a bare object or a gerund and no preposition: ✗ oppose to the merger, ✗ oppose against the bill; opposed extending the deadline is correct. The to belongs to the adjective opposed, which then takes a noun or -ing: opposed to extending the deadline, ✗ opposed to extend.
entries.passive: restricted — the true passive is fine with a by-phrase: the rezoning was opposed by every county commissioner. But the union is opposed to reopening the contract is the adjective, not a passive — it has no active counterpart ✗ something opposes the union to reopening.
entries.see also: object to · disapprove of · protest · agree with · argue against · opposed to

entries.meaning: Object publicly to something.
examples: Several hundred people protested the closure outside the county building.
Students protested the tuition increase for most of the spring.
She protested the charge in writing and got half of it reversed.
In Britain they would say the crowd protested against the bill.
He protested to the commissioner and was told to file a form.
He protested that nobody had ever explained the deadline to him.
She signed it under protest.
entries.русский: протестовать против — в амер. англ. без предлога: protest the ruling
entries.register: neutral — the transitive form is characteristically American
entries.complement: a direct object naming what you object to, or a that-clause (protested that he had never been told) — in American English, no preposition: protest the ruling, protest the war. British English requires protest against the ruling. Protest to names the person you complain to, and is correct in both varieties.
entries.pattern: protest [a decision, a policy, a verdict] — American · protest against [something] — British, and also used in the U.S. · protest to [an official] · protest that [clause] · protest (intransitive) · under protest
entries.contrast: This is a genuine transatlantic split, and the American form is the bare transitive. Thousands protested the ruling is standard in the United States and reads as an error to some British ears, where protested against the ruling is required. Both are current in American writing, with the bare form dominant in news copy. Note the third pattern, which is neither: protest to the commissioner names the person you complain to. And protest that introduces a denial (he protested that nobody had told him), which is where protest too much comes from.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and atelic in the demonstrating sense (students protested the tuition increase for most of the spring), dynamic and performative in he protested that nobody had told him.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a bare object in American English (protest the ruling, where British English requires protest against the ruling), intransitive when the crowd simply protests, and with to for the official you complain to.
entries.passive: yes in the American transitive — the closure was protested by several hundred people, the charge was protested in writing and half of it reversed. No passive of protest to: ✗ the commissioner was protested to.
entries.see also: complain to · object to · argue with · comply with · vote against

entries.meaning: Arrive at something, get in touch with someone, or attain a level.
examples: We reached the trailhead about twenty minutes before dark.
You can reach me at the office until five.
The jury reached a verdict on the second day.
Temperatures reached a hundred and four in the valley.
He reached for the railing and missed it.
Somebody from the office will reach out to you this week.
entries.русский: достигать, добираться до; дозвониться до — без предлога: reach Denver
entries.complement: a direct object naming a place, a person, a level, or a decision — no preposition: ✗ reach to the summit, ✗ reach at the office. The genuine reach for means extend a hand toward something, and reach out to means make contact — both are real and both mean something else.
entries.pattern: reach [a place, a person, a figure, an agreement] · reach for [something] · reach out to [someone] · reach into [a bag, a pocket] · within reach of [something] — the noun takes of
entries.contrast: Reach the airport, not ✗ reach to the airport. The verb is transitive for arriving, contacting, and attaining: reach Denver, reach me at this number, reach a verdict, reach ninety degrees. Reach for is the physical gesture (reached for the salt), and reach out to is the American business idiom for making contact — now so common that it has largely displaced contact in email. Compare arrive at and arrive in, which do take prepositions, and get to, which takes to: three ways of saying the same thing with three different requirements.
entries.verb type: action — an achievement verb, dynamic and telic (we reached the trailhead about twenty minutes before dark, the jury reached a verdict on the second day).
entries.transitivity: transitive with a bare object in the arriving, contacting, and attaining senses: ✗ reach to the summit, ✗ reach at the office. The prepositional frames are separate verbs of gesture and contact: reach for the railing, reach into a pocket, reach out to someone.
entries.passive: restricted — routine with abstract objects and with people: a verdict was reached on the second day, she could not be reached for comment. Weak with plain destinations: ?the trailhead was reached before dark belongs to expedition prose, not ordinary speech.
entries.see also: arrive at · approach · contact · enter

entries.meaning: Look or be like something else.
examples: She resembles her mother more every year.
The finished building resembled the rendering in almost no respect.
His second novel resembles the first one a little too closely.
Nothing on the plate resembled what the menu had described.
The two dialects resemble each other more than either resembles the standard.
The child bears a strong resemblance to his grandfather.
entries.русский: быть похожим на — без предлога: resemble his father, не ✗ resemble to
entries.complement: a direct object — no preposition: ✗ resemble to her mother, ✗ resemble with her mother. Resemble is stative and does not take the progressive: ✗ is resembling her mother. The noun takes to: a resemblance to her mother.
entries.pattern: resemble [someone / something] · bear a resemblance to [someone] · take after [a relative] — the idiomatic alternative · look like [someone] — the everyday one
entries.contrast: Resemble to is an error imported from French ressembler à and Spanish parecerse a. The verb takes a bare object; only the noun takes to — a striking resemblance to her mother. In American speech the verb is rare: people say she looks like her mother or she takes after her mother, and resemble is reserved for writing. Note the useful passive-free construction X and Y resemble each other, which avoids choosing a direction.
entries.verb type: stative — the entry says it directly: a relation of likeness, not an act, and it refuses the progressive: ✗ she is resembling her mother.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with a bare object that is obligatory: ✗ resemble to her mother, ✗ resemble with her mother. The noun is where to lives: a striking resemblance to her mother.
entries.passive: no — the textbook case of a transitive stative that refuses promotion: ✗ her mother is resembled by her, ✗ the rendering was resembled by the building. The symmetric active is the way around it: the two dialects resemble each other.
entries.see also: compare to · differ from · separate from
